24---  Sometimes, though, we want less freedom: rather than leaving `α`
25---  completely generic, we want to partially specify its behavior. In Lean,

1+import TS.SFLCompat
2+
3+-- # Typeclasses
4+
5+-- So far we have discussed **parametric polymorphism**, where in Lean we can
6+-- declare a type variable
7+
8+variable (α : Type)
9+
10+-- without any further information about the details of the type `α`. Here we
11+-- are able to work with a type like `List α`, and can write functions like
12+-- `List.reverse` or `List.length` that only operate on the structure of a
13+-- list independently of its contents. Along with these we have corresponding
14+-- proofs like `List.length_reverse` that are similarly structural in nature.
15+
16+-- This is somewhat limiting, as we cannot inspect or non-trivially use any
17+-- particular `a : α`. What we might want in some situations rather than `α`
18+-- being completely generic is to partially specify its behavior. In Lean,
19+-- this happens through a form of "ad hoc polymorphism" called
20+-- **typeclasses**. This concept originated in the Haskell programming
21+-- language, and is analogous to features you may be familiar with in other
22+-- languages such as traits in Rust.
23+
24+-- ## First Example: Inhabited Types
25+
26+-- Suppose we wanted to specify that a type has at least one inhabitant —
27+-- i.e., that it is not empty. We have previously seen `structure`, which
28+-- would allow us to express this as
29+
30+structure HasOneStruct (α : Type) where
31+  one : α
32+
33+-- As discussed previously, a structure is just an inductive type that comes
34+-- with a single constructor, in this case `HasOneStruct.mk`, along with a few
35+-- different syntaxes for convenience:
36+
37+def nat_hasOneStruct_mk : HasOneStruct Nat := HasOneStruct.mk 1
38+
39+def nat_hasOneStruct_brace : HasOneStruct Nat := {one := 1}
40+
41+def nat_hasOneStruct_where : HasOneStruct Nat where
42+  one := 1
43+
44+-- All of these are the same value, a structure of type `HasOneStruct Nat`
45+-- that we can thing of as carrying a piece of data (a term that is not a
46+-- proposition), the number `1`, as evidence that this type is not empty. We
47+-- can use this in proofs such as
48+
49+theorem nat_hasOneStruct_eq_one : nat_hasOneStruct_mk.one = 1 := rfl
50+
51+-- to see how this structure provably contains the value that we have placed
52+-- within it. In Lean, typeclasses work very similarly, and in fact are
53+-- implemented as structures. The only difference in defining a typeclass is
54+-- that we instead use the `class` keyword:
55+
56+class HasOne (α : Type) where
57+  one : α
58+
59+-- While the definition is essentially the same, including the constructor
60+-- `HasOne.mk`, the usage of typeclasses is different, and what allows us to
61+-- use them to express ad hoc polymorphism. Instead of using `def` to define
62+-- inhabitants of this type, we will instead use the `instance` keyword:
63+
64+-- Note to developers:
65+--     From GitHub (@chenson2018): Part of the point here is that we don't
66+--     usually refer to instances explicitly, even me providing an explicit
67+--     name is for pedagogy reasons. I'll make it more explicit in the text
68+--     that what we're looking for in the infoview is the presence of this
69+--     instance.
70+
71+instance instHasOneNat : HasOne Nat where
72+  one := 1
73+
74+-- The definition is exactly the same as above (and any of the alternative
75+-- syntaxes work as well), but instead of being used as a definition that we
76+-- pass around, Lean will try to infer its usage through a process called
77+-- **typeclass synthesis** or **typeclass inference**. To help see this, let's
78+-- define another instance of `HasOne` for `Int`, the type of integers ... -2,
79+-- -1, 0, 1, 2, ...
80+
81+instance instHasOneInt : HasOne Int where
82+  one := -1
83+
84+-- Instead of explicitly referring to a structure like we did in the proof
85+-- `nat_hasOneStruct_eq_one`, we can instead use `HasOne.one`, and Lean will
86+-- use typeclass inference to determine the intended meaning. As an example,
87+-- you can write
88+
89+example : HasOne.one = (1 : Nat) := rfl
90+example : HasOne.one = (-1 : Int) := rfl
91+
92+-- and based on the type annotations Lean will infer which of these instances
93+-- you intended to use. So these proofs are equivalent to
94+
95+example : instHasOneNat.one = (1 : Nat) := rfl
96+example : instHasOneInt.one = (-1 : Int) := rfl
97+
98+-- but without needing to explicitly refer to the instances `instHasOneNat`
99+-- and `instHasOneInt`. Another way that we can inspect what instance is being
100+-- using with the constructor of a typeclass is the option `pp.all`. For
101+-- example looking at
102+
103+set_option pp.all true in
104+example : HasOne.one = (1 : Nat) := rfl
105+
106+set_option pp.all true in
107+example : HasOne.one = (-1 : Int) := rfl
108+
109+-- we can see that `@HasOne.one Nat instHasOneNat` and
110+-- `@HasOne.one Int instHasOneInt` are the respective terms that appear on the
111+-- right hand side of each equality.
112+
113+-- Lean also has a command `#synth` that allows you to search for an instance
114+-- of a given type. So the command
115+
116+#synth HasOne Nat
117+
118+-- for instance prints `instHasOneNat`, informing us that this is the instance
119+-- found that has type `HasOne Nat`. In general, the assumption is that for
120+-- typeclasses like `HasOne` that include data, as opposed to solely proofs,
121+-- that these these instances should be unique to avoid ambiguity.
122+
123+-- Note to developers:
124+--     @chenson2018: I don't really want to explain diamonds here, is the
125+--     above white lie hand-waving okay??
126+
127+-- ## Proof-Carrying Typeclasses
128+
129+-- Notably, the above examples enforce no conditions on the data that they
130+-- carry, and we could provide any value that we would like for `HasOne.one`.
131+-- This could be misleading, for instance if we had instead defined an
132+-- instance
133+
134+sf_experiment
135+  instance : HasOne Nat where
136+    one := 2
137+
138+-- we might have some counterintuitive proofs based on the name leading us to
139+-- believe the class contained the element `1`. In most languages that support
140+-- typeclasses it is not possible to enforce a notion of "lawfulness" as part
141+-- of the typeclass, and it falls to the author to ensure that any desired
142+-- invariants are satisfied.
143+
144+-- As an example, suppose that we wanted to express the idea that a type has
145+-- at least two distinct elements. A first attempt might be
146+
147+sf_experiment
148+  class HasTwoIncomplete (α : Type) where
149+    one : α
150+    two : α
151+
152+-- but this does not disallow the case where `one` and `two` are equal. In a
153+-- proof assistant, however, typeclasses can also carry proofs along with
154+-- data, so we can write
155+
156+class HasTwo (α : Type) where
157+  one : α
158+  two : α
159+  one_neq_two : one ≠ two
160+
161+-- to enforce that these are two distinct entries. Declaring instances works
162+-- in much the same way as before, except that now `HasTwo.one_neq_two`
163+-- requires a proof:
164+
165+instance : HasTwo Nat where
166+  one := 1
167+  two := 2
168+  one_neq_two := by intro contra; contradiction
169+
170+-- ### Exercise (1 star): HasThree ⭐
171+
172+-- Following the pattern of `HasOne` and `HasTwo`, define a class `HasThree`
173+-- that specifies a type with at least three distinct elements.
174+
175+-- Note to developers (Claude, NOW):
176+--     Rendering bug in this exercise and `instHasThree` below. Both use the
177+--     `-- SOLUTION`/`-- END SOLUTION` comment-marker idiom to hide **some**
178+--     class fields / instance fields, but the Verso HTML build does not
179+--     process those markers (only the `solution!` tactic is handled). In
180+--     **student** and **terse** the class shows only the visible fields while
181+--     the `instHasThree` instance then reports a spurious
182+--     `Fields missing: one_neq_three, two_neq_three` error; in **solutions**
183+--     the hidden fields are shown but the literal `-- SOLUTION` /
184+--     `-- END SOLUTION` comment lines leak into the displayed code. The
185+--     generated `.lean` is fine — HTML-only. Fix by expressing the hidden
186+--     fields with `solution!` rather than the comment markers.
187+
188+class HasThree (α : Type) where
189+  one : α
190+  two : α
191+  three : α
192+  one_neq_two : one ≠ two
193+  one_neq_three : one ≠ three
194+  two_neq_three : two ≠ three
195+
196+-- ### Exercise (1 star): instHasThree ⭐
197+
198+-- Provide an instance of `HasThree` for `Nat`.
199+
200+instance : HasThree Nat where
201+  one := 1
202+  two := 2
203+  three := 3
204+  one_neq_two := (by intro contra; contradiction)
205+  one_neq_three := (by intro contra; contradiction)
206+  two_neq_three := (by intro contra; contradiction)
207+

79---  Typeclasses automate this — instead of the programmer passing the
80---  function explicitly, Lean searches for one and provides it on its own.
81---  We specify something we want Lean to search for by declaring a `class`
82---  with the needed function as a field; a `class` is like an interface in
83---  Java or a trait in Rust. Particular implementations of that class are
84---  called *instance*; each type can have its own instance of a class. For
85---  functions that would use such instances, we specify the name of the
86---  class in a *instance implicit* on the polymorphic variable that the
87---  instance's function applies to. This directs Lean to rely on the class
88---  inside the function, and to find and fill in the appropriate instance
89---  when the function is called.

284+-- that mentions a typeclass `BEq`. Perhaps a better question is what exactly
285+-- the `==` notation meant in our original `List.elem_nat`. Let's look at a
286+-- usage of this notation with natural numbers, but turn off notation:
287+
288+set_option pp.notation false in
289+#check 1 == 2
290+
291+-- This may be a bit surprising, as you may have been expecting to see
292+-- `Nat.beq`, the function for boolean equality on natural numbers. What we
293+-- instead find is that `==` is a notation for the typeclass `BEq`:
294+
295+-- class BEq (α : Type u) where
296+--   /-- Boolean equality, notated as `a == b`. -/
297+--   beq : α → α → Bool
298+
299+-- What is happening in the background when we use the `a == b` notation is
300+-- that Lean is searching for an *instance* of the `BEq` typeclasses that
301+-- applies for `Nat`. An example of such an instance would be
302+
303+instance (priority := low) : BEq Nat where
304+  beq := Nat.beq
305+
306+-- where we are specifying that the usage of `==` for natural numbers should
307+-- correspond to the expected `Nat.beq`. So in order to write a function that
308+-- uses the notation for boolean equality over a generic type, we need a way
309+-- to express that there is some instance for `BEq α`. This is done using
310+-- **instance implicits**, where we place a desired typeclass assumption in
311+-- square brackets. Our corrected definition is then
312+
313+@[irreducible]
93314 def List.elem_poly {α : Type} [BEq α] (a : α) (xs : List α) : Bool :=
94315   match xs with
95316   | [] => false
96317   | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_poly a tl
97318

105---  Comparing `List.elem_poly_eq` with `List.elem_poly`, we see three
106---  differences. First, `List.elem_poly_eq` takes an *explicit* parameter
107---  `eq`, whereas `List.elem_poly` specifies an instance implicit
108---  `[BEq α]`. The instance implicit indicates that an instance of `BEq`
109---  must be provided at call sites for the particular type `α` that is
110---  used. Second, whereas `List.elem_poly_eq` invokes parameter `eq` to
111---  test equality, `List.elem_poly` uses `==` instead. As Lists noted when
112---  we first used it, `==` on `Nat` comes from the `BEq` typeclass.
113---  Finally, whereas `[0, 1].elem_poly_eq Nat.beq 0` passes the equality
114---  function `Nat.beq` explicitly, in `[0, 1].elem_poly 0` Lean fills it in
115---  automatically based on the type `Nat` of the `List`.

133---  ## Defining Your Own Typeclasses

137---  that made `==` resolve automatically above.

156---  Getting Lean to fill in `defaultValue` automatically takes two things.
157---  One is marking the parameter as "searchable," rather than something the
158---  caller always supplies explicitly. The other is giving Lean some
159---  information about what it should search *for*.

161---  Considering the second problem first: the way to provide this
162---  information is to *name* the data we're after — the **default value**
163---  of a type. In particular, a `structure` (chapter Lists) is a good way
164---  to give this information a name; structures can also bundle together
165---  more than one piece of data, which will come in handy later, though we
166---  only need a single field here.
167-
168---  To address the first problem, we need to mark this particular structure
169---  as one Lean should search for automatically — not every
170---  `structure`-typed argument should be.
171-
172---  Let's build up to what we want in two steps: first the naming, as a
173---  plain `structure`; then the marking, by upgrading it to a `class`.
174---  Here's the structure — we'll put it in its own namespace so we can
175---  reuse the name `DefaultValue` for the class version below:

177-namespace DefaultValueScratch

394-namespace Algebra
395-
396---  This facility is very powerful, and is used extensively in Lean to
397---  define mathematical structures that carry both operators and laws about
398---  how those operators interact. As a simple example, let's use a
399---  typeclass to define a *monoid*, a simple algebraic structure that
400---  includes four things:
401-
402---  - an underlying set of data, represented by a type `α`,
403-
404---  - an operator (which we'll write `⊗`, typed otimes) that combines two
405---    elements of type `α` into one,
406-
407---  - a particular element `id` of type `α`, which we call the "identity
408---    element", and
409-
410---  - some laws about the interaction of `⊗` and `id`, namely that:
411-
412---    - `∀ x, id ⊗ x = x = x ⊗ id`, and
413-
414---    - `∀ x y z, x ⊗ (y ⊗ z) = (x ⊗ y) ⊗ z` (i.e., that `⊗` is
415---      associative)
416-
417---  We can express these requirements in the form of a typeclass:
418-
419--- first we define a notation typeclass for our operator ⊗
420-class OpSet (α : Type) where
421-  op : α → α → α
422-
423-infixr:70 " ⊗ " => OpSet.op
424-
425-class Monoid (α : Type) extends (OpSet α) where
426-  id : α
427-  left_id : ∀ (x : α), id ⊗ x = x
428-  right_id : ∀ (x : α), x ⊗ id = x
429-  assoc : ∀ (x y z : α), x ⊗ (y ⊗ z) = (x ⊗ y) ⊗ z
430-
431---  The `extends` keyword indicates that the `Monoid` typeclass extends the
432---  `OpSet` typeclass, which just defines a set with an operator and some
433---  notation for it. The `Monoid` typeclass "inherits" the fields of
434---  `OpSet`, similar to how a class would in an object-oriented language.
435-
436---  As one might expect, the `+` operator over `Nat`s forms a monoid, where
437---  `0` is the identity element. Note that we don't have to define `Nat`'s
438---  `OpSet` instance separately, we can define a single instance that
439---  implements both classes.
440-
441-instance : Monoid Nat where
442-  op := Nat.add
443-  id := 0
444-  left_id := by lia
445-  right_id := by lia
446-  assoc := by lia

468---  science, lists of any type also form a monoid, with `List.append` as
469---  the operator in question:

478---  In addition to defining instances of `Monoid`, we can also prove some
479---  properties about monoids in general, just based on the laws defined on
480---  the typeclass. One simple theorem about monoids is that the identity
481---  element of a monoid is unique. That is, if we have two monoids over the
482---  same set with the same operator, their identity elements must also be
483---  the same:
484-
485-theorem id_unique {α : Type} {m₁ m₂ : Monoid α} (h : m₁.op = m₂.op) : m₁.id = m₂.id := by
486-  obtain @⟨op₁, id₁, left_id₁, right_id₁, assoc₁⟩ := m₁
487-  obtain @⟨op₂, id₂, left_id₂, right_id₂, assoc₂⟩ := m₂
488-  have h' : id₁ = id₂ := by
489-    -- this introduces a use of m₁'s operator
490-    rw [← left_id₁ id₂]
491-    -- we use our hypothesis to rewrite m₁'s operator into m₂'s
492-    rw [h]
493-    -- then, we can use m₂'s right id
494-    rw [right_id₂]
495-  -- the goal `m₁.id = m₂.id` is equivalent with `id₁ = id₂` even though it displays `Monoid.id = Monoid.id`
496-  exact h'
497-
498---  In the above proof, we can destructure the monoid instances `m₁` and
499---  `m₂` with the `obtain` tactic we saw in the Logic chapter. When we do
500---  so however, because these are class instances instead of normal
501---  structures, we preface our tuple with the `@` symbol. When stepping
502---  through the above proof, if the notation is confusing to you, remember
503---  that you can set `set_option pp.all true` or
504---  `set_option pp.explicit true` to make Lean show you more clearly what
505---  is going on. For example, the goal is displayed as
506---  `Monoid.id = Monoid.id` since the instances `m₁` and `m₂` are implicit
507---  arguments to `Monoid.id`. Setting `pp.explicit true` displays the goal
508---  as `@Eq α (@Monoid.id α m₁) (@Monoid.id α m₂)`.

510---  A *group* is a special kind of monoid with an *inverse* operation
511---  `inv`, which has the property that `∀ x, inv x ⊗ x = id = x ⊗ inv x`.
512---  We can extend the definition of a `Monoid` to capture this new feature:
513-
514-class Group (α : Type) extends (Monoid α) where
515-  inv : α → α
516-  left_inv : ∀ (x : α), inv x ⊗ x = id
517-  right_inv: ∀ (x : α), x ⊗ inv x = id
518-
519---  Now, the monoids we described earlier are not groups: there is no
520---  inverse operation on the natural numbers such that
521---  `∀ x, x + inv x = 0 = inv x + x`, for example. However, addition does
522---  form a group over the integers:

612---  ## Maps
613-
614---  *Maps* (or "dictionaries") are ubiquitous data structures both in
615---  ordinary programming and in the theory of programming languages; we're
616---  going to need them in many places in later volumes.
617-
618---  We'll define two flavors of maps: *total maps*, which include a
619---  "default" element to be returned when a key being looked up doesn't
620---  exist, and *partial maps*, which instead return an option to indicate
621---  success or failure. Partial maps are defined in terms of total maps,
622---  using `none` as the default element.
623-
624---  ### Key and Value Types
625-
626---  To define maps, we first need a type for the keys that we will use to
627---  index into our maps and a type for the values the maps return. In this
628---  section, we'll use the type variable `α` for the type of keys and `β`
629---  for values. In addition to `BEq`, which we have already seen, our key
630---  type `α` requires instances of the `ReflBEq` and `LawfulBEq`
631---  typeclasses:

635-      rfl {a : α} : a == a

639-      eq_of_beq : {a b : α} → a == b → a = b

641---  These classes refine `BEq`, specifying that (`==`) is reflexive and
642---  coincides with proposition equality `=`.

647-
648---  The Lists chapter introduced a partial map abstraction, `PartialMap`,
649---  with a `find` function for lookup, based on lists of key-value pairs.
650---  Here, we are going to build a map abstraction using functions instead.
651---  The advantage of this representation is that it offers a more
652---  *extensional* view of maps, as we saw with functions in the Logic
653---  chapter: two maps that respond to every query in the same way will be
654---  represented as exactly the same function, rather than just as
655---  "equivalent" list structures. This simplifies proofs that use maps.

344+-- ## Maps
345+
346+-- Maps (or dictionaries) are ubiquitous data structures both in ordinary
347+-- programming and in the theory of programming languages; we're going to need
348+-- them in many places in the coming chapters.
349+
350+-- We'll define two flavors of maps: total maps, which include a "default"
351+-- element to be returned when a key being looked up doesn't exist, and
352+-- partial maps, which instead return an option to indicate success or
353+-- failure. Partial maps are defined in terms of total maps, using None as the
354+-- default element.
355+
356+-- ### Identifiers
357+
358+-- To define maps, we first need a type for the keys that we will use to index
359+-- into our maps. Instead of using concrete types, we will use a type
360+-- variables
361+
362+universe u v
363+variable {α : Type u} {β : Type v} [BEq α] [ReflBEq α] [LawfulBEq α]
364+
365+set_option linter.unusedSectionVars false
366+
367+-- where `α` is the type of our map keys and `β` the corresponding values.
368+-- Looking at `ReflBEq` and `LawfulBEq`, we see that these typeclasses:
369+
370+-- /-- `ReflBEq α` says that the `BEq` implementation is reflexive. -/
371+-- class ReflBEq (α) [BEq α] : Prop where
372+--   /-- `==` is reflexive, that is, `(a == a) = true`. -/
373+--   protected rfl {a : α} : a == a
374+
375+-- /--
376+-- A Boolean equality test coincides with propositional equality.
377+
378+-- In other words:
379+--  * `a == b` implies `a = b`.
380+--  * `a == a` is true.
381+-- -/
382+-- class LawfulBEq (α : Type u) [BEq α] : Prop extends ReflBEq α where
383+--   /-- If `a == b` evaluates to `true`, then `a` and `b` are equal in the logic. -/
384+--   eq_of_beq : {a b : α} → a == b → a = b
385+
386+-- provide the assumption that we have an boolean equality (`==`) on our keys
387+-- that is reflexive and coincides with proposition equality `=`.
388+
389+-- ### Total Maps
390+
391+-- Our main job in this chapter will be to build a definition of partial maps
392+-- that is similar in behavior to the one we saw in the Lists chapter, plus
393+-- accompanying lemmas about its behavior.
394+
395+-- This time around, though, we're going to use functions, rather than lists
396+-- of key-value pairs, to build maps. The advantage of this representation is
397+-- that it offers a more "extensional" view of maps: two maps that respond to
398+-- queries in the same way will be represented as exactly the same function,
399+-- rather than just as "equivalent" list structures. This simplifies proofs
400+-- that use maps.
401+
402+-- We build up to partial maps in two steps. First, we define a type of total
403+-- maps that return a default value when we look up a key that is not present
404+-- in the map.
405+

441+-- More interesting is the map-updating function, which (as always) takes a

450+-- takes a function `m` and yields a new function `fun x' ↦ ...` that behaves
451+-- like the desired map.

851459     |>.update "foo" true

827+-- We've seen two different ways of expressing logical claims in Lean: with
828+-- booleans (of type `Bool`), and with propositions (of type `Prop`).
829+
830+-- Here are the key differences between `Bool` and `Prop`:
831+
832+-- - ⠀
833+-- - `Bool`
834+-- - `Prop`
835+-- - decidable?
836+-- - yes
837+-- - no
838+-- - useable with `match`?
839+-- - yes
840+-- - no
841+-- - works with `rewrite` tactic?
842+-- - no
843+-- - yes
844+
845+-- The crucial difference between the two worlds is decidability. Every
846+-- (closed) Lean expression of type `Bool` can be simplified in a finite
847+-- number of steps to either `true` or `false` — i.e., there is a terminating
848+-- mechanical procedure for deciding whether or not it is true.
849+
850+-- This means that, for example, the type `Nat → Bool` is inhabited only by
851+-- functions that, given a `Nat`, always yield either `true` or `false` in
852+-- finite time; and this, in turn, means (by a standard computability
853+-- argument) that there is no function in `Nat → Bool` that checks whether a
854+-- given number is the code of a terminating Turing machine.
855+
856+-- By contrast, the type `Prop` includes both decidable and undecidable
857+-- mathematical propositions; in particular, the type `Nat → Prop` does
858+-- contain functions representing properties like "the nth Turing machine
859+-- halts." The second row in the table follows directly from this essential
860+-- difference. To evaluate a pattern match (or conditional) on a boolean, we
861+-- need to know whether the scrutinee evaluates to `true` or `false`; this
862+-- only works for `Bool`, not `Prop`.
863+
864+-- The third row highlights an important practical difference: equality
865+-- functions like `Nat.beq` that return a boolean cannot be used directly to
866+-- justify rewriting with the rewrite tactic; propositional equality is
867+-- required for this. Since `Prop` includes both decidable and undecidable
868+-- properties, we have two options when we want to formalize a property that
869+-- happens to be decidable: we can express it either as a boolean computation
870+-- or as a function into Prop.
871+
872+-- As an example, we can write
873+
874+unseal isEven in
875+example : isEven 42 := rfl
876+
877+-- or that there exists some `k` such that `42 = double k`.
878+
879+unseal double in
880+example : Even 42 := by exists 21
881+
882+-- Of course, it would be deeply strange if these two characterizations of
883+-- evenness did not describe the same set of natural numbers!
884+
885+-- Fortunately, they do! To prove this, we first need two helper lemmas.
886+
887+theorem even_double (k : Nat) : isEven (double k) = true := by

1682---      fit.
1683-
1684-end Reflection

SFLCompat/Experiment.lean

1-module
2-
3-public meta import Lean.Elab.BuiltinCommand
4-
5-namespace SFLCompat.Experiment
6-
7-open Lean Elab Command
8-
9-meta section
10-
11--- Copied from `SubVerso.Compat` to avoid making generated projects depend on verso.
12--- We want to have info state and messages available right after the elaboration,
13--- so we need to disable `Elab.async` which would let diagnostics produced asynchronously
14--- through spanshot tasks.
15-private def commandWithoutAsync (act : CommandElabM Unit) : CommandElabM Unit := do
16-  match (← get).scopes with
17-  | [] => act
18-  | h :: t =>
19-    let mut orig : Option Bool := none
20-    try
21-      orig := h.opts.get? `Elab.async
22-      modify fun s => { s with scopes := { h with opts := h.opts.setBool `Elab.async false } :: t }
23-      act
24-    finally
25-      if let h :: t := (← get).scopes then
26-        let opts := orig.map (h.opts.setBool `Elab.async) |>.getD (h.opts.erase `Elab.async)
27-        modify fun s => { s with scopes := { h with opts := opts } :: t }
28-
29-private def withRestoringState (keepMsgs : Bool) (m : CommandElabM Unit) : CommandElabM Unit := do
30-  let savedState ← get
31-  try
32-    m
33-  finally
34-    let state ← get
35-    set { savedState with
36-      -- Preserve the info tree
37-      infoState := state.infoState
38-      messages := if keepMsgs then state.messages else savedState.messages }
39-
40-namespace IndentedCommands
41-
42-/-! # Block Commands Parser
43-  Parse an indented command block. Commands are separated by new lines.
44-  Since we want to capture parsing errors in `sf_expect_failure_in`,
45-  we can't use Lean command parser directly in our command's syntax,
46-  because any parsing error occurred would fail `sf_expect_failure_in` itself.
47-  One possible solution is to first parse the whole indented body as raw syntax,
48-  and then run Lean's command parser followed by command elaboration.
49--/
50-
51-open Parser
52-
53-private def rawLineEndFn : ParserFn :=
54-  eoiFn <|> satisfyFn (· == '\n') "line break"
55-
56-/-- Consumes everything until the next newline and then consumes the newline itself. -/
57-private def rawLineFn : ParserFn :=
58-  takeUntilFn (· == '\n') >> rawLineEndFn
59-
60-/- For each line after the first body line, consumes leading whitespaces.
61-  If it's blank, consumes the newline; otherwise consumes the line
62-  requiring the indentation.
63--/
64-private def rawIndentedLineFn : ParserFn := atomicFn <|
65-  takeWhileFn (· == ' ') >>
66-  (satisfyFn (· == '\n') "line break" <|>
67-    (checkColGeFn "indented command sequence" >> rawLineFn))
68-
69-private def rawCommandBlockFn : ParserFn :=
70-  rawFn (rawLineFn >> manyFn rawIndentedLineFn) (trailingWs := true)
71-
72-private def rawCommandBlock : Parser := { fn := rawCommandBlockFn }
73-
74-@[combinator_parenthesizer rawCommandBlock]
75-private def rawCommandBlock.parenthesizer := PrettyPrinter.Parenthesizer.visitToken
76-
77-@[combinator_formatter rawCommandBlock]
78-private def rawCommandBlock.formatter := PrettyPrinter.Formatter.visitAtom Name.anonymous
79-
80-private partial def runRawCmdsAux
81-    (ictx : InputContext) (pstate : ModuleParserState) : CommandElabM Unit := do
82-  let state ← get
83-  let scope := state.scopes.head!
84-  let pctx :=  {
85-      env := state.env
86-      options := scope.opts
87-      currNamespace := scope.currNamespace
88-      openDecls := scope.openDecls : ParserModuleContext
89-    }
90-  let (cmd, pstate, messages) := parseCommand ictx pctx pstate state.messages
91-  modify fun state => { state with messages }
92-  unless cmd.isOfKind ``Command.eoi do
93-    elabCommand cmd
94-    runLinters cmd
95-    unless isTerminalCommand cmd do
96-      runRawCmdsAux ictx pstate
97-
98-/- Recovers the source info and elaborates the commands -/
99-private def runRawCmds (body : Syntax) : CommandElabM Unit := do
100-  let some source := body.getSubstring? (withLeading := false) (withTrailing := false)
101-    | throwErrorAt body "command sequence has no source range"
102-  let fileName ← getFileName
103-  let fileMap ← getFileMap
104-  -- Recall that `rawIndentedLineFn` may consume whitespaces after the newline.
105-  -- Here we move the ending back to the last non-whitespace character to produce
106-  -- correctly positioned diagnostics.
107-  let stopPos := source.trimRight.stopPos
108-  if h : stopPos ≤ fileMap.source.rawEndPos then
109-    let ictx := InputContext.mk fileMap.source fileName
110-      (fileMap := fileMap) (endPos := stopPos) (endPos_valid := h)
111-    runRawCmdsAux ictx { pos := source.startPos, recovering := false, hasLeading := false }
112-  else
113-    throwErrorAt body "invalid command-sequence source range"
114-
115-end IndentedCommands
116-
117-end
118-
119-public meta section
120-
121-open Parser IndentedCommands
122-
123-/--
124-Elaborates the enclosed commands and reports their diagnostics,
125-but discards their effects afterwards.
126-
127-Example:
128-```lean
129-sf_experiment
130-  def hidden : Nat := 1
131-  #check hidden
132--- `hidden` is not available here.
133-```
134--/
135-def experimentTk := leading_parser
136-  "sf_experiment"
137-
138-@[command_parser] def experimentCmd := leading_parser
139-  experimentTk >> checkLinebreakBefore "indented command sequence" >>
140-    checkColGt "indented command sequence" >> withPosition rawCommandBlock
141-
142-/--
143-Succeeds only if the enclosed commands fail.
144-Diagnostics from the expected failure are suppressed.
145-
146-Example:
147-```lean
148-sf_expect_failure_in
149-  example : 1 = 2 := rfl
150-```
151--/
152-def expectFailureTk := leading_parser
153-  "sf_expect_failure_in"
154-
155-/-
156-  Like `sf_expect_failure_in` but reports the diagnostics.
157--/
158-def expectFailureInfoTk := leading_parser
159-  "sf_expect_failure_in?"
160-
161-@[command_parser] def expectFailureCmd := leading_parser
162-  expectFailureTk >> checkLinebreakBefore "indented command sequence" >>
163-    checkColGt "indented command sequence" >> withPosition rawCommandBlock
164-
165-@[command_parser] def expectFailureInfoCmd := leading_parser
166-  expectFailureInfoTk >> checkLinebreakBefore "indented command sequence" >>
167-    checkColGt "indented command sequence" >> withPosition rawCommandBlock
168-
169-@[command_elab experimentCmd]
170-def elabExperimentCmd : CommandElab := fun stx => do
171-  let body := stx.getArgs.back!
172-  commandWithoutAsync <| withRestoringState true do
173-    runRawCmds body
174-
175-@[command_elab expectFailureCmd, command_elab expectFailureInfoCmd]
176-def elabExpectFailureCmd : CommandElab := fun stx => do
177-  let keepMsgs := stx.isOfKind ``expectFailureInfoCmd
178-  unless keepMsgs || stx.isOfKind ``expectFailureCmd do
179-    throwUnsupportedSyntax
180-  let tk := stx[0]
181-  let body := stx.getArgs.back!
182-  commandWithoutAsync <| withRestoringState keepMsgs do
183-    withRef tk <| failIfSucceeds <| runRawCmds body
184-
185-end
186-

190-@ +3:11...+4:8
191-info: unexpected token '#check'; expected 'with'

SFLCompat/Recall/Check.lean

1-module
2-
3--- For testing cases in this file
4-meta import all Init.Prelude
5-public meta import SFLCompat.Recall.Common
6-
7-/-!
8-# Recall, checked by elaboration
9-
10-`sf_recall` lets a chapter restate a definition from earlier in the
11-development while the build checks that the restatement means the same
12-thing. The restated declaration is elaborated for real, inside a hidden
13-namespace, and compared with the original up to definitional equality; the
14-temporary declaration is then rolled back.
15-
16-Two forms:
17-
18-```
19-sf_recall
20-  def twice (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) : Nat := f <| f n
21-
22-sf_recall statement twice_id : twice id 3 = 3
23-```
24-
25-What is compared:
26-
27-* types, always;
28-* a `def`'s value, safety, and abbreviation status;
29-* an inductive's constructors, one by one (names, parameter and index
30-  counts, and each constructor's type);
31-* a structure's fields, field defaults, and type-class registration;
32-* a theorem's statement, never its proof.
33-
34-So a recalled definition may be reformatted or rephrased into something
35-definitionally equal, and a theorem may be reproved differently or, with
36-the `statement` form, restated without any proof. The command is global and
37-available wherever this module is imported.
38--/
39-
40-
41-namespace SFLCompat.Recall.Check
42-
43-open Lean Elab Command Meta
44-
45-meta section
46-
47-structure DeclId where
48-  /-- This could be a private name. -/
49-  actual : Name
50-  display : Name
51-
52-def DeclId.ofActual (actual : Name) : DeclId :=
53-  { actual, display := privateToUserName actual }
54-
55-/-- Look up the actual name in temp elaboration namespace -/
56-def tempDeclId (userName : Name) : CommandElabM DeclId := do
57-  let env ← getEnv
58-  let privateName := mkPrivateName env userName
59-  let actual ←
60-    if env.contains privateName then pure privateName
61-    else if env.contains userName then pure userName
62-    else throwError "the re-elaborated declaration '{userName}' was not found"
63-  return .ofActual actual
64-
65-def renameBackName (chk orig n : Name) : Name :=
66-  if chk.isPrefixOf n then n.replacePrefix chk orig
67-  else
68-    let chk := privateToUserName chk
69-    if chk.isPrefixOf n then n.replacePrefix chk orig else n
70-
71-/--
72-Replaces the name prefix `chk` with `orig` in every constant that `e`
73-mentions: `chk` itself becomes `orig`, and a longer name such as a hidden
74-constructor `chk.mk` becomes `orig.mk`. Constructor types mention the
75-hidden inductive type's name in argument and resulting positions, so this
76-rewrite is what makes a re-elaborated declaration comparable with the
77-original.
78--/
79-def renameBack (chk orig : DeclId) (e : Expr) : Expr :=
80-  e.replace fun
81-    | .const n us =>
82-      let n' := renameBackName chk.actual orig.actual n
83-      if n == n' then none else some (.const n' us)
84-    | _ => none
85-
86-/--
87-Applies `renameBack` to the expressions recorded in an info tree. The info
88-recorded while elaborating the hidden copy mentions the hidden constants,
89-so hovers over a recalled declaration would otherwise display the hidden
90-names; rewriting before the trees are stored makes them display the
91-originals, which also exist after the hidden copy is rolled back.
92--/
93-partial def renameBackInfoTree (chk orig : DeclId) (t : InfoTree) : InfoTree :=
94-  match t with
95-  | .context (.parentDeclCtx n) t' =>
96-    .context (.parentDeclCtx (renameBackName chk.actual orig.actual n))
97-      (renameBackInfoTree chk orig t')
98-  | .context ctx t' => .context ctx (renameBackInfoTree chk orig t')
99-  | .node i children =>
100-    let i := match i with
101-      | .ofTermInfo ti => .ofTermInfo (reTerm ti)
102-      | .ofDelabTermInfo dti => .ofDelabTermInfo { dti with toTermInfo := reTerm dti.toTermInfo }
103-      | other => other
104-    .node i (children.map (renameBackInfoTree chk orig))
105-  | .hole m => .hole m
106-where
107-  reTerm (ti : TermInfo) : TermInfo :=
108-    { ti with
109-      expr := renameBack chk orig ti.expr
110-      expectedType? := ti.expectedType?.map (renameBack chk orig) }
111-
112-/-- A specialization of universe parameters to a declaration.
113-  It stores level parameters of a `ConstantInfo` and mvars created from these parameters.
114--/
115-abbrev Specialization := List Name × List Level
116-
117-def renameBackS (specialization? : Option Specialization)
118-    (chk orig : DeclId) (e : Expr) : Expr :=
119-  match specialization? with
120-  | none => renameBack chk orig e
121-  | some (_params, levels) =>
122-    e.replace fun
123-      | .const n _ =>
124-        let n' := renameBackName chk.actual orig.actual n
125-        if n == n' then none else some <| .const n' levels
126-      | _ => none
127-
128-def levelsFor (specialization : Specialization) (info : ConstantInfo) :
129-    TermElabM (List Level) :=
130-  let (params, levels) := specialization
131-  info.levelParams.mapM fun param =>
132-    match params.findIdx? (· == param) with
133-    | some index => pure levels[index]!
134-    | none => throwError
135-      "universe parameter '{param}' of '{info.name}' is not a parameter of the recalled declaration"
136-
137-/--
138-Checks that the types of the original constant `x` and its re-elaborated
139-counterpart `chk` agree, definitionally. The restated type is first
140-rewritten by `renameBack renChk renOrig`; the defaults compare a
141-declaration against its own hidden copy, and the constructor check
142-overrides them with the enclosing inductive types, whose names the
143-constructor types mention. The restatement's universe parameters are
144-instantiated with the original's.
145--/
146-def checkTypesMatch (x chk : DeclId) (ref : Syntax)
147-    (specialization? : Option Specialization)
148-    (renChk : DeclId := chk) (renOrig : DeclId := x) (hint : MessageData := .nil) :
149-    TermElabM Unit := do
150-  let origInfo ← getConstInfo x.actual
151-  let chkInfo ← getConstInfo chk.actual
152-  if specialization?.isNone then
153-    -- no specialization, do strict check first
154-    unless origInfo.levelParams.length == chkInfo.levelParams.length do
155-      throwErrorAt ref (m!"universe parameters of '{x.display}' do not match" ++ hint)
156-  let origType ← match specialization? with
157-    | none => pure origInfo.type
158-    | some s => origInfo.instantiateTypeLevelParams <$> levelsFor s origInfo
159-  let chkType := match specialization? with
160-    | none => (renameBackS specialization? renChk renOrig chkInfo.type).instantiateLevelParams
161-        chkInfo.levelParams (origInfo.levelParams.map .param)
162-    | some _ => renameBackS specialization? renChk renOrig chkInfo.type
163-  unless ← isDefEq chkType origType do
164-    throwErrorAt ref
165-      (m!"the statement of '{x.display}' does not match.\n\
166-          Original:{indentD origInfo.type}\nRestated:{indentD chkType}" ++ hint)
167-
168-/--
169-All constructor syntax nodes of a command, in source order: an inductive
170-type's `| name : ...` alternatives and a structure's `name ::` header.
171--/
172-partial def ctorStxs (stx : Syntax) : Array Syntax :=
173-  let inner := stx.getArgs.flatMap ctorStxs
174-  if stx.isOfKind ``Lean.Parser.Command.ctor
175-      || stx.isOfKind ``Lean.Parser.Command.structCtor then
176-    #[stx] ++ inner
177-  else inner
178-
179-/-- Does the syntax contain a doc comment? -/
180-def hasDocComment (stx : Syntax) : Bool :=
181-  (stx.find? (·.isOfKind ``Lean.Parser.Command.docComment)).isSome
182-
183-/--
184-Suggestions localized to a mismatched constructor, returned as a pair of
185-hints for name errors and for type errors. An inductive type's `| name : ...` alternative is replaced
186-with the original constructor's own source. A structure's `name ::` header
187-can carry a name fix but not a field fix, so its type errors keep `outer`,
188-the suggestion that replaces the whole restatement. A constructor without
189-syntax also falls back to `outer`.
190--/
191-def ctorHints (ctorRef : Syntax) (origCtor origShort : Name) (outer : MessageData) :
192-    TermElabM (MessageData × MessageData) := do
193-  try
194-    if ctorRef.isOfKind ``Lean.Parser.Command.ctor then
195-      let origSrc := dedent (← sourceOf origCtor)
196-      -- A restatement without a doc comment gets a suggestion without one;
197-      -- the meaning check does not compare documentation.
198-      let origSrc := if hasDocComment ctorRef then origSrc
199-        else stripLeadingComments origSrc
200-      let restatedSrc ← sourceOfSyntax ctorRef
201-      let h ← replaceWithOriginalHint ctorRef origSrc restatedSrc
202-      return (h, h)
203-    if ctorRef.isOfKind ``Lean.Parser.Command.structCtor then
204-      let restatedSrc ← sourceOfSyntax ctorRef
205-      let h ← replaceWithOriginalHint ctorRef s!"{origShort} ::" restatedSrc
206-      return (h, outer)
207-    return (outer, outer)
208-  catch _ => return (outer, outer)
209-
210-/--
211-Checks a re-elaborated declaration against the original, definitionally.
212-Errors point at `ref`, the restated command, except for constructor
213-mismatches, which point at the offending constructor within it.
214--/
215-def checkMatchCore (x chk : DeclId) (ref : Syntax)
216-    (specialization? : Option (List Name × List Level))
217-    (hint : MessageData := .nil) : TermElabM Unit := do
218-  checkTypesMatch x chk ref specialization? (hint := hint)
219-  let origInfo ← getConstInfo x.actual
220-  let chkInfo ← getConstInfo chk.actual
221-  match origInfo, chkInfo with
222-  | .defnInfo orig, .defnInfo restated =>
223-    let origVal ← match specialization? with
224-      | none => pure orig.value
225-      | some s => origInfo.instantiateValueLevelParams! <$> levelsFor s origInfo
226-    let chkVal := match specialization? with
227-      | none => (renameBackS specialization? chk x restated.value).instantiateLevelParams
228-          restated.levelParams (orig.levelParams.map .param)
229-      | some _ => renameBackS specialization? chk x restated.value
230-    unless ← isDefEq chkVal origVal do
231-      throwErrorAt ref
232-        (m!"the value of '{x.display}' does not match.\n\
233-            Original:{indentD orig.value}\nRestated:{indentD chkVal}" ++ hint)
234-  | .inductInfo orig, .inductInfo restated =>
235-    unless orig.numParams == restated.numParams && orig.numIndices == restated.numIndices do
236-      throwErrorAt ref (m!"parameters or indices of '{x.display}' do not match" ++ hint)
237-    unless orig.ctors.length == restated.ctors.length do
238-      throwErrorAt ref
239-        (m!"'{x.display}' has {orig.ctors.length} constructors, \
240-            the restatement has {restated.ctors.length}" ++ hint)
241-    -- A `structure` that writes no `name ::` header has a constructor
242-    -- without syntax; the whole command remains the fallback position.
243-    let ctorRefs := ctorStxs ref
244-    let mut i := 0
245-    for origCtorActual in orig.ctors, chkCtorActual in restated.ctors do
246-      let origCtor := DeclId.ofActual origCtorActual
247-      let chkCtor := DeclId.ofActual chkCtorActual
248-      let ctorRef := ctorRefs[i]?.getD ref
249-      let origShort := origCtor.actual.replacePrefix x.actual .anonymous
250-      let (nameHint, typeHint) ← ctorHints ctorRef origCtor.actual origShort hint
251-      let renamedChkCtor := DeclId.ofActual <|
252-        chkCtor.actual.replacePrefix chk.actual x.actual
253-      unless origCtor.actual == renamedChkCtor.actual do
254-        throwErrorAt ctorRef
255-          (m!"constructor '{renamedChkCtor.display}' does not match \
256-              '{origCtor.display}'" ++ nameHint)
257-      checkTypesMatch origCtor chkCtor ctorRef specialization?
258-        (renChk := chk) (renOrig := x) (hint := typeHint)
259-      i := i + 1
260-    -- A structure's field names are part of its interface, and the
261-    -- constructor's type does not record them, so they are compared
262-    -- through the environment's structure information.
263-    let env ← getEnv
264-    match getStructureInfo? env x.actual, getStructureInfo? env chk.actual with
265-    | some origSi, some chkSi =>
266-      let origFields := origSi.fieldNames.map DeclId.ofActual
267-      let chkFields := chkSi.fieldNames.map DeclId.ofActual
268-      unless origFields.map (·.actual) == chkFields.map (·.actual) do
269-        throwErrorAt ref
270-          (m!"the fields of '{x.display}' do not match.\n\
271-              Original:{indentD (toMessageData (origFields.map (·.display)).toList)}\n\
272-              Restated:{indentD (toMessageData (chkFields.map (·.display)).toList)}" ++ hint)
273-      unless getOutParamPositions? env x.actual == getOutParamPositions? env chk.actual
274-          && getOutLevelParamPositions? env x.actual == getOutLevelParamPositions? env chk.actual do
275-        throwErrorAt ref (m!"the type-class metadata of '{x.display}' does not match" ++ hint)
276-    | some _, none =>
277-      throwErrorAt ref (m!"'{x.display}' is a structure, but the restatement is not" ++ hint)
278-    | none, some _ =>
279-      throwErrorAt ref (m!"'{x.display}' is not a structure, but the restatement is one" ++ hint)
280-    | none, none => pure ()
281-  -- A theorem's proof is not compared; restating it as a `def` is also
282-  -- accepted, since only the statement matters.
283-  | .thmInfo _, .thmInfo _ => pure ()
284-  | .thmInfo _, .defnInfo _ => pure ()
285-  | .axiomInfo _, .axiomInfo _ => pure ()
286-  | .opaqueInfo _, .opaqueInfo _ => pure ()
287-  | _, _ =>
288-    throwErrorAt ref
289-      (m!"'{x.display}' and its restatement are different kinds of declaration" ++ hint)
290-
291-/--
292-Run `checkpointDefEq` in `TermElabM`.
293-Note: this is only for universe level constraints solving in `isDefEq` and
294-has nothing to do with the elaborator.
295--/
296-def checkpointDefEq' (action : TermElabM Bool) : TermElabM Bool :=
297-  controlAt MetaM fun runInBase =>
298-    checkpointDefEq (mayPostpone := false) (runInBase action)
299-
300-def checkMatch (x chk : DeclId) (ref : Syntax)
301-    (strictUniverse : Bool) (hint : MessageData := .nil) : TermElabM Unit := do
302-  let origInfo ← getConstInfo x.actual
303-  let chkInfo ← getConstInfo chk.actual
304-  if origInfo.levelParams.length == chkInfo.levelParams.length then
305-    -- if the definition being to check has exactly the same number of the parameters,
306-    -- treat it as no specialization in checking
307-    checkMatchCore x chk ref none hint
308-  else if !strictUniverse && !origInfo.levelParams.isEmpty && chkInfo.levelParams.isEmpty then
309-    -- if all parameters have been specified (monomorphic), do check with specialization
310-    let succeeded ← checkpointDefEq' do
311-      let levels ← mkFreshLevelMVarsFor origInfo
312-      checkMatchCore x chk ref (some (origInfo.levelParams, levels)) hint
313-      pure true
314-    unless succeeded do
315-      throwErrorAt ref (m!"the statement of '{x.display}' does not match" ++ hint)
316-  else
317-    throwErrorAt ref (m!"universe parameters of '{x.display}' do not match" ++ hint)
318-
319-
320-/--
321-`sf_recall` restates a definition from earlier in the development and checks
322-that the restatement means the same thing. `sf_recall statement x : T` checks
323-that `T` matches the statement of the theorem `x`.
324--/
325-syntax (name := recallChk) "sf_recall " command : command
326-
327-@[inherit_doc recallChk]
328-syntax (name := recallChkStrict) "sf_recall" " +" noWs &"strictUniverse" ppSpace command : command
329-
330-@[inherit_doc recallChk]
331-syntax (name := recallChkStmt) "sf_recall " &"statement " ident " : " term : command
332-
333-
334-def elabRecallCommand (cmd : Syntax) (strictUniverse : Bool) : CommandElabM Unit := do
335-  let decl ← declaredName cmd
336-  let xActual ← liftCoreM <| withoutExporting <|
337-    realizeGlobalConstNoOverloadWithInfo decl.ident
338-  let x := DeclId.ofActual xActual
339-  -- The restatement elaborates unchanged inside a fresh hidden namespace:
340-  -- self-references (an inductive's own name in its constructor types, in
341-  -- resulting-type position included) resolve to the hidden copy, and
342-  -- every other name resolves as it would at the recall site. The
343-  -- namespace comes from the name generator: `_uniq` names cannot be
344-  -- written in source, so it is collision-free, and unlike a macro-scoped
345-  -- name it is an ordinary component, so declarations under it keep the
346-  -- prefix structure that `renameBack` and the constructor comparison
347-  -- rely on.
348-  let ns ← liftCoreM (mkFreshId : CoreM Name)
349-  -- Any mismatch gets a clickable fix: replace the restatement with the
350-  -- original's source text, indented like the restatement. The helpers
351-  -- for recovering and re-indenting source are shared with the
352-  -- byte-for-byte variant.
353-  -- A failed hint must not fail the check: not every constant has a
354-  -- declaration range or sources on the search path.
355-  let hint ←
356-    try
357-      let original := dedent (← sourceOf x.actual)
358-      let original := if hasDocComment cmd then original
359-        else stripLeadingComments original
360-      let restated ← sourceOfSyntax cmd
361-      liftCoreM <| replaceWithOriginalHint cmd original restated
362-    catch _ => pure .nil
363-  let envBefore ← getEnv
364-  try
365-    let chk ← withScope (fun sc => { sc with currNamespace := sc.currNamespace ++ ns }) do
366-      let saved ← getResetInfoTrees
367-      try
368-        elabCommand cmd
369-        -- this could be a private name
370-        let userName := (← getScope).currNamespace ++ decl.written
371-        let chk ← tempDeclId userName
372-        let inner ← getResetInfoTrees
373-        modifyInfoState fun s => { s with trees := saved ++ inner.map (renameBackInfoTree chk x) }
374-        return chk
375-      catch e =>
376-        let inner ← getResetInfoTrees
377-        modifyInfoState fun s => { s with trees := saved ++ inner }
378-        throw e
379-    runTermElabM fun _ => checkMatch x chk cmd strictUniverse (hint := hint)
380-  finally
381-    setEnv envBefore
382-
383-def elabRecallStatement (ident stmt : Syntax) : CommandElabM Unit := do
384-  let xActual ← liftCoreM <| withoutExporting <|
385-    realizeGlobalConstNoOverloadWithInfo ident
386-  let x := DeclId.ofActual xActual
387-  addConstInfo ident x.actual
388-  let region := mkNullNode #[ident, stmt]
389-  let restated ← sourceOfSyntax region
390-  runTermElabM fun _ => do
391-    -- The suggestion restates the original's type as the pretty-printer
392-    -- renders it. The statement cannot be carved out of the original's
393-    -- source, since finding its boundary would require parsing the
394-    -- source in the elaboration context of its declaration site.
395-    let hint ←
396-      try
397-        let origInfo ← getConstInfo x.actual
398-        let printed ← ppExpr origInfo.type
399-        replaceWithOriginalHint region
400-          s!"{ident.getId} : {printed}" restated
401-      catch _ => pure .nil
402-    let t ← Term.elabType stmt
403-    Term.synthesizeSyntheticMVarsNoPostponing
404-    let t ← instantiateMVars (← Term.levelMVarToParam t)
405-    let origInfo ← getConstInfo x.actual
406-    let stParams := (collectLevelParams {} t).params
407-    unless stParams.size == origInfo.levelParams.length do
408-      throwErrorAt stmt (m!"universe parameters of '{x.display}' do not match" ++ hint)
409-    let t := t.instantiateLevelParams stParams.toList
410-      (origInfo.levelParams.map .param)
411-    unless ← isDefEq t origInfo.type do
412-      throwErrorAt stmt
413-        (m!"the restated statement of '{x.display}' does not match.\n\
414-            Original:{indentD origInfo.type}\nRestated:{indentD t}" ++ hint)
415-
416-
417-elab_rules : command
418-  | `(sf_recall $cmd:command) => elabRecallCommand cmd false
419-  | `(sf_recall +strictUniverse $cmd:command) => elabRecallCommand cmd true
420-  | `(sf_recall statement $ident:ident : $stmt:term) => elabRecallStatement ident stmt
421-
422-end

SFLCompat/Recall/Common.lean

1-module
2-
3-public meta import Lean.Elab.Command
4-
5-namespace SFLCompat.Recall
6-
7-open Lean Elab Command
8-public meta section
9-
10-/-- All `declId` nodes in a command, in source order. -/
11-partial def declIds (stx : Syntax) : Array Syntax :=
12-  let inner := stx.getArgs.flatMap declIds
13-  if stx.isOfKind ``Lean.Parser.Command.declId then #[stx] ++ inner else inner
14-
15-/-- The syntax and written name of the single declaration in a recall command. -/
16-structure DeclSyntax where
17-  ident : Syntax
18-  written : Name
19-
20-/--
21-The `declId` node of a declaration command, together with the name written
22-in it. A command that declares several names (a `mutual` block) or none (an
23-anonymous `instance`, an `example`) is rejected.
24--/
25-def declaredName (cmd : Syntax) : CommandElabM DeclSyntax := do
26-  let defined := declIds cmd
27-  match h : defined.size with
28-  | 0 => throwErrorAt cmd "the restated command does not declare a name"
29-  | 1 =>
30-    let declId := defined[0]
31-    return { ident := declId[0], written := declId[0].getId }
32-  | n + 2 =>
33-    for h : i in 0...(n + 1) do
34-      logErrorAt defined[i]
35-        "the restated command declares several names; recall one declaration at a time"
36-    throwErrorAt defined[n + 1]
37-      "the restated command declares several names; recall one declaration at a time"
38-
39-/--
40-Removes the block indentation of a declaration's source text. The first
41-line starts at the declaration's first token and has no indentation of its
42-own; each following line is stripped of the smallest indentation found
43-among the non-blank ones. Restatements of the same text at different block
44-depths dedent to identical strings, and every other difference survives
45-dedenting.
46--/
47-def dedent (s : String) : String :=
48-  match indentWidth s, s.splitOn "\n" with
49-  | some n, first :: rest =>
50-    "\n".intercalate (first :: rest.map (fun l => String.ofList (l.toList.drop n)))
51-  | _, _ => s
52-where
53-  /-- The smallest indentation among the non-blank continuation lines. -/
54-  indentWidth (s : String) : Option Nat :=
55-    s.splitOn "\n" |>.drop 1 |>.map (·.toList)
56-      |>.filter (fun l => !l.all (·.isWhitespace))
57-      |>.map (fun l => (l.takeWhile (· == ' ')).length)
58-      |>.min?
59-
60-/--
61-Indents the continuation lines of dedented source text by `n` spaces, so
62-that the text reads correctly at the block depth of a restatement.
63--/
64-def reindent (s : String) (n : Nat) : String :=
65-  match s.splitOn "\n" with
66-  | [] => s
67-  | first :: rest =>
68-    let pad := String.ofList (List.replicate n ' ')
69-    "\n".intercalate (first :: rest.map fun l =>
70-      if l.toList.all (·.isWhitespace) then l else pad ++ l)
71-
72-/--
73-Removes the comments from the front of dedented source text, together with
74-the whitespace around them, so that a suggestion offered for a restatement
75-that carries no comments does not introduce any. The text of a declaration
76-or of a constructor begins with its doc comment when it has one, possibly
77-accompanied by ordinary comments, and a leading block comment ends at its
78-depth-balanced closing delimiter, so a character scan recognizes the
79-leading run of comments exactly. A comment elsewhere in the text cannot be
80-recognized without lexing and is left in place.
81--/
82-def stripLeadingComments (s : String) : String := Id.run do
83-  let mut cs := s.toList.dropWhile (·.isWhitespace)
84-  repeat
85-    if cs.take 2 == ['/', '-'] then
86-      cs := cs.drop 2
87-      let mut depth := 1
88-      while depth > 0 do
89-        match cs with
90-        | [] => return s
91-        | '/' :: '-' :: rest => depth := depth + 1; cs := rest
92-        | '-' :: '/' :: rest => depth := depth - 1; cs := rest
93-        | _ :: rest => cs := rest
94-    else if cs.take 2 == ['-', '-'] then
95-      cs := cs.dropWhile (· != '\n')
96-    else
97-      break
98-    cs := cs.dropWhile (·.isWhitespace)
99-  return String.ofList cs
100-
101-/--
102-A clickable suggestion that replaces the restated text at `span` with
103-`original`, which must already be dedented. The original's indentation is
104-moved to match the restatement's: the restatement's own indentation width
105-when it has continuation lines, one step past the span's start column when
106-it does not.
107--/
108-def replaceWithOriginalHint [Monad m] [MonadFileMap m] [MonadLiftT CoreM m]
109-    (span : Syntax) (original restated : String) : m MessageData := do
110-  let fileMap ← getFileMap
111-  let k := match dedent.indentWidth restated, span.getRange? with
112-    | some k, _ => k
113-    | none, some r => (fileMap.toPosition r.start).column + 2
114-    | none, none => 2
115-  MessageData.hint m!"Replace the restatement with the original:"
116-    #[{ suggestion := .string (reindent original k), span? := some span }]
117-
118-/--
119-The source text of the declaration of `x`, from the file that declared it.
120-
121-The location comes from the declaration range that Lean records for every
122-constant. A declaration from the current file is read out of the file map;
123-one from an imported module is read from its source file, found on the
124-source search path. In a book build the whole project's sources are on that
125-path, so definitions can be recalled across chapters.
126--/
127-def sourceOf [Monad m] [MonadEnv m] [MonadError m] [MonadFileMap m]
128-    [MonadLiftT IO m] [MonadLiftT BaseIO m] (x : Name) : m String := do
129-  let some ranges ← findDeclarationRanges? x
130-    | throwError "no declaration range recorded for '{x}'"
131-  let env ← getEnv
132-  let text ←
133-    match env.getModuleIdxFor? x with
134-    | none => pure (← getFileMap)
135-    | some idx => do
136-      let modName := env.allImportedModuleNames[idx.toNat]!
137-      let sp ← getSrcSearchPath
138-      let some path ← sp.findModuleWithExt "lean" modName
139-        | throwError "source for module '{modName}' is not on the search path"
140-      pure (FileMap.ofString (← IO.FS.readFile path))
141-  return String.Pos.Raw.extract text.source
142-    (text.ofPosition ranges.range.pos) (text.ofPosition ranges.range.endPos)
143-
144-/-- The source text of a piece of syntax in the current file. -/
145-def sourceOfSyntax [Monad m] [MonadError m] [MonadFileMap m]
146-    (stx : Syntax) : m String := do
147-  let some r := stx.getRange?
148-    | throwErrorAt stx "no source range"
149-  return String.Pos.Raw.extract (← getFileMap).source r.start r.stop
150-
151-end
152-
153-end SFLCompat.Recall

5-/-!
6-# Recall, checked byte for byte
7-
8-`sf_recall_source` lets a chapter restate a definition from earlier in the
9-development while the build checks that the restatement matches the
10-original's source text, byte for byte. The restated text is what the
11-reader already saw, and it can never drift from the original.
12-
13-```
14-sf_recall_source
15-  def twice (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) : Nat := f (f n)
16-```
17-
18-The restated declaration is parsed but never elaborated; the check is
19-purely textual: after the block indentation is removed from each side, the
20-two texts must be equal, byte for byte. The restatement may sit at a
21-different indentation depth, but it may not be reflowed or respaced.
22-
23-The comparison covers whole declarations only. Carving a statement out of
24-the original's source would require parsing it, which is only possible in
25-the elaboration context of its declaration site; restating only a theorem
26-statement is therefore the province of `sf_recall statement`, which compares
27-elaborated types.
28--/
29-
30-namespace SFLCompat.Recall.Source
31-
32-open Lean Elab Command
33-
34-/--
35-`recall_source` restates a definition from earlier in the development and
36-checks that the restatement matches the original's source text, byte for
37-byte, modulo block indentation.
38--/
39-syntax (name := recallSrc) "sf_recall_source " command : command
40-
41-elab_rules : command
42-  | `(sf_recall_source $cmd:command) => do
43-    let decl ← declaredName cmd
44-    let x ← liftCoreM <| withoutExporting <|
45-      realizeGlobalConstNoOverloadWithInfo decl.ident
46-    -- The restatement is never elaborated, so it produces no info of its
47-    -- own. The whole compared region is one big reference to the original:
48-    -- hovering anywhere in it shows the original, and go-to-definition
49-    -- jumps to it.
50-    addConstInfo cmd x
51-    let restated ← sourceOfSyntax cmd
52-    let original ← sourceOf x
53-    unless dedent restated == dedent original do
54-      throwErrorAt cmd
55-        (m!"the restatement of '{privateToUserName x}' does not match its source.\n\
56-            Original:{indentD original}\nRestated:{indentD restated}"
57-          ++ (← liftCoreM <| replaceWithOriginalHint cmd (dedent original) restated))
58-

62-  | red | green | blue
63-
64-def twice (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) : Nat := f (f n)
65-

79-#guard SFLCompat.Recall.stripLeadingComments

1+module
2+
3+public meta import Lean.Elab.BuiltinCommand
4+
5+namespace SLFCommand
6+
7+open Lean Elab Command
8+
9+meta section
10+
11+-- Copied from `SubVerso.Compat` to avoid making generated projects depend on verso.
12+-- We want to have info state and messages available right after the elaboration,
13+-- so we need to disable `Elab.async` which would let diagnostics produced asynchronously
14+-- through spanshot tasks.
15+private def commandWithoutAsync (act : CommandElabM Unit) : CommandElabM Unit := do
16+  match (← get).scopes with
17+  | [] => act
18+  | h :: t =>
19+    let mut orig : Option Bool := none
20+    try
21+      orig := h.opts.get? `Elab.async
22+      modify fun s => { s with scopes := { h with opts := h.opts.setBool `Elab.async false } :: t }
23+      act
24+    finally
25+      if let h :: t := (← get).scopes then
26+        let opts := orig.map (h.opts.setBool `Elab.async) |>.getD (h.opts.erase `Elab.async)
27+        modify fun s => { s with scopes := { h with opts := opts } :: t }
28+
29+private def withRestoringState (keepMsgs : Bool) (m : CommandElabM Unit) : CommandElabM Unit := do
30+  let savedState ← get
31+  try
32+    m
33+  finally
34+    let state ← get
35+    set { savedState with
36+      -- Preserve the info tree
37+      infoState := state.infoState
38+      messages := if keepMsgs then state.messages else savedState.messages }
39+
40+namespace IndentedCommands
41+
42+/-! # Block Commands Parser
43+  Parse an indented command block. Commands are separated by new lines.
44+  Since we want to capture parsing errors in `sf_expect_failure`,
45+  we can't use Lean command parser directly in our command's syntax,
46+  because any parsing error occurred would fail `sf_expect_failure` itself.
47+  One possible solution is to first parse the whole indented body as raw syntax,
48+  and then run Lean's command parser followed by command elaboration.
49+-/
50+
51+open Parser
52+
53+private def rawLineEndFn : ParserFn :=
54+  eoiFn <|> satisfyFn (· == '\n') "line break"
55+
56+/-- Consumes everything until the next newline and then consumes the newline itself. -/
57+private def rawLineFn : ParserFn :=
58+  takeUntilFn (· == '\n') >> rawLineEndFn
59+
60+/- For each line after the first body line, consumes leading whitespaces.
61+  If it's blank, consumes the newline; otherwise consumes the line
62+  requiring the indentation.
63+-/
64+private def rawIndentedLineFn : ParserFn := atomicFn <|
65+  takeWhileFn (· == ' ') >>
66+  (satisfyFn (· == '\n') "line break" <|>
67+    (checkColGeFn "indented command sequence" >> rawLineFn))
68+
69+private def rawCommandBlockFn : ParserFn :=
70+  rawFn (rawLineFn >> manyFn rawIndentedLineFn) (trailingWs := true)
71+
72+private def rawCommandBlock : Parser := { fn := rawCommandBlockFn }
73+
74+@[combinator_parenthesizer rawCommandBlock]
75+private def rawCommandBlock.parenthesizer := PrettyPrinter.Parenthesizer.visitToken
76+
77+@[combinator_formatter rawCommandBlock]
78+private def rawCommandBlock.formatter := PrettyPrinter.Formatter.visitAtom Name.anonymous
79+
80+private partial def runRawCmdsAux
81+    (ictx : InputContext) (pstate : ModuleParserState) : CommandElabM Unit := do
82+  let state ← get
83+  let scope := state.scopes.head!
84+  let pctx :=  {
85+      env := state.env
86+      options := scope.opts
87+      currNamespace := scope.currNamespace
88+      openDecls := scope.openDecls : ParserModuleContext
89+    }
90+  let (cmd, pstate, messages) := parseCommand ictx pctx pstate state.messages
91+  modify fun state => { state with messages }
92+  unless cmd.isOfKind ``Command.eoi do
93+    elabCommand cmd
94+    runLinters cmd
95+    unless isTerminalCommand cmd do
96+      runRawCmdsAux ictx pstate
97+
98+/- Recovers the source info and elaborates the commands -/
99+private def runRawCmds (body : Syntax) : CommandElabM Unit := do
100+  let some source := body.getSubstring? (withLeading := false) (withTrailing := false)
101+    | throwErrorAt body "command sequence has no source range"
102+  let fileName ← getFileName
103+  let fileMap ← getFileMap
104+  -- Recall that `rawIndentedLineFn` may consume whitespaces after the newline.
105+  -- Here we move the ending back to the last non-whitespace character to produce
106+  -- correctly positioned diagnostics.
107+  let stopPos := source.trimRight.stopPos
108+  if h : stopPos ≤ fileMap.source.rawEndPos then
109+    let ictx := InputContext.mk fileMap.source fileName
110+      (fileMap := fileMap) (endPos := stopPos) (endPos_valid := h)
111+    runRawCmdsAux ictx { pos := source.startPos, recovering := false, hasLeading := false }
112+  else
113+    throwErrorAt body "invalid command-sequence source range"
114+
115+end IndentedCommands
116+
117+end
118+
119+public meta section
120+
121+open Parser IndentedCommands
122+
123+/--
124+Elaborates the enclosed commands and reports their diagnostics,
125+but discards their effects afterwards.
126+
127+Example:
128+```lean
129+sf_experiment
130+  def hidden : Nat := 1
131+  #check hidden
132+-- `hidden` is not available here.
133+```
134+-/
135+def experimentTk := leading_parser
136+  "sf_experiment"
137+
138+@[command_parser] def experimentCmd := leading_parser
139+  experimentTk >> checkLinebreakBefore "indented command sequence" >>
140+    checkColGt "indented command sequence" >> withPosition rawCommandBlock
141+
142+/--
143+Succeeds only if the enclosed commands fail.
144+Diagnostics from the expected failure are suppressed.
145+
146+Example:
147+```lean
148+sf_expect_failure
149+  example : 1 = 2 := rfl
150+```
151+-/
152+def expectFailureTk := leading_parser
153+  "sf_expect_failure"
154+
155+/-
156+  Like `sf_expect_failure` but reports the diagnostics.
157+-/
158+def expectFailureInfoTk := leading_parser
159+  "sf_expect_failure?"
160+
161+@[command_parser] def expectFailureCmd := leading_parser
162+  expectFailureTk >> checkLinebreakBefore "indented command sequence" >>
163+    checkColGt "indented command sequence" >> withPosition rawCommandBlock
164+
165+@[command_parser] def expectFailureInfoCmd := leading_parser
166+  expectFailureInfoTk >> checkLinebreakBefore "indented command sequence" >>
167+    checkColGt "indented command sequence" >> withPosition rawCommandBlock
168+
169+@[command_elab experimentCmd]
170+def elabExperimentCmd : CommandElab := fun stx => do
171+  let body := stx.getArgs.back!
172+  commandWithoutAsync <| withRestoringState true do
173+    runRawCmds body
174+
175+@[command_elab expectFailureCmd, command_elab expectFailureInfoCmd]
176+def elabExpectFailureCmd : CommandElab := fun stx => do
177+  let keepMsgs := stx.isOfKind ``expectFailureInfoCmd
178+  unless keepMsgs || stx.isOfKind ``expectFailureCmd do
179+    throwUnsupportedSyntax
180+  let tk := stx[0]
181+  let body := stx.getArgs.back!
182+  commandWithoutAsync <| withRestoringState keepMsgs do
183+    withRef tk <| failIfSucceeds <| runRawCmds body
184+
185+end
186+
187+namespace Tests
188+
189+/--
190+@ +3:11...+4:8
191+info: unexpected token '#check'; expected 'with'
192+---
193+@ +3:4...9
194+info: Missing cases:
195+_
196+---
197+@ +4:2...8
198+info: 1 : Nat
199+-/
200+#guard_msgs (positions := true) in
201+sf_expect_failure?
202+  def f (n : Nat) : Nat :=
203+    match n
204+  #check 1
205+
206+/-- info: Nat : Type -/
207+#guard_msgs in
208+#check Nat
209+
210+/--
211+info: SLFCommand.Tests.x : Nat
212+---
213+info: 3
214+-/
215+#guard_msgs in
216+sf_experiment
217+  def x : Nat := 1
218+  #check x
219+  def f : Nat → Nat
220+    | 0 => 0
221+    | n + 1 => n + 2
222+  #eval f 2
223+
224+/-- error: Unknown identifier `x` -/
225+#guard_msgs in
226+#check x
227+
228+/--
229+error: Type mismatch
230+  "qwq"
231+has type
232+  String
233+but is expected to have type
234+  Nat
235+-/
236+#guard_msgs in
237+sf_experiment
238+  def y : Nat := "qwq"
239+
240+/-- info: invalid 'import' command, it must be used in the beginning of the file -/
241+#guard_msgs in
242+sf_expect_failure?
243+  import Lean
244+
245+/-- warning: using 'exit' to interrupt Lean -/
246+#guard_msgs in
247+sf_experiment
248+  #exit
249+
250+end Tests
251+
252+end SLFCommand

3---  # Slang: Arithmetic and Boolean Expressions
4-
5---  Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):

7---      proofs. Quite a few proofs here don't render into the chosen page

9-
10---  In **Logical Foundations** (LF) we went through the basics of how to
11---  use Lean to prove theorems and write functional programs. Now, we begin
12---  to shift gears to using it to reason about properties of programs and
13---  programming languages. We begin by looking at a language we call
14---  **Slang** (for *simple language*). Despite its simplicity, Slang lets
15---  us introduce key concepts for specifying the *syntax* and *semantics*
16---  of programming languages and show how those concepts are realized in
17---  Lean.
18-
19---  (This chapter is shared, word for word, between two volumes: **Type
20---  Systems** (TS) and **Hoare Logic** (HL). If you have already worked
21---  through it in the other volume, you can safely skip ahead to the next
22---  chapter of this one.)
23-
24---  ## Arithmetic and Boolean Expressions
25-
26---  Slang is a simple core language of *arithmetic and boolean expressions*
27---  sufficient to express simple computations and logical predicates.
28-
29---  ### Syntax
1+import TS.SFLCompat
2+
3+-- # Slang: Arithmetic and Boolean Expressions
4+
5+-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce  @bcpierce00):
6+--     We need to figure out our approach to text width, especially for
7+--     proofs. Quite a few proofs here don't render into the chosen page
8+--     width, and for terse mode it will be worse.
9+
10+-- We begin by looking at a language we call **Slang** (for *simple
11+-- language*). Despite its simplicity, Slang lets us introduce key concepts
12+-- for specifying the *syntax* and *semantics* of programming languages and
13+-- show how those concepts are realized in Lean.
14+
15+-- (This chapter is shared, word for word, between two volumes: **Type
16+-- Systems** (TS) and **Hoare Logic** (HL). If you have already worked through
17+-- it in the other volume, you can safely skip ahead to the next chapter of
18+-- this one.)
19+
20+-- ## Arithmetic and Boolean Expressions
21+
22+-- Slang is a simple core language of *arithmetic and boolean expressions*
23+-- sufficient to express simple computations and logical predicates.
24+
25+-- ### Syntax
3026 
3127 namespace Slang

47+-- In this chapter, we'll ignore the translation from the *concrete syntax*

55+-- a ::= nat
56+--     | a + a

58+--     | a * a

67+-- Compared to the Lean version above...
68+
69+-- - The BNF is more informal -- for example, it gives some suggestions about
70+--   the surface syntax of expressions (like the fact that the addition
71+--   operation is written with an infix `+`) while leaving other aspects of
72+--   lexical analysis and parsing (like the relative precedence of `+`, `-`, and
73+--   `*`, the use of parens to group subexpressions, etc.) unspecified. Some
74+--   additional information -- and human intelligence -- would be required to
75+--   turn this description into a formal definition, e.g., for implementing a
76+--   compiler. The Lean version consistently omits all this information and
77+--   concentrates on the abstract syntax only.
78+
79+-- - Conversely, the BNF version is lighter and easier to read. Its informality
80+--   makes it flexible, a big advantage in situations like discussions at the
81+--   blackboard, where conveying general ideas is more important than nailing
82+--   down every detail precisely.
83+
84+--   Indeed, there are dozens of BNF-like notations and people switch freely
85+--   among them -- usually without bothering to say which kind of BNF they're
86+--   using, because there is no need to: a rough-and-ready informal
87+--   understanding is all that's important.
88+
89+-- It's good to be comfortable with both sorts of notations: informal ones for

332+-- ### Inference Rule Notation
333+
334+-- In informal discussions, it is convenient to write the rules for
335+-- `Aexp.EvalR` and similar relations in the more readable graphical form of
336+-- *inference rules*, where the premises above the line justify the conclusion
337+-- below the line. For example, the constructor `plus` can be written like
338+-- this as an inference rule:
339+
340+-- e1 ⇓ n1
341+--                          e2 ⇓ n2
342+--                     ------------------          (plus)
343+--                     plus e1 e2 ⇓ n1+n2
344+
345+-- Notice the structural correspondence between this rule and our version of
346+-- the inductive type with unnamed hypotheses:
347+
348+-- | plus (a1 a2 : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat) :
349+--         EvalR a1 n1 →
350+--         EvalR a2 n2 →
351+--         EvalR (.plus a1 a2) (n1 + n2)
352+
353+-- Formally, there is nothing deep about inference rules: they are just an
354+-- informal notation for implications. You can read the rule name on the right
355+-- as the name of the constructor and read each of the linebreaks between the
356+-- premises above the line (as well as the line itself) as `→`. All the
357+-- variables mentioned in the rule (`e1`, `n1`, etc.) are implicitly bound by
358+-- universal quantifiers at the beginning. (Such variables are often called
359+-- *metavariables* to distinguish them from the variables of whatever language
360+-- we are defining. At the moment, our arithmetic expressions don't include
361+-- variables, but we'll soon be adding them.) The whole collection of rules is
362+-- understood as being wrapped, implicitly, in an inductive declaration. In
363+-- informal prose, this is sometimes indicated by saying something like "Let
364+-- `Aexp.EvalR` be the smallest relation closed under the following rules...".
365+
366+-- To summarize: a group of inference rules corresponds to a single inductive
367+-- definition; each rule's name corresponds to a constructor name; above the
368+-- line are the premises, below the line the conclusion; metavariables like
369+-- `e1` and `n1` are implicitly universally quantified. The whole collection
370+-- of rules defines `⇓` as the smallest relation closed under them:
371+
372+-- ---------                (num)
373+--                         num n ⇓ n
374+
375+--                          e1 ⇓ n1
376+--                          e2 ⇓ n2
377+--                     ------------------           (plus)
378+--                     plus e1 e2 ⇓ n1+n2
379+
380+--                          e1 ⇓ n1
381+--                          e2 ⇓ n2
382+--                    -------------------           (minus)
383+--                    minus e1 e2 ⇓ n1-n2
384+
385+--                          e1 ⇓ n1
386+--                          e2 ⇓ n2
387+--                     ------------------           (mult)
388+--                     mult e1 e2 ⇓ n1*n2
389+

400+-- `plus` (E) `num`, `mult`, and `plus`

658---  At this point you may be wondering: which of these styles should I use
659---  by default?
660-
661---  Where the thing being defined is not easy to express as a function,
662---  definitions are often simpler. When both styles are workable,
663---  relational definitions can be more elegant and easier to understand,
664---  and Lean generates useful inversion and induction principles from them.
665---  On the other hand, functional definitions are automatically
666---  deterministic and total -- whereas, for a relation, we must *prove*
667---  these if we need them -- and we can use Lean's computation mechanism to
668---  simplify them during proofs.
669-
670---  In large developments it is common to give a definition in *both*
671---  styles plus a lemma that the two coincide, allowing later proofs to
672---  switch between points of view at will -- exactly what we did above in
673---  `Slang.Aexp.evalR_iff_eval` and `Slang.Bexp.evalR_iff_eval`.

610+-- Note to developers (Michael Hicks  @mwhicks1, before next release):
611+--     The following text seems not quite right to me. First, you can use
612+--     options for partial functions, and that's very natural to do in Lean as
613+--     a monad. Second, and related, monadic functions need not even be
614+--     terminating if the implement the `CCPO` typeclass and are labeled as a
615+--     `partial_fixpoint`. Maybe we don't want to get into the second thing
616+--     here, but failing to mention options (which I think were introduced in
617+--     LF) seems a bit surprising.
618+
619+-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce  @bcpierce00):
620+--     Agreed.
621+
622+-- At this point you may be wondering: which of these styles should I use by
623+-- default?
624+
625+-- Where the thing being defined is not easy to express as a function -- or is
626+-- genuinely *not* a function -- there is no real choice. When both styles are
627+-- workable, relational definitions can be more elegant and easier to
628+-- understand, and Lean generates useful inversion and induction principles
629+-- from them. On the other hand, functional definitions are automatically
630+-- deterministic and total -- whereas, for a relation, we must *prove* these
631+-- if we need them -- and we can use Lean's computation mechanism to simplify
632+-- them during proofs.
633+
634+-- In large developments it is common to give a definition in *both* styles
635+-- plus a lemma that the two coincide, allowing later proofs to switch between
636+-- points of view at will -- exactly what we did above.
