51---  ## Big-step and Small-step Evaluation
52-
53---  The evaluators we saw for Slang were formulated in a "big-step" style:
54---  they specify how a given expression can be evaluated to its final value
55---  "all in one big step":
56-
57---  2 + 2 + 3 * 4 ⇓ 16
58-
59---  This style is simple and natural for many purposes — indeed, Gilles
60---  Kahn, who popularized it, called it *natural semantics*. But there are
61---  some things it does not do well. In particular, it does not give us a
62---  convenient way of talking about *concurrent* programming languages,
63---  where the semantics of a program — the essence of how it behaves —
64---  includes not just which input states get mapped to which output states,
65---  but also the intermediate states that it passes through along the way;
66---  this is crucial, since these states can also be observed by
67---  concurrently executing code.
68-
69---  Another shortcoming of the big-step style is more technical but equally
70---  critical in many situations. Suppose we want to define a variant of our
71---  expression language where a value could be *either* a number *or* a
72---  list of numbers. In the syntax of this extended language, it will be
73---  possible to write strange expressions like `2 + nil`, and our semantics
74---  for arithmetic expressions will then need to say something about how
75---  such expressions behave. One possibility is to maintain the convention
76---  that every arithmetic expression evaluates to some number by choosing
77---  some way of viewing a list as a number — e.g., by specifying that a
78---  list should be interpreted as `0` when it occurs in a context expecting
79---  a number. But this would be a bit of a hack.
80-
81---  A much more natural approach is simply to say that the behavior of the
82---  expression `2 + nil` is *undefined* — i.e., it doesn't evaluate to any
83---  result at all. And we can easily do this: we just have to formulate
84---  `aeval` and `beval` as inductive propositions rather than functions, so
85---  that we can make them partial functions instead of total ones.
86-
87---  Now, however, we encounter a subtlety that will become important once
88---  we move to a full programming language with looping. There, a program
89---  might fail to produce a result for *two quite different reasons*:
90---  either because the execution gets into an infinite loop or because, at
91---  some point, the program tries to do an operation that makes no sense,
92---  such as adding a number to a list, so that none of the evaluation rules
93---  can be applied.
94-
95---  These two outcomes — nontermination vs. getting stuck in an erroneous
96---  configuration — should not be confused. In particular, we want to
97---  *allow* the first (because permitting the possibility of infinite loops
98---  is the price we pay for the convenience of programming with general
99---  looping constructs) but *prevent* the second (which is just wrong), for
100---  example by adding some form of *typechecking* to the language. Indeed,
101---  this will be a major topic of the next chapter, on *types*. As a first
102---  step, we need a way of presenting the semantics that allows us to
103---  distinguish nontermination from erroneous "stuck states."
104-

109---  program, how its atomic steps of computation are performed. In the
110---  *small-step* style, we show how to "reduce" an expression to a simpler
111---  form by performing a single step of computation:

51+-- ## Big-step and Small-step Evaluation
52+
53+-- The evaluators we saw for Slang were formulated in a "big-step" style: they
54+-- specify how a given expression can be evaluated to its final value "all in
55+-- one big step":
56+
57+-- 2 + 2 + 3 * 4 ⇓ 16
58+
59+-- This style is simple and natural for many purposes — indeed, Gilles Kahn,
60+-- who popularized it, called it *natural semantics*. But there are some
61+-- things it does not do well. In particular, it does not give us a convenient
62+-- way of talking about *concurrent* programming languages, where the
63+-- semantics of a program — the essence of how it behaves — includes not just
64+-- which input states get mapped to which output states, but also the
65+-- intermediate states that it passes through along the way; this is crucial,
66+-- since these states can also be observed by concurrently executing code.
67+
68+-- Another shortcoming of the big-step style is more technical but equally
69+-- critical in many situations. Suppose we want to define a variant of our
70+-- expression language where a value could be *either* a number *or* a list of
71+-- numbers. In the syntax of this extended language, it will be possible to
72+-- write strange expressions like `2 + nil`, and our semantics for arithmetic
73+-- expressions will then need to say something about how such expressions
74+-- behave. One possibility is to maintain the convention that every arithmetic
75+-- expression evaluates to some number by choosing some way of viewing a list
76+-- as a number — e.g., by specifying that a list should be interpreted as `0`
77+-- when it occurs in a context expecting a number. But this would be a bit of
78+-- a hack.
79+
80+-- A much more natural approach is simply to say that the behavior of the
81+-- expression `2 + nil` is *undefined* — i.e., it doesn't evaluate to any
82+-- result at all. And we can easily do this: we just have to formulate `aeval`
83+-- and `beval` as inductive propositions rather than functions, so that we can
84+-- make them partial functions instead of total ones.
85+
86+-- Now, however, we encounter a subtlety that will become important once we
87+-- move to a full programming language with looping. There, a program might
88+-- fail to produce a result for *two quite different reasons*: either because
89+-- the execution gets into an infinite loop or because, at some point, the
90+-- program tries to do an operation that makes no sense, such as adding a
91+-- number to a list, so that none of the evaluation rules can be applied.
92+
93+-- These two outcomes — nontermination vs. getting stuck in an erroneous
94+-- configuration — should not be confused. In particular, we want to *allow*
95+-- the first (because permitting the possibility of infinite loops is the
96+-- price we pay for the convenience of programming with general looping
97+-- constructs) but *prevent* the second (which is just wrong), for example by
98+-- adding some form of *typechecking* to the language. Indeed, this will be a
99+-- major topic of the next chapter, on *types*. As a first step, we need a way
100+-- of presenting the semantics that allows us to distinguish nontermination
101+-- from erroneous "stuck states."
102+
103+-- So, for lots of reasons, we'd like to have a finer-grained way of defining
104+-- and reasoning about program behaviors. This is the topic of the present
105+-- chapter. Our goal is to replace the "big-step" `Eval` relation with a
106+-- "small-step" relation that specifies, for a given program, how its atomic
107+-- steps of computation are performed. In the *small-step* style, we show how
108+-- to "reduce" an expression to a simpler form by performing a single step of
109+-- computation:
110+
111+-- 2 + 2 + 3 * 4
112+-- ⟶ 2 + 2 + 12
113+-- ⟶ 4 + 12
114+-- ⟶ 16
115+
116+-- ## A Toy Language
117+
118+-- To save space, we start with an incredibly simple language of just
119+-- constants and addition. (We use single-letter constructors `c` and `p` —
120+-- for Constant and Plus — for brevity.) The same techniques scale up to
121+-- richer languages.

268-

271---  of elements of `X`.

256+-- ## Relations
257+
258+-- We will be working with several different single-step relations, so it is
259+-- helpful to generalize a bit and state a few definitions and theorems about
260+-- relations in general. (The optional chapter `Rel` in *Logical Foundations*
261+-- develops some of these ideas in a bit more detail; reviewing that chapter

263+

265+-- by two elements of `X` — i.e., a proposition about pairs of elements of
266+-- `X`.

278273 def Relation (X : Type) := X → X → Prop
279274 
280---  Our main examples of such relations in this chapter will be the
281---  single-step reduction relation, `⟶`, and its multi-step variant, `⟶*`,
282---  defined below, but there are many other examples — e.g., the "equals,"
283---  "less than," "less than or equal to," and "is the square of" relations
284---  on numbers, and the "prefix of" relation on lists and strings.
285-
286---  One simple property a relation may have is being *deterministic*: like
287---  Slang's big-step evaluation, each element is related to at most one
288---  other.
289-
290---  *Theorem*: For each `t`, there is at most one `t'` such that `t` steps
291---  to `t'`. We prove it by induction on the derivation of the first step.
292-
293---  *Proof sketch*: We show that if `x` steps to both `y₁` and `y₂`, then
294---  `y₁` and `y₂` are equal, by induction on a derivation of `x ⟶ y₁`.
295---  There are several cases, depending on the last rule used in this
296---  derivation and the last rule in the given derivation of `x ⟶ y₂`.
297-
298---  - If both are `plus`, the result is immediate.
299-
300---  - The cases when both derivations end with `plusLeft` or `plusRight`
301---    follow by the induction hypothesis.
302-
303---  - It cannot happen that one is `plus` and the other is
304---    `plusLeft`/`plusRight`, since this would imply that `x` has the form
305---    `p t₁ t₂` where both `t₁` and `t₂` are constants (by `plus`) *and*
306---    one of `t₁` or `t₂` has the form `p _`.
307-
308---  - Similarly, it cannot happen that one is `plusLeft` and the other is
309---    `plusRight`, since this would imply that `x` has the form `p t₁ t₂`
310---    where `t₁` has both the form `p t₁₁ t₁₂` and the form `c n`.
311-

275+-- Our main examples of such relations in this chapter will be the single-step
276+-- reduction relation, `⟶`, and its multi-step variant, `⟶*`, defined below,
277+-- but there are many other examples — e.g., the "equals," "less than," "less
278+-- than or equal to," and "is the square of" relations on numbers, and the
279+-- "prefix of" relation on lists and strings.
280+
281+-- One simple property a relation may have is being *deterministic*: like
282+-- Slang's big-step evaluation, each element is related to at most one other.
283+
284+-- *Theorem*: For each `t`, there is at most one `t'` such that `t` steps to
285+-- `t'`. We prove it by induction on the derivation of the first step.
286+
287+-- *Proof sketch*: We show that if `x` steps to both `y1` and `y2`, then `y1`
288+-- and `y2` are equal, by induction on a derivation of `x ⟶ y1`. There are
289+-- several cases, depending on the last rule used in this derivation and the
290+-- last rule in the given derivation of `x ⟶ y2`.
291+
292+-- - If both are `plus`, the result is immediate.
293+
294+-- - The cases when both derivations end with `plusLeft` or `plusRight` follow
295+--   by the induction hypothesis.
296+
297+-- - It cannot happen that one is `plus` and the other is
298+--   `plusLeft`/`plusRight`, since this would imply that `x` has the form
299+--   `p t1 t2` where both `t1` and `t2` are constants (by `plus`) *and* one of
300+--   `t1` or `t2` has the form `p _`.
301+
302+-- - Similarly, it cannot happen that one is `plusLeft` and the other is
303+--   `plusRight`, since this would imply that `x` has the form `p t1 t2` where
304+--   `t1` has both the form `p t11 t12` and the form `c n`.
305+
306+-- Formally,

309+  ∀ x y1 y2 : X, R x y1 → R x y2 → y1 = y2

338---  ### Values
339-
340---  Next, it will be useful to slightly reformulate the definition of
341---  single-step reduction by stating it in terms of "values."
342-
343---  It can be useful to think of the `⟶` relation as defining an *abstract
344---  machine*:
345-
346---  - At any moment, the *state* of the machine is a term.
347-
348---  - A *step* of the machine is an atomic unit of computation — here, a
349---    single "add" operation.
350-
351---  - The *halting states* of the machine are ones where there is no more
352---    computation to be done.
353-
354---  We can then *execute* a term `t` as follows:
355-
356---  - Take `t` as the starting state of the machine.
357-
358---  - Repeatedly use the `⟶` relation to find a sequence of machine states,
359---    starting with `t`, where each state steps to the next.
360-
361---  - When no more reduction is possible, "read out" the final state of the
362---    machine as the result of execution.
363-
364---  Intuitively, it is clear that the final states of our machine are
365---  always terms of the form `c n` for some `n`. We call such terms
366---  *values*.

332+-- ### Values
333+
334+-- Next, it will be useful to slightly reformulate the definition of
335+-- single-step reduction by stating it in terms of "values."
336+
337+-- It can be useful to think of the `⟶` relation as defining an *abstract
338+-- machine*:
339+
340+-- - At any moment, the *state* of the machine is a term.
341+
342+-- - A *step* of the machine is an atomic unit of computation — here, a single
343+--   "add" operation.
344+
345+-- - The *halting states* of the machine are ones where there is no more
346+--   computation to be done.
347+
348+-- We can then *execute* a term `t` as follows:
349+
350+-- - Take `t` as the starting state of the machine.
351+
352+-- - Repeatedly use the `⟶` relation to find a sequence of machine states,
353+--   starting with `t`, where each state steps to the next.
354+
355+-- - When no more reduction is possible, "read out" the final state of the
356+--   machine as the result of execution.
357+
358+-- Intuitively, it is clear that the final states of our machine are always
359+-- terms of the form `c n` for some `n`. We call such terms *values*.

462---  ### Strong Progress and Normal Forms
463-
464---  The definition of single-step reduction for our toy language is fairly
465---  simple, but for a larger language it would be easy to forget one of the

454+-- ### Strong Progress and Normal Forms
455+
456+-- The definition of single-step reduction for our toy language is fairly
457+-- simple, but for a larger language it would be easy to forget one of the
458+-- rules and accidentally create a situation where some term cannot take a
459+-- step even though it has not been completely reduced to a value. The
460+-- following theorem shows that we did not, in fact, make such a mistake here.
461+
462+-- *Theorem* (*Strong Progress*): If `t` is a term, then either `t` is a value
463+-- or else there exists a term `t'` such that `t ⟶ t'`.
464+
465+-- *Proof*: By induction on `t`.
466+
467+-- - Suppose `t = c n`. Then `t` is a value.
468+
469+-- - Suppose `t = p t1 t2`, where (by the IH) `t1` either is a value or can step
470+--   to some `t1'`, and where `t2` is either a value or can step to some `t2'`.
471+--   We must show `p t1 t2` is either a value or steps to some `t'`.
472+
473+--   - If `t1` and `t2` are both values, then `t` can take a step, by `plus`.
474+
475+--   - If `t1` is a value and `t2` can take a step, then so can `t`, by
476+--     `plusRight`.
477+
478+--   - If `t1` can take a step, then so can `t`, by `plusLeft`.
479+

663+-- ## Multi-Step Reduction
664+
665+-- We've been working so far with the *single-step reduction* relation `⟶`,
666+-- which formalizes the individual steps of an abstract machine for executing
667+-- programs. We can use the same machine to reduce programs to completion — to
668+-- find out what final result they yield. This can be formalized as follows:
669+
670+-- - First, we define a *multi-step reduction relation* `⟶*`, which relates
671+--   terms `t` and `t'` if `t` can reach `t'` by any number (including zero) of
672+--   single reduction steps.
673+
674+-- - Then we define a "result" of a term `t` as a normal form that `t` can reach
675+--   by multi-step reduction.
676+
677+-- Since we'll want to reuse the idea of multi-step reduction many times with
678+-- many different single-step relations, let's define the concept generically.
679+-- Given a relation `R` (e.g., the step relation `⟶`), we define a new
680+-- relation `Multi R`, called the *multi-step closure of `R`*, as follows.
700681 
701682 inductive Multi {X : Type} (R : Relation X) : X → X → Prop where
702683   | refl (x : X) : Multi R x x
703-  | step (x y z : X) (h₁ : R x y) (h₂ : Multi R y z) : Multi R x z

711---  `x` and `y` if
712-

714-
715---  - `R x y`, or
716-
717---  - there is some nonempty sequence `z₁`, `z₂` , ..., `zₙ` such that
718-
719---    `R x₁ z₁,
720---    R z₁ z₂,
721---    ...,
722---    R zₙ y.`
723-
724---  Intuitively, if `R` describes a single-step of computation, then
725---  `z₁ ... zₙ` are the intermediate steps of computation that get us from
726---  `x` to `y`.

713+-- The relation `Multi R` has several crucial properties.
714+
715+-- First, it is obviously *reflexive* (a term can execute to itself by taking
716+-- zero steps). That is just what the `Multi.refl` constructor says, so such a
717+-- goal can always be closed with `exact .refl _`. It comes up often enough
718+-- that it is worth registering the constructor as a *reflexivity lemma*, with
719+-- the `@[refl]` attribute. The `rfl` tactic then closes a zero-step execution

759740     Multi R x y :=
760741   .step x y y h (.refl y)

879+--   using `multistep_congr_1` and `multistep_congr_2` to prove that `p t1 t2`
880+--   reduces in many steps to `t' = c (n1 + n2)`. Finally, `c (n1 + n2)` is a
881+--   value, which is in turn a normal form.

949+-- ### Exercise (3 stars): multistep_of_eval_inf ⭐⭐⭐

951+-- Write a detailed informal version of the proof of `multistep_of_eval`. (A
952+-- paper exercise — there is no Lean proof to fill in here.)
953+
954+-- _Theorem_: for all `t`, `n`, if `t ⇓ n` then `t ⟶* c n`.
955+
956+-- _Proof_: By induction on a derivation of `t ⇓ n`.
957+
958+--   - Suppose the final rule used to show `t ⇓ n` is `const`.  Then `t = c n`.
959+--     We must show `c n ⟶* c n`.  This holds by `refl`.
960+
961+--   - Suppose the final rule used to show `t ⇓ n` is `plus`.  Then
962+--     `t = p t1 t2`, and we know that `t1 ⇓ c n1` and `t2 ⇓ c n2` for some
963+--     `n1` and `n2`, with `n = n1 + n2`.  The IH tells us that `t1 ⟶* c n1` and
964+--     `t2 ⟶* c n2`.  We must show that `p t1 t2 ⟶* c (n1 + n2)`.
965+
966+--     First, `p t1 t2 ⟶* p (c n1) t2` by `multistep_congr_1` and the multistep
967+--     derivation for `t1`.  Observing that `c n1` is a value, we also have
968+--     `p (c n1) t2 ⟶* p (c n1) (c n2)` by `multistep_congr_2` and the multistep
969+--     derivation for `t2`.  It's also easy to see by `plus` that

1355+-- Now put the pieces together: prove that the deterministic and
1356+-- nondeterministic semantics always compute the *same* final result. That is,
1357+-- if `a` fully reduces to `.num n1` under `⟶a` and to `.num n2` under `⟶n`,
1358+-- then `n1 = n2`.
1359+
1360+-- *Hint:* both `.num n1` and `.num n2` are reachable by `⟶n` (use
1361+-- `multi_astep_imp_anstep` for the first), and `⟶n` preserves `eval`.
1362+
1363+theorem astep_anstep_agree (a : Aexp) (n1 n2 : Nat)
1364+    (hd : Multi AStep a (.num n1)) (hn : Multi ANStep a (.num n2)) : n1 = n2 := by
1365+  all_goals
1366+    have e1 := multi_anstep_preserves_eval a (.num n1)
1367+      (multi_astep_imp_anstep a (.num n1) hd)
1368+    have e2 := multi_anstep_preserves_eval a (.num n2) hn
1369+    simp only [Aexp.eval] at e1 e2
1370+    lia
1371+
1372+-- So even though `⟶n` is genuinely nondeterministic, the value it eventually
1373+-- produces is completely determined — and it is the same value the
1374+-- deterministic machine (and the big-step evaluator) computes. This
1375+-- *confluence to a unique result* is exactly the property one wants when
1376+-- reordering or parallelizing the evaluation of pure expressions.

9-
10---  The simply typed lambda-calculus (STLC) is a tiny core calculus
11---  embodying the key concept of *functional abstraction*. This concept
12---  shows up in pretty much every real-world programming language in some
13---  form (functions, procedures, methods, etc.).
14-

16---  formalizing this calculus (syntax, small-step semantics, typing rules)
17---  and its main properties (progress and preservation). The new technical
18---  challenges arise from the mechanisms of *variable binding* and
19---  *substitution*. It will take some work to deal with these.
20-

22---  cube* (also called the *Barendregt Cube*), which visualizes three sets
23---  of features that can be added to its simple core:
24-

29---  polymorphism +--------+  |

55---  much — the definition of the language as well as its theoretical

58---  we'll see how to add more base types, and in later chapters we'll

6+import TS.SFLCompat
7+
8+-- # Stlc: The Simply Typed Lambda-Calculus
9+
10+-- The simply typed lambda-calculus (STLC) is a tiny core calculus embodying
11+-- the key concept of *functional abstraction*. This concept shows up in
12+-- pretty much every real-world programming language in some form (functions,
13+-- procedures, methods, etc.).
14+
15+-- We will follow exactly the same pattern as in the previous chapter when
16+-- formalizing this calculus (syntax, small-step semantics, typing rules) and
17+-- its main properties (progress and preservation). The new technical
18+-- challenges arise from the mechanisms of *variable binding* and
19+-- *substitution*. It will take some work to deal with these.
20+
21+-- The STLC lives in the lower-left front corner of the famous *lambda cube*
22+-- (also called the *Barendregt Cube*), which visualizes three sets of
23+-- features that can be added to its simple core:
24+
25+-- Calculus of Constructions
26+--  type operators +--------+
27+--                /|       /|
28+--               / |      / |
29+-- polymorphism +--------+  |
30+--              |  |     |  |
31+--              |  +-----|--+
32+--              | /      | /
33+--              |/       |/
34+--              +--------+ dependent types
35+--            STLC
36+
37+-- Moving from bottom to top in the cube corresponds to adding *polymorphic
38+-- types* like `∀ α : Type, α → α`. Adding *just* polymorphism gives us the
39+-- famous Girard-Reynolds calculus, System F.
40+
41+-- Moving from front to back corresponds to adding *type operators* like
42+-- `List`.
43+
44+-- Moving from left to right corresponds to adding *dependent types* like
45+-- `∀ n, ArrayOfSize n`.
46+
47+-- The top right corner on the back, which combines all three features, is
48+-- called the *Calculus of Constructions*. First studied by Coquand and Huet,
49+-- it forms the foundation of Lean's logic.
50+
51+-- ## Overview
52+
53+-- The STLC is built on some collection of *base types*: booleans, numbers,
54+-- strings, etc. The exact choice of base types doesn't matter much — the
55+-- definition of the language as well as its theoretical properties work out
56+-- the same no matter what we choose — so for the sake of brevity let's take
57+-- just `Bool` for the moment. In the next chapter we'll see how to add more
58+-- base types, and in later chapters we'll enrich the pure STLC with other
59+-- useful constructs like pairs, records, subtyping, and mutable state.
60+
61+-- Starting from boolean constants and conditionals, we add three things:
62+
63+-- - variables
64+-- - function abstractions
65+-- - application
66+
67+-- This gives us the following collection of abstract syntax constructors
68+-- (written out first in informal BNF notation — we'll formalize it below) for
69+-- STLC terms `t`.
70+
71+-- t ::= x                     (variable)
72+--     | λ x : T . t           (abstraction)
73+--     | t t                   (application)
74+--     | true                  (constant true)
75+--     | false                 (constant false)
76+--     | if t then t else t    (conditional)
77+
78+-- The Greek letter λ ("lambda") in a function abstraction `λx:T. t` is what
79+-- gives the calculus its name. The variable `x` is called the *parameter* to
80+-- the function; the term `t` is its *body*. The annotation `:T` specifies the
81+-- *type* of arguments that the function can be applied to.
82+
83+-- The types of the STLC include `Bool`, which classifies the boolean
84+-- constants `true` and `false` as well as more complex computations that
85+-- yield booleans, plus *arrow types* that classify functions (as is the case
86+-- in Lean).
87+
88+-- T ::= Bool
89+--     | T → T
90+
91+-- Some examples of STLC terms:
92+
93+-- `λx:Bool. x`
94+
95+-- The identity function for booleans.
96+
97+-- `(λx:Bool. x) true`
98+
99+-- The identity function for booleans, applied to the boolean `true`.
100+
101+-- `λx:Bool. if x then false else true`
102+
103+-- The boolean "not" function.
104+
105+-- `λx:Bool. true`
106+
107+-- The constant function that takes every (boolean) argument to `true`.
108+
109+-- `λx:Bool. λy:Bool. x`
110+
111+-- A two-argument function that takes two booleans and returns the first one.
112+
113+-- (As in Lean, a two-argument function in the lambda-calculus is really a
114+-- one-argument function whose body is also a one-argument function.)
115+
116+-- `(λx:Bool. λy:Bool. x) false true`
117+
118+-- A two-argument function that takes two booleans and returns the first one,
119+-- applied to the booleans `false` and `true`.
120+
121+-- (As in Lean, application associates to the left — i.e., this expression is
122+-- parsed as `((λx:Bool. λy:Bool. x) false) true`.)
123+
124+-- `λf:Bool → Bool. f (f true)`
125+
126+-- A higher-order function that takes a *function* `f` (from booleans to
127+-- booleans) as an argument, applies `f` to `true`, and applies `f` again to
128+-- the result.
129+
130+-- `(λf:Bool → Bool. f (f true)) (λx:Bool. false)`
131+
132+-- The same higher-order function, applied to the constantly `false` function.
133+
134+-- The last two examples show, the STLC is a language of *higher-order*
135+-- functions: we can write down functions that take other functions as
136+-- arguments and/or return other functions as results.
137+
138+-- The STLC doesn't provide any primitive syntax for defining *named*
139+-- functions: i.e., all functions are "anonymous." We'll see in chapter
140+-- `MoreStlc` that it is easy to add named functions — indeed, the fundamental
141+-- naming and binding mechanisms are exactly the same.
142+
143+-- Now reconsider our examples, each along with its type:
144+
145+-- - `λx:Bool. x` has type `Bool → Bool`
146+
147+-- - `(λx:Bool. x) true` has type `Bool`
148+
149+-- - `λx:Bool. if x then false else true` has type `Bool → Bool`
150+
151+-- - `λx:Bool. true` has type `Bool → Bool`
152+
153+-- - `λx:Bool. λy:Bool. x` has type `Bool → Bool → Bool` (i.e.,
154+--   `Bool → (Bool → Bool)`)
155+
156+-- - `(λx:Bool. λy:Bool. x) false true` has type `Bool`
157+
158+-- The last two, higher-order examples are left off the list on purpose —
159+-- working out their types is the subject of the quizzes that follow.
160+
161+-- _Quiz:_
162+
163+-- What is the type of the following term?
164+
165+--   λf:Bool → Bool. f (f true)
166+
167+-- (A) `Bool → (Bool → Bool)`
168+
169+-- (B) `(Bool → Bool) → Bool`
170+
171+-- (C) `Bool → Bool`
172+
173+-- (D) `Bool`
174+
175+-- (E) none of the above
176+
177+-- _Quiz:_
178+
179+-- How about the type of this one?
180+
181+--   (λf:Bool → Bool. f (f true)) (λx:Bool. false)
182+
183+-- (A) `Bool → (Bool → Bool)`
184+
185+-- (B) `(Bool → Bool) → Bool`
186+
187+-- (C) `Bool → Bool`
188+
189+-- (D) `Bool`
190+
191+-- (E) none of the above
192+
193+-- ## Syntax
194+
195+-- We next formalize the syntax of the STLC.

217+
218+-- The upshot of this section is that STLC types and terms are both written
219+-- inside one pair of brackets, `<{ … }>`, and that `~e` inside the brackets
220+-- escapes back to an arbitrary Lean expression:
221+
222+-- - `<{ Bool → Bool }>` is a type;
223+
224+-- - `<{ λ x : Bool . x }>` is a term — a bare identifier inside the brackets is
225+--   the object-language variable of that name, so `<{ x }>` is the variable
226+--   `x`;
227+
228+-- - `<{ ~t₁ ~t₂ }>` applies one Lean-level term to another.
229+
230+-- Lean works out from context which of the two a given bracket holds, so the
231+-- same brackets serve for types, for terms, and — when we come to typing —
232+-- for typing judgments too. How that works is in the collapsed blocks below;
233+-- nothing later in the chapter depends on it.
234+
235+-- _Details:_ Notation encoding: types
236+
237+-- The `stlcTy` grammar covers `Bool`, arrows (written `→` or `->`,
238+-- associating to the right), parentheses, and `~e`. A bare identifier other
239+-- than `Bool` is spliced in as a Lean term, so a local `T` — or any Lean
240+-- expression of type `Ty` — can appear directly inside the brackets.
241+
242+-- To extend the grammar, a later chapter adds a `syntax` line to the category
243+-- and a matching `macro_rules` case; that is all it takes to add a new type
244+-- construct.

473+-- ## Operational Semantics
474+
475+-- To define the small-step semantics of STLC terms, we begin, as always, by
476+-- defining the set of values. Next, we define the critical notions of *free
477+-- variables* and *substitution*, which are used in the reduction rule for
478+-- application expressions. And finally we give the small-step relation
479+-- itself.
480+
481+-- ### Values
482+
483+-- To define the values of the STLC, we have a few cases to consider.
484+
485+-- First, for the boolean part of the language, the situation is clear: `true`
486+-- and `false` are the only values. An `if` expression is never a value.
487+
488+-- Second, an application is not a value: it represents a function being
489+-- invoked on some argument, which clearly still has work left to do.
490+
491+-- Third, for abstractions, we have a choice:
492+
493+-- - We can say that `λx:T. t` is a value only when `t` is a value — i.e., only
494+--   if the function's body has been reduced (as much as it can be without
495+--   knowing what argument it is going to be applied to).
496+
497+-- - Or we can say that `λx:T. t` is always a value, no matter whether `t` is
498+--   one or not — in other words, we can say that reduction stops at
499+--   abstractions.
500+
501+-- Our usual way of evaluating expressions in Lean makes the first choice —
502+-- for example,

529+-- Note to developers:
530+--     The Rocq source follows each inductive definition in this chapter with
531+--     a `Hint Constructors … : core`, registering the constructors with
532+--     `auto`; the proofs then lean on `auto`/`eauto` to assemble derivations.

536+
537+-- ### STLC Programs
538+
539+-- Finally, we must consider what constitutes a *complete* program.
540+
541+-- Intuitively, a "complete program" must not refer to any undefined
542+-- variables. We'll see shortly how to define the *free* variables in a STLC
543+-- term. A complete program, then, is one that is *closed* — that is, that
544+-- contains no free variables.
545+
546+-- (Conversely, a term that may contain free variables is often called an
547+-- *open term*.)
548+
549+-- Note to developers (Chris Henson  @chenson2018, before next release):
550+--     Is the "shortly" above setting wrong expectations? Where exactly are we
551+--     defining the free variables in a STLC term? BCP 25: Indeed, we need to
552+--     define "free"!
553+
554+-- Having made the choice not to reduce under abstractions, we don't need to
555+-- worry about whether variables are values, since we'll always be reducing
556+-- programs "from the outside in," and that means the `step` relation will
557+-- always be working with closed terms.
558+
559+-- ### Substitution
560+
561+-- Now we come to the heart of the STLC: the operation of *substituting* one
562+-- term for a variable in another term. This operation is used below to define
563+-- the operational semantics of function application, where we will need to
564+-- substitute the argument term for the function parameter in the function's
565+-- body. For example, we reduce
566+
567+--   (λx:Bool. if x then true else x) false
568+
569+-- to
570+
571+--   if false then true else false
572+
573+-- by substituting `false` for the parameter `x` in the body of the function.
574+
575+-- In general, we need to be able to substitute some given term `s` for
576+-- occurrences of some variable `x` in another term `t`. Informally, this is
577+-- written `[x:=s]t` and pronounced "substitute `s` for `x` in `t`."
578+
579+-- Here are some examples:
580+
581+-- - `[x:=true] (if x then true else false)` yields
582+--   `if true then true else false`
583+
584+-- - `[x:=true] x` yields `true`
585+
586+-- - `[x:=true] (if x then x else y)` yields `if true then true else y`
587+
588+-- - `[x:=true] y` yields `y`
589+
590+-- - `[x:=true] false` yields `false` (vacuous substitution)
591+
592+-- - `[x:=true] (λy:Bool. if y then x else false)` yields
593+--   `λy:Bool. if y then true else false`
594+
595+-- - `[x:=true] (λy:Bool. x)` yields `λy:Bool. true`
596+
597+-- - `[x:=true] (λy:Bool. y)` yields `λy:Bool. y`
598+
599+-- - `[x:=true] (λx:Bool. x)` yields `λx:Bool. x`
600+
601+-- The last example is illuminating: substituting `x` with `true` in
602+-- `λx:Bool. x` does *not* yield `λx:Bool. true`! The reason for this is that
603+-- the `x` in the body of `λx:Bool. x` is *bound* by the abstraction: it is a
604+-- new, local name that just happens to be spelled the same as some global
605+-- name `x`.
606+
607+-- Here is the definition, informally...
608+
609+--   [x:=s]x               = s
610+--   [x:=s]y               = y                     if x ≠ y
611+--   [x:=s](λx:T. t)       = λx:T. t
612+--   [x:=s](λy:T. t)       = λy:T. [x:=s]t         if x ≠ y
613+--   [x:=s](t₁ t₂)         = ([x:=s]t₁) ([x:=s]t₂)
614+--   [x:=s]true            = true
615+--   [x:=s]false           = false
616+--   [x:=s](if t₁ then t₂ else t₃) =
617+--                   if [x:=s]t₁ then [x:=s]t₂ else [x:=s]t₃
618+
619+-- ... and formally:

724-
725---  What is the result of the following substitution?
726-
727---    [x:=s](λy:T₁. x (λx:T₂. x))
728-
729---  (1) `(λy:T₁. x (λx:T₂. x))`
730-
731---  (2) `(λy:T₁. s (λx:T₂. s))`
732-
733---  (3) `(λy:T₁. s (λx:T₂. x))`
734-
735---  (4) none of the above
736-
737---  *Technical note*: Substitution becomes trickier to define if we
738---  consider the case where `s`, the term being substituted for a variable
739---  in some other term, may itself contain free variables. We say that `s`
740---  is an *open* term.
741-
742---  Here is an example. Using the above definition to substitute the open
743---  term
744-
745---    s = λx:Bool. r
746-
747---  (where `r` is a *free* reference to some global resource) for the free
748---  variable `z` in the term
749-
750---    t = λr:Bool. z
751-
752---  where `r` is a bound variable, we would get
753-
754---    λr:Bool. λx:Bool. r
755-
756---  where the free reference to `r` in `s` has been "captured" by the
757---  binder at the beginning of `t`.
758-
759---  Why would this be bad? Because it violates the principle that the names
760---  of bound variables do not matter. For example, if we rename the bound
761---  variable in `t`, e.g., let
762-
763---    t' = λw:Bool. z
764-
765---  then `[z:=s]t'` is
766-
767---    λw:Bool. λx:Bool. r
768-
769---  which does not behave the same as the substituting in the original `t`:
770-
771---    [z:=s]t = λr:Bool. λx:Bool. r
772-
773---  That is, renaming a bound variable in `t` would change how `t` behaves
774---  under our simple substitution. So substitution gets more complicated in
775---  that setting, but fortunately we don't have that problem in our STLC
776---  variant.
777-
778---  Fortunately, since we are only interested here in defining the `step`
779---  relation on *closed* terms (i.e., terms like `λx:Bool. x` that include
780---  binders for all of the variables they mention), we can sidestep this
781---  extra complexity, but it must be dealt with when formalizing richer
782---  languages.

698+
699+-- (1) `(λy:T₁. x (λx:T₂. x))`
700+
701+-- (2) `(λy:T₁. s (λx:T₂. s))`
702+
703+-- (3) `(λy:T₁. s (λx:T₂. x))`
704+
705+-- (4) none of the above
706+
707+-- *Technical note*: Substitution becomes trickier to define if we consider
708+-- the case where `s`, the term being substituted for a variable in some other
709+-- term, may itself contain free variables. We say that `s` is an *open* term.
710+
711+-- Here is an example. Using the above definition to substitute the open term
712+
713+--   s = λx:Bool. r
714+
715+-- (where `r` is a *free* reference to some global resource) for the free
716+-- variable `z` in the term
717+
718+--   t = λr:Bool. z
719+
720+-- where `r` is a bound variable, we would get
721+
722+--   λr:Bool. λx:Bool. r
723+
724+-- where the free reference to `r` in `s` has been "captured" by the binder at
725+-- the beginning of `t`.
726+
727+-- Why would this be bad? Because it violates the principle that the names of
728+-- bound variables do not matter. For example, if we rename the bound variable
729+-- in `t`, e.g., let
730+
731+--   t' = λw:Bool. z
732+
733+-- then `[z:=s]t'` is
734+
735+--   λw:Bool. λx:Bool. r
736+
737+-- which does not behave the same as the substituting in the original `t`:
738+
739+--   [z:=s]t = λr:Bool. λx:Bool. r
740+
741+-- That is, renaming a bound variable in `t` would change how `t` behaves
742+-- under our simple substitution. So substitution gets more complicated in
743+-- that setting, but fortunately we don't have that problem in our STLC
744+-- variant.
745+
746+-- Fortunately, since we are only interested here in defining the `step`
747+-- relation on *closed* terms (i.e., terms like `λx:Bool. x` that include
748+-- binders for all of the variables they mention), we can sidestep this extra
749+-- complexity, but it must be dealt with when formalizing richer languages.
750+

805+-- ### Reduction
806+
807+-- The small-step reduction relation for STLC now follows the same pattern as
808+-- the ones we have seen before. Intuitively, to reduce a function
809+-- application, we first reduce its left-hand side (the function) until it
810+-- becomes an abstraction; then we reduce its right-hand side (the argument)
811+-- until it is also a value; and finally we substitute the argument for the
812+-- bound variable in the body of the abstraction. This last rule, written
813+-- informally as
814+
815+--   (λx:T. t₁₂) v₂ ⟶ [x:=v₂] t₁₂
816+
817+-- is traditionally called *beta-reduction*.
818+
819+-- v.IsValue
820+--                        -----------------------      (appAbs)
821+--                         (λx:T. t) v ⟶ [x:=v]t
822+
823+--                               t₁ ⟶ t₁'
824+--                           ----------------          (app1)
825+--                            t₁ t₂ ⟶ t₁' t₂
826+
827+--                               v.IsValue
828+--                               t₂ ⟶ t₂'
829+--                           ----------------          (app2)
830+--                            v₁ t₂ ⟶ v₁ t₂'
831+
832+-- ... plus the usual rules for conditionals:
833+
834+-- --------------------------------                (ifTrue)
835+--                    (if true then t₁ else t₂) ⟶ t₁
836+
837+--                   ---------------------------------               (ifFalse)
838+--                    (if false then t₁ else t₂) ⟶ t₂
839+
840+--                               t₁ ⟶ t₁'
841+--         ----------------------------------------------------      (ifStep)
842+--          (if t₁ then t₂ else t₃) ⟶ (if t₁' then t₂ else t₃)
843+
844+-- This is *call by value* reduction: to reduce an application `(t₁ t₂)`, we
845+
846+-- - first reduce `t₁` to a value: a function `λx:T. t`
847+
848+-- - then reduce the argument `t₂` to a value `v`
849+
850+-- - then reduce the application itself by substituting `v` for the bound
851+--   variable `x` in the body `t`.
852+

1104---  ### Contexts

1106---  Although we are primarily interested in the binary relation `⊢ t ⦂ T`,
1107---  relating a closed term `t` to its type `T`, we need to generalize a bit
1108---  to make the definitions work.

1110---  Consider checking that `λx:T₁₁. t₁₂` has type `T₁₁ → T₁₂`. Intuitively,
1111---  we need to check that `t₁₂` has type `T₁₂`. However, we have removed
1112---  the binder `λx`, so `x` may occur free in `t₁₂` (that is, `t₁₂` may be
1113---  *open*). While checking that `t₁₂` has type `T₁₂`, we must remember
1114---  that `x` has type `T₁₁`, in order to deal with these free occurrences
1115---  of `x`. Similarly, `t₁₂` itself could contain abstractions, and
1116---  typechecking their bodies could require looking up the declared types
1117---  of yet more free variables.
1118-

1121---  occur free in a term — that is, Γ is a partial map from variables to
1122---  types.

1072+
1073+-- Although we are primarily interested in the binary relation `⊢ t ⦂ T`,
1074+-- relating a closed term `t` to its type `T`, we need to generalize a bit to
1075+-- make the definitions work.
1076+
1077+-- Consider checking that `λx:T₁₁. t₁₂` has type `T₁₁ → T₁₂`. Intuitively, we
1078+-- need to check that `t₁₂` has type `T₁₂`. However, we have removed the
1079+-- binder `λx`, so `x` may occur free in `t₁₂` (that is, `t₁₂` may be *open*).
1080+-- While checking that `t₁₂` has type `T₁₂`, we must remember that `x` has
1081+-- type `T₁₁`, in order to deal with these free occurrences of `x`. Similarly,
1082+-- `t₁₂` itself could contain abstractions, and typechecking their bodies
1083+-- could require looking up the declared types of yet more free variables.
1084+
1085+-- To keep track of all this, we add a third element to the relation, a
1086+-- *typing context* `Γ`, which records the types of the variables that may
1087+-- occur free in a term — that is, Γ is a partial map from variables to types.
1088+
1089+-- The new *typing judgment* is written `Γ ⊢ t ⦂ T` and informally read as
1090+-- "term `t` has type `T`, given the types of free variables in `t` as
1091+-- specified by `Γ`".
1092+
1093+-- We'll also write `x ↦ T ; Γ` for "update the partial map `Γ` so that it
1094+-- maps `x` to `T`," following the notation from the `Typeclasses` chapter.
1095+
1096+-- With these refinements, we are ready to give informal and formal
1097+-- specifications of the typing relation.

31+-- In this chapter, we develop the fundamental theory of the Simply Typed
32+-- Lambda Calculus — in particular, the type safety theorem.
33+
34+-- We pick up where the Stlc chapter left off, so everything below lives in
35+-- the same namespace as the definitions it is about.
36+
37+namespace Stlc
38+
39+-- ## Canonical Forms
40+
41+-- As we saw for the very simple language in the Types chapter, the first step
42+-- in establishing basic properties of reduction and types is to identify the
43+-- possible *canonical forms* (i.e., well-typed values) belonging to each
44+-- type. For `Bool`, these are again the boolean values `true` and `false`;
45+-- for arrow types, they are lambda-abstractions.
46+
47+-- Formally, we will need these lemmas only for terms that are not only well
48+-- typed but *closed* — i.e., well typed in the empty context.
49+
50+theorem canonical_forms_bool (t : Tm) (hT : <{ ∅ ⊢ ~t ⦂ Bool }>) (hv : t.IsValue) :
51+    t = <{ true }> ∨ t = <{ false }> := by
52+  cases hv with
53+  | abs x T t₁ => cases hT
54+  | tru => exact .inl rfl
55+  | fls => exact .inr rfl
56+
57+theorem canonical_forms_fun (t : Tm) (T₁ T₂ : Ty)
58+    (hT : <{ ∅ ⊢ ~t ⦂ ~T₁ → ~T₂ }>) (hv : t.IsValue) :
59+    ∃ x u, t = <{ λ ~x : ~T₁ . ~u }> := by
60+  cases hv with
61+  | abs x T t₁ => cases hT with | abs _ _ _ _ _ _ => exact ⟨x, t₁, rfl⟩
62+  | tru => cases hT
63+  | fls => cases hT
64+
65+-- ## Progress
66+
67+-- The *progress* theorem tells us that closed, well-typed terms are not
68+-- stuck: either a well-typed term is a value, or it can take a reduction
69+-- step. The proof is a relatively straightforward extension of the progress
70+-- proof we saw in the Types chapter. We give the proof in English first, then
71+-- the formal version.
72+
73+theorem progress (t : Tm) (T : Ty) (hT : <{ ∅ ⊢ ~t ⦂ ~T }>) :
74+    t.IsValue ∨ ∃ t', t ⟶ t' := by
75+  generalize hΓ : (∅ : Context) = Γ at hT
76+  induction hT with
77+  | var Γ x T₁ h =>
78+    subst hΓ
79+    -- Contradictory: variables cannot be typed in an empty context.
80+    rw [PartialMap.apply_empty] at h
81+    cases h
82+  | abs => exact .inl (.abs ..)
83+  | tru => exact .inl .tru
84+  | fls => exact .inl .fls
85+  | app Γ T₁ T₂ t₁ t₂ h₁ h₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
86+    -- `t = t₁ t₂`.  Proceed by cases on whether `t₁` is a value or steps.
87+    right
88+    cases ih₁ hΓ with
89+    | inl hv₁ =>
90+      cases ih₂ hΓ with
91+      | inl hv₂ =>
92+        obtain ⟨x, u, rfl⟩ := canonical_forms_fun t₁ _ _ (hΓ ▸ h₁) hv₁
93+        exact ⟨<{ [~x := ~t₂] ~u }>, .appAbs x T₂ u t₂ hv₂⟩
94+      | inr hs₂ => obtain ⟨t₂', h⟩ := hs₂; exact ⟨<{ ~t₁ ~t₂' }>, .app2 t₁ t₂ t₂' hv₁ h⟩
95+    | inr hs₁ => obtain ⟨t₁', h⟩ := hs₁; exact ⟨<{ ~t₁' ~t₂ }>, .app1 t₁ t₁' t₂ h⟩
96+  | ite Γ t₁ t₂ t₃ T₁ h₁ h₂ h₃ ih₁ ih₂ ih₃ =>
97+    right
98+    cases ih₁ hΓ with
99+    | inl hv₁ =>
100+      cases canonical_forms_bool t₁ (hΓ ▸ h₁) hv₁ with
101+      | inl he => subst he; exact ⟨t₂, .ifTrue t₂ t₃⟩
102+      | inr he => subst he; exact ⟨t₃, .ifFalse t₂ t₃⟩
103+    | inr hs₁ =>
104+      obtain ⟨t₁', h⟩ := hs₁
105+      exact ⟨<{ if ~t₁' then ~t₂ else ~t₃ }>, .ifStep t₁ t₁' t₂ t₃ h⟩
106+
107+-- *Proof*: By induction on the derivation of `⊢ t ⦂ T`.
108+
109+-- - The last rule of the derivation cannot be `HasType.var`, since a variable
110+--   is never well typed in an empty context.
111+
112+-- - The `HasType.tru`, `HasType.fls`, and `HasType.abs` cases are trivial,
113+--   since in each of these cases we can see by inspecting the rule that `t` is
114+--   a value.
115+
116+-- - If the last rule of the derivation is `HasType.app`, then `t` has the form
117+--   `t₁ t₂` for some `t₁` and `t₂`, where `⊢ t₁ ⦂ T₂ → T` and `⊢ t₂ ⦂ T₂` for
118+--   some type `T₂`. The induction hypothesis for the first subderivation says
119+--   that either `t₁` is a value or else it can take a reduction step.
120+
121+--   - If `t₁` is a value, then consider `t₂`, which by the induction hypothesis
122+--     for the second subderivation must also either be a value or take a step.
123+
124+--     - Suppose `t₂` is a value. Since `t₁` is a value with an arrow type, it must
125+--       be a lambda abstraction; hence `t₁ t₂` can take a step by `Step.appAbs`.
126+
127+--     - Otherwise, `t₂` can take a step, and hence so can `t₁ t₂` by `Step.app2`.
128+
129+--   - If `t₁` can take a step, then so can `t₁ t₂` by `Step.app1`.
130+
131+-- - If the last rule of the derivation is `HasType.ite`, then
132+--   `t = if t₁ then t₂ else t₃`, where `t₁` has type `Bool`. The first IH says
133+--   that `t₁` either is a value or takes a step.
134+
135+--   - If `t₁` is a value, then since it has type `Bool` it must be either `true`
136+--     or `false`. If it is `true`, then `t` steps to `t₂`; otherwise it steps to
137+--     `t₃`.
138+
139+--   - Otherwise, `t₁` takes a step, and therefore so does `t` (by `Step.ifStep`).
140+
141+-- ### Exercise (3 stars): progress_from_term_ind (Advanced) ⭐⭐⭐
142+
143+-- Show that progress can also be proved by induction on terms instead of
144+-- induction on typing derivations.
145+
146+theorem progress' (t : Tm) (T : Ty) (hT : <{ ∅ ⊢ ~t ⦂ ~T }>) :
147+    t.IsValue ∨ ∃ t', t ⟶ t' := by
148+  all_goals
149+    induction t generalizing T with
150+    | var x =>
151+      cases hT with
152+      | var _ _ _ h => rw [PartialMap.apply_empty] at h; cases h
153+    | abs x T₂ t₁ _ => exact .inl (.abs ..)
154+    | tru => exact .inl .tru
155+    | fls => exact .inl .fls
156+    | app t₁ t₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
157+      right
158+      cases hT with
159+      | app _ _ T₂ _ _ h₁ h₂ =>
160+        cases ih₁ _ h₁ with
161+        | inl hv₁ =>
162+          obtain ⟨x, u, rfl⟩ := canonical_forms_fun t₁ _ _ h₁ hv₁
163+          cases ih₂ _ h₂ with
164+          | inl hv₂ => exact ⟨<{ [~x := ~t₂] ~u }>, .appAbs x T₂ u t₂ hv₂⟩
165+          | inr hs₂ => obtain ⟨t₂', h⟩ := hs₂; exact ⟨_, .app2 _ t₂ t₂' hv₁ h⟩
166+        | inr hs₁ => obtain ⟨t₁', h⟩ := hs₁; exact ⟨_, .app1 t₁ t₁' t₂ h⟩
167+    | ite t₁ t₂ t₃ ih₁ ih₂ ih₃ =>
168+      right
169+      cases hT with
170+      | ite _ _ _ _ _ h₁ h₂ h₃ =>
171+        cases ih₁ _ h₁ with
172+        | inl hv₁ =>
173+          cases canonical_forms_bool t₁ h₁ hv₁ with
174+          | inl he => subst he; exact ⟨t₂, .ifTrue t₂ t₃⟩
175+          | inr he => subst he; exact ⟨t₃, .ifFalse t₂ t₃⟩
176+        | inr hs₁ => obtain ⟨t₁', h⟩ := hs₁; exact ⟨_, .ifStep t₁ t₁' t₂ t₃ h⟩
177+
178+-- ## Preservation
179+
180+-- The other half of the type soundness property is the preservation of types
181+-- during reduction. For this part, we'll need to develop some technical
182+-- machinery for reasoning about variables and substitution. Working from top
183+-- to bottom (from the high-level property we are actually interested in to
184+-- the lowest-level technical lemmas that are needed by various cases of the
185+-- more interesting proofs), the story goes like this:
186+
187+-- - The *preservation theorem* is proved by induction on a typing derivation
188+--   and case analysis on the step relation, pretty much as we did in the Types
189+--   chapter. The one case that is significantly different is the one for the
190+--   `Step.appAbs` rule, whose definition uses the substitution operation. To
191+--   see that this step preserves typing, we need to know that the substitution
192+--   itself does. So we prove a...
193+
194+-- - *substitution lemma*, stating that substituting a (closed, well-typed) term
195+--   `s` for a variable `x` in a term `t` preserves the type of `t`. The proof
196+--   goes by induction on the form of `t` and requires looking at all the
197+--   different cases in the definition of substitition. This time, for the
198+--   variables case, we discover that we need to deduce from the fact that a
199+--   term `s` has type S in the empty context the fact that `s` has type S in
200+--   every context. For this we prove a...
201+
202+-- - *weakening* lemma, showing that typing is preserved under "extensions" to
203+--   the context `Γ`.
204+
205+-- To make Lean happy, though, we need to formalize the story in the opposite
206+-- order, starting with weakening...
207+
208+-- ### The Weakening Lemma
209+
210+-- First, we show that typing is preserved under "extensions" to the context
211+-- `Γ`. (Recall map inclusion, `Γ ⊆ Γ'`, from the `Typeclasses` chapter.)
212+
213+theorem weakening (Γ Γ' : Context) (t : Tm) (T : Ty)
214+    (hi : Γ ⊆ Γ') (hT : <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~t ⦂ ~T }>) : <{ ~Γ' ⊢ ~t ⦂ ~T }> := by
215+  induction hT generalizing Γ' with
216+  | var _ x _ h => exact .var _ x _ (hi x _ h)
217+  | abs _ x _ _ _ _ ih => exact .abs _ x _ _ _ (ih _ (PartialMap.update_subset _ _ _ _ hi))
218+  | app _ _ _ _ _ _ _ ih₁ ih₂ => exact .app _ _ _ _ _ (ih₁ _ hi) (ih₂ _ hi)
219+  | tru => exact .tru _
220+  | fls => exact .fls _
221+  | ite _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ ih₁ ih₂ ih₃ => exact .ite _ _ _ _ _ (ih₁ _ hi) (ih₂ _ hi) (ih₃ _ hi)
222+
223+-- The following simple corollary is what we actually need below.
224+
225+theorem weakening_empty (Γ : Context) (t : Tm) (T : Ty) (hT : <{ ∅ ⊢ ~t ⦂ ~T }>) :
226+    <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~t ⦂ ~T }> :=
227+  weakening _ _ _ _
228+    (fun x T h => by rw [PartialMap.apply_empty] at h; cases h) hT
229+
230+-- ### The Substitution Lemma
231+
232+-- Now we come to the conceptual heart of the proof that reduction preserves
233+-- types — namely, the observation that *substitution* preserves types.
234+
235+-- Formally, the so-called *substitution lemma* says this: Suppose we have a
236+-- term `t` with a free variable `x`, and suppose we've assigned a type `T` to
237+-- `t` under the assumption that `x` has some type `U`. Also, suppose that we
238+-- have some other term `v` and that we've shown that `v` has type `U`. Then,
239+-- since `v` satisfies the assumption we made about `x` when typing `t`, we
240+-- can substitute `v` for each of the occurrences of `x` in `t` and obtain a
241+-- new term that still has type `T`.
242+
243+theorem substitution_preserves_typing (Γ : Context) (x : String) (U : Ty)
244+    (t v : Tm) (T : Ty)
245+    (hT : <{ ~x ↦ ~U ; ~Γ ⊢ ~t ⦂ ~T }>) (hv : <{ ∅ ⊢ ~v ⦂ ~U }>) :
246+    <{ ~Γ ⊢ [~x := ~v] ~t ⦂ ~T }> := by
247+  -- By induction on `t`; in each case we get at the derivation of `hT`.
248+  induction t generalizing Γ T with
249+  | var y =>
250+    cases hT with
251+    | var _ _ _ h =>
252+      by_cases hxy : x = y
253+      · subst hxy
254+        rw [PartialMap.update_eq] at h
255+        rw [subst_var_eq]
256+        have hUT : U = T := Option.some.inj h
257+        subst hUT
258+        exact weakening_empty _ _ _ hv
259+      · rw [PartialMap.update_neq _ _ _ hxy] at h
260+        rw [subst_var_ne _ _ _ hxy]
261+        exact .var _ y _ h
262+  | app t₁ t₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
263+    cases hT with
264+    | app _ _ _ _ _ h₁ h₂ => rw [subst_app]; exact .app _ _ _ _ _ (ih₁ _ _ h₁) (ih₂ _ _ h₂)
265+  | abs y S t₁ ih =>
266+    cases hT with
267+    | abs _ _ _ _ _ h =>
268+      by_cases hxy : x = y
269+      · subst hxy
270+        rw [subst_abs_eq]
271+        rw [PartialMap.update_shadow] at h
272+        exact .abs _ _ _ _ _ h
273+      · rw [subst_abs_ne _ _ _ _ _ hxy]
274+        rw [PartialMap.update_permute _ _ _ _ _ (Ne.symm hxy)] at h
275+        exact .abs _ _ _ _ _ (ih _ _ h)
276+  | tru => cases hT with | tru => rw [subst_tru]; exact .tru _
277+  | fls => cases hT with | fls => rw [subst_fls]; exact .fls _
278+  | ite c t e ihc iht ihe =>
279+    cases hT with
280+    | ite _ _ _ _ _ h₁ h₂ h₃ =>
281+      rw [subst_ite]
282+      exact .ite _ _ _ _ _ (ihc _ _ h₁) (iht _ _ h₂) (ihe _ _ h₃)
283+
284+-- The substitution lemma can be viewed as a kind of "commutation property."
285+-- Intuitively, it says that substitution and typing can be done in either
286+-- order: we can either assign types to the terms `t` and `v` separately
287+-- (under suitable contexts) and then combine them using substitution, or we
288+-- can substitute first and then assign a type to ` `x:=v` t`; the result is
289+-- the same either way.
290+
291+-- *Proof*: We show, by induction on `t`, that for all `T` and `Γ`, if
292+-- `x ↦ U; Γ ⊢ t ⦂ T` and `⊢ v ⦂ U`, then `Γ ⊢ [x:=v]t ⦂ T`.
293+
294+-- - If `t` is a variable there are two cases to consider, depending on whether
295+--   `t` is `x` or some other variable.
296+
297+--   - If `t = x`, then from the fact that `x ↦ U; Γ ⊢ x ⦂ T` we conclude that
298+--     `U = T`. We must show that `[x:=v]x = v` has type `T` under `Γ`, given the
299+--     assumption that `v` has type `U = T` under the empty context. This follows
300+--     from the weakening lemma.
301+
302+--   - If `t` is some variable `y` that is not equal to `x`, then we need only
303+--     note that `y` has the same type under `x ↦ U; Γ` as under `Γ`.
304+
305+-- - If `t` is an abstraction `λy:S. t₀`, then `T = S→T₁` and the IH tells us,
306+--   for all `Γ'` and `T₀`, that if `x ↦ U; Γ' ⊢ t₀ ⦂ T₀`, then
307+--   `Γ' ⊢ [x:=v]t₀ ⦂ T₀`. Moreover, by inspecting the typing rules we see it
308+--   must be the case that `y ↦ S; x ↦ U; Γ ⊢ t₀ ⦂ T₁`.
309+
310+--   The substitution in the conclusion behaves differently depending on whether
311+--   `x` and `y` are the same variable.
312+
313+--   First, suppose `x = y`. Then, by the definition of substitution,
314+--   `[x:=v]t = t`, so we just need to show `Γ ⊢ t ⦂ T`. Using `HasType.abs`, we
315+--   need to show that `y ↦ S; Γ ⊢ t₀ ⦂ T₁`. But we know
316+--   `y ↦ S; x ↦ U; Γ ⊢ t₀ ⦂ T₁`, and the claim follows since `x = y`.
317+
318+--   Second, suppose `x <> y`. Again, using `HasType.abs`, we need to show that
319+--   `y ↦ S; Γ ⊢ [x:=v]t₀ ⦂ T₁`. Since `x <> y`, we have
320+--   `y ↦ S; x ↦ U; Γ = x ↦ U; y ↦ S; Γ`. So we have
321+--   `x ↦ U; y ↦ S; Γ ⊢ t₀ ⦂ T₁`. Then, the the IH applies (taking
322+--   `Γ' = y ↦ S; Γ`), giving us `y ↦ S; Γ ⊢ [x:=v]t₀ ⦂ T₁`, as required.
323+
324+-- - If `t` is an application `t₁ t₂`, the result follows straightforwardly from
325+--   the definition of substitution and the induction hypotheses.
326+
327+-- - The remaining cases are similar to the application case.
328+
329+-- One technical subtlety in the statement of the above lemma is that we
330+-- assume `v` has type `U` in the *empty* context — in other words, we assume
331+-- `v` is closed. (Since we are using a simple definition of substition that
332+-- is not capture-avoiding, it doesn't make sense to substitute non-closed
333+-- terms into other terms. Fortunately, closed terms are all we need!)
334+
335+-- ### Exercise (3 stars): substitution_preserves_typing_from_typing_ind (Advanced) ⭐⭐⭐
336+
337+-- Show that substitution*preserves*typing can also be proved by induction on
338+-- typing derivations instead of induction on terms.
339+
340+theorem substitution_preserves_typing_from_typing_ind (Γ : Context) (x : String) (U : Ty)
341+    (t v : Tm) (T : Ty)
342+    (hT : <{ ~x ↦ ~U ; ~Γ ⊢ ~t ⦂ ~T }>) (hv : <{ ∅ ⊢ ~v ⦂ ~U }>) :
343+    <{ ~Γ ⊢ [~x := ~v] ~t ⦂ ~T }> := by
344+  all_goals
345+    generalize hΓ : (x →ₚ U ; Γ) = Γ₀ at hT
346+    induction hT generalizing Γ with
347+    | var _ y T₁ h =>
348+      subst hΓ
349+      by_cases hxy : x = y
350+      · subst hxy
351+        rw [PartialMap.update_eq] at h
352+        rw [subst_var_eq]
353+        have hUT : U = T₁ := Option.some.inj h
354+        subst hUT
355+        exact weakening_empty _ _ _ hv
356+      · rw [PartialMap.update_neq _ _ _ hxy] at h
357+        rw [subst_var_ne _ _ _ hxy]
358+        exact .var _ y _ h
359+    | abs _ y _ _ _ hb ih =>
360+      subst hΓ
361+      by_cases hxy : x = y
362+      · subst hxy
363+        rw [subst_abs_eq]
364+        rw [PartialMap.update_shadow] at hb
365+        exact .abs _ _ _ _ _ hb
366+      · rw [subst_abs_ne _ _ _ _ _ hxy]
367+        exact .abs _ _ _ _ _ (ih _ (PartialMap.update_permute _ _ _ _ _ hxy))
368+    | app _ _ _ _ _ _ _ ih₁ ih₂ =>
369+      rw [subst_app]; exact .app _ _ _ _ _ (ih₁ _ hΓ) (ih₂ _ hΓ)
370+    | tru => rw [subst_tru]; exact .tru _
371+    | fls => rw [subst_fls]; exact .fls _
372+    | ite _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ ih₁ ih₂ ih₃ =>
373+      rw [subst_ite]; exact .ite _ _ _ _ _ (ih₁ _ hΓ) (ih₂ _ hΓ) (ih₃ _ hΓ)
374+
375+-- ### Main Theorem
376+
377+-- We now have the ingredients we need to prove preservation: if a closed,
378+-- well-typed term `t` has type `T` and takes a step to `t'`, then `t'` is
379+-- also a closed term with type `T`. In other words, the small-step reduction
380+-- relation preserves types.
381+
382+theorem preservation (t t' : Tm) (T : Ty)
383+    (hT : <{ ∅ ⊢ ~t ⦂ ~T }>) (hs : t ⟶ t') : <{ ∅ ⊢ ~t' ⦂ ~T }> := by
384+  generalize hΓ : (∅ : Context) = Γ at hT
385+  induction hT generalizing t' with
386+  | var => cases hs
387+  | abs => cases hs
388+  | tru => cases hs
389+  | fls => cases hs
390+  | app Γ T₁ T₂ t₁ t₂ h₁ h₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
391+    subst hΓ
392+    cases hs with
393+    | appAbs _ _ _ _ _ =>
394+      -- The one interesting case: the desired result is the substitution lemma.
395+      cases h₁ with
396+      | abs _ _ _ _ _ hb => exact substitution_preserves_typing _ _ _ _ _ _ hb h₂
397+    | app1 _ t₁' _ h => exact .app _ _ _ _ _ (ih₁ t₁' h rfl) h₂
398+    | app2 _ _ t₂' _ h => exact .app _ _ _ _ _ h₁ (ih₂ t₂' h rfl)
399+  | ite Γ t₁ t₂ t₃ T₁ h₁ h₂ h₃ ih₁ ih₂ ih₃ =>
400+    subst hΓ
401+    cases hs with
402+    | ifTrue => exact h₂
403+    | ifFalse => exact h₃
404+    | ifStep _ t₁' _ _ h => exact .ite _ _ _ _ _ (ih₁ t₁' h rfl) h₂ h₃
405+
406+-- *Proof*: By induction on the derivation of `⊢ t ⦂ T`.
407+
408+-- - We can immediately rule out `HasType.var`, `HasType.abs`, `HasType.tru`,
409+--   and `HasType.fls` as final rules in the derivation, since in each of these
410+--   cases `t` cannot take a step.
411+
412+-- - If the last rule in the derivation is `HasType.app`, then `t = t₁ t₂`, and
413+--   there are subderivations showing that `⊢ t₁ ⦂ T₂→T` and `⊢ t₂ ⦂ T₂` plus
414+--   two induction hypotheses: (1) `t₁ ⟶ t₁'` implies `⊢ t₁' ⦂ T₂→T` and (2)
415+--   `t₂ ⟶ t₂'` implies `⊢ t₂' ⦂ T₂`. There are now three subcases to consider,
416+--   one for each rule that could be used to show that `t₁ t₂` takes a step to
417+--   `t'`.
418+
419+--   - If `t₁ t₂` takes a step by `Step.app1`, with `t₁` stepping to `t₁'`, then,
420+--     by the first IH, `t₁'` has the same type as `t₁` (`⊢ t₁' ⦂ T₂→T`), and
421+--     hence by `HasType.app` `t₁' t₂` has type `T`.
422+
423+--   - The `Step.app2` case is similar, using the second IH.
424+
425+--   - If `t₁ t₂` takes a step by `Step.appAbs`, then `t₁ = λx:T₀. t₀` and `t₁ t₂`
426+--     steps to `[x0:=t₂]t₀`; the desired result now follows from the substitution
427+--     lemma.
428+
429+-- - If the last rule in the derivation is `HasType.ite`, then
430+--   `t = if t₁ then t₂ else t₃`, with `⊢ t₁ ⦂ Bool`, `⊢ t₂ ⦂ T₁`, and
431+--   `⊢ t₃ ⦂ T₁`, and with three induction hypotheses: (1) `t₁ ⟶ t₁'` implies
432+--   `⊢ t₁' ⦂ Bool`, (2) `t₂ ⟶ t₂'` implies `⊢ t₂' ⦂ T₁`, and (3) `t₃ ⟶ t₃'`
433+--   implies `⊢ t₃' ⦂ T₁`.
434+
435+--   There are again three subcases to consider, depending on how `t` steps.
436+
437+--   - If `t` steps to `t₂` or `t₃` by `Step.ifTrue` or `Step.ifFalse`, the result
438+--     is immediate, since `t₂` and `t₃` have the same type as `t`.
439+
440+--   - Otherwise, `t` steps by `Step.ifStep`, and the desired conclusion follows
441+--     directly from the first induction hypothesis.
442+
443+-- ### Exercise (2 stars): subject_expansion_stlc (manually graded) ⭐⭐
444+
445+-- An exercise in the Types chapter asked about the *subject expansion*
446+-- property for the simple language of arithmetic and boolean expressions.
447+-- This property did not hold for that language, and it also fails for STLC.
448+-- That is, it is not always the case that, if `t ⟶ t'` and `empty ⊢ t' ⦂ T`,
449+-- then `empty ⊢ t ⦂ T`. Show this by giving a counter-example that does *not
450+-- involve conditionals*.
451+
452+-- COMMENT:
453+-- `untagged (* .. *) comment at prose position in the Rocq source — probably an error there; decide whether it is book prose or an author note`
454+-- For example, `((\a:Bool→Bool, λy:Bool. y) true)` is ill typed, but it
455+-- evaluates to the well-typed term `λy:Bool. y`,
456+
457+theorem not_subject_expansion :
458+    ∃ (t t' : Tm) (T : Ty), t ⟶ t' ∧ <{ ∅ ⊢ ~t' ⦂ ~T }> ∧ ¬ <{ ∅ ⊢ ~t ⦂ ~T }> := by
459+  all_goals
460+    refine ⟨<{ (λ x : Bool → Bool . λ y : Bool . y) true }>, <{ λ y : Bool . y }>,
461+            <{ Bool → Bool }>, ?_, ?_, ?_⟩
462+    · exact .appAbs "x" _ _ _ .tru
463+    · exact .abs _ _ _ _ _ (.var _ "y" _ rfl)
464+    · intro hc
465+      cases hc with
466+      | app _ _ _ _ _ hf ha => cases ha with | tru => cases hf
467+
468+-- ## Type Soundness
469+
470+-- ### Exercise (2 stars): type_soundness ⭐⭐
471+
472+-- Put progress and preservation together and show that a well-typed term can
473+-- *never* reach a stuck state.
474+
475+def Tm.IsStuck (t : Tm) : Prop := IsNormalForm Step t ∧ ¬ t.IsValue
476+
477+theorem type_soundness (t t' : Tm) (T : Ty)
478+    (hT : <{ ∅ ⊢ ~t ⦂ ~T }>) (hm : t ⟶* t') : ¬ t'.IsStuck := by
479+  intro hst
480+  obtain ⟨hnf, hnv⟩ := hst
481+  all_goals
482+    induction hm with
483+    | refl u =>
484+      cases progress u T hT with
485+      | inl hv => exact hnv hv
486+      | inr hs => exact hnf hs
487+    | step u w z h₁ _ ih => exact ih (preservation u w T hT h₁) hnf hnv
488+
489+-- ## Uniqueness of Types
490+
491+-- ### Exercise (3 stars): unique_types ⭐⭐⭐
492+
493+-- Another nice property of the STLC is that types are unique: a given term
494+-- (in a given context) has at most one type.
495+
496+theorem unique_types (Γ : Context) (e : Tm) (T T' : Ty)
497+    (h : <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~e ⦂ ~T }>) (h' : <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~e ⦂ ~T' }>) : T = T' := by
498+  all_goals
499+    induction h generalizing T' with
500+    | var _ _ _ hx => cases h' with | var _ _ _ hx' => exact Option.some.inj (hx.symm.trans hx')
501+    | abs _ _ _ _ _ _ ih => cases h' with | abs _ _ _ _ _ hb' => rw [ih _ hb']
502+    | app _ _ _ _ _ _ _ ih₁ _ =>
503+      cases h' with
504+      | app _ _ _ _ _ hf' _ => exact (Ty.arrow.inj (ih₁ _ hf')).2
505+    | tru => cases h' with | tru => rfl
506+    | fls => cases h' with | fls => rfl
507+    | ite _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ ih₂ _ => cases h' with | ite _ _ _ _ _ _ h₂' _ => exact ih₂ _ h₂'
508+
509+-- ## Context Invariance (Optional)
510+
511+-- Another standard technical lemma associated with typed languages is
512+-- *context invariance*. It states that typing is preserved under "inessential
513+-- changes" to the context `Γ` — in particular, changes that do not affect any
514+-- of the free variables of the term. In this section, we establish this
515+-- property for our system, introducing some other standard terminology on the
516+-- way.
517+
518+-- First, we need to define the *free variables* in a term — i.e., variables
519+-- that are used in the term in positions that are *not* in the scope of an
520+-- enclosing function abstraction binding a variable of the same name.
521+
522+-- More technically, a variable `x` *appears free in* a term *t* if `t`
523+-- contains some occurrence of `x` that is not under an abstraction labeled
524+-- `x`. For example:
525+
526+-- - `y` appears free, but `x` does not, in `λx:T→U. x y`
527+-- - both `x` and `y` appear free in `(λx:T→U. x y) x`
528+-- - no variables appear free in `λx:T→U. λy:T. x y`
529+
530+-- We write this `x ∈ᶠ t`, reading the relation as "`x` is one of the free
531+-- variables of `t`". Formally:
532+
533+section
534+set_option hygiene false in
535+local infix:50 " ∈ᶠ " => AppearsFreeIn
536+
537+inductive AppearsFreeIn (x : String) : Tm → Prop where
538+  | var : x ∈ᶠ (Tm.var x)
539+  | app1 (t₁ t₂ : Tm) (h : x ∈ᶠ t₁) : x ∈ᶠ <{ ~t₁ ~t₂ }>
540+  | app2 (t₁ t₂ : Tm) (h : x ∈ᶠ t₂) : x ∈ᶠ <{ ~t₁ ~t₂ }>
541+  | abs (y : String) (T₁ : Ty) (t₁ : Tm) (hne : y ≠ x) (h : x ∈ᶠ t₁) :
542+      x ∈ᶠ <{ λ ~y : ~T₁ . ~t₁ }>
543+  | ite1 (t₁ t₂ t₃ : Tm) (h : x ∈ᶠ t₁) : x ∈ᶠ <{ if ~t₁ then ~t₂ else ~t₃ }>
544+  | ite2 (t₁ t₂ t₃ : Tm) (h : x ∈ᶠ t₂) : x ∈ᶠ <{ if ~t₁ then ~t₂ else ~t₃ }>
545+  | ite3 (t₁ t₂ t₃ : Tm) (h : x ∈ᶠ t₃) : x ∈ᶠ <{ if ~t₁ then ~t₂ else ~t₃ }>
546+end
547+
548+scoped infix:50 " ∈ᶠ " => AppearsFreeIn
549+
550+-- The *free variables* of a term are just the variables that appear free in
551+-- it. This gives us another way to define *closed* terms — arguably a better
552+-- one, since it applies even to ill-typed terms. Indeed, this is the standard
553+-- definition of the term "closed."
554+
555+def Tm.Closed (t : Tm) : Prop := ∀ x, ¬ x ∈ᶠ t
556+
557+-- Conversely, an *open* term is one that may contain free variables. (I.e.,
558+-- every term is an open term; the closed terms are a subset of the open ones.
559+-- "Open" precisely means "possibly containing free variables.")
560+
561+-- ### Exercise (1 star): afi ⭐
562+
563+-- (Officially optional, but strongly recommended!) In the space below, write
564+-- out the rules of the `∈ᶠ` relation in informal inference-rule notation.
565+-- (Use whatever notational conventions you like — the point of the exercise
566+-- is just for you to think a bit about the meaning of each rule.) Although
567+-- this is a rather low-level, technical definition, understanding it is
568+-- crucial to understanding substitution and its properties, which are really
569+-- the crux of the lambda-calculus.
570+
571+-- COMMENT:
572+-- `untagged (* .. *) comment at prose position in the Rocq source — probably an error there; decide whether it is book prose or an author note`
573+-- (no solution yet) -/ /- LATER: Fill in an official solution
574+
575+-- Next, we show that if a variable `x` appears free in a term `t`, and if we
576+-- know `t` is well typed in context `Γ`, then it must be the case that `Γ`
577+-- assigns a type to `x`.
578+
579+theorem free_in_context (x : String) (t : Tm) (T : Ty) (Γ : Context)
580+    (ha : x ∈ᶠ t) (hT : <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~t ⦂ ~T }>) : ∃ T', Γ[x] = some T' := by
581+  all_goals
582+    induction ha generalizing Γ T with
583+    | var => cases hT with | var _ _ _ h => exact ⟨_, h⟩
584+    | app1 _ _ _ ih => cases hT with | app _ _ _ _ _ h₁ _ => exact ih _ _ h₁
585+    | app2 _ _ _ ih => cases hT with | app _ _ _ _ _ _ h₂ => exact ih _ _ h₂
586+    | abs y _ _ hne _ ih =>
587+      cases hT with
588+      | abs _ _ _ _ _ hb =>
589+        obtain ⟨T', h⟩ := ih _ _ hb
590+        rw [PartialMap.update_neq _ _ _ hne] at h
591+        exact ⟨T', h⟩
592+    | ite1 _ _ _ _ ih => cases hT with | ite _ _ _ _ _ h₁ _ _ => exact ih _ _ h₁
593+    | ite2 _ _ _ _ ih => cases hT with | ite _ _ _ _ _ _ h₂ _ => exact ih _ _ h₂
594+    | ite3 _ _ _ _ ih => cases hT with | ite _ _ _ _ _ _ _ h₃ => exact ih _ _ h₃
595+
596+-- *Proof*: We show, by induction on the proof that `x` appears free in `t`,
597+-- that, for all contexts `Γ`, if `t` is well typed under `Γ`, then `Γ`
598+-- assigns some type to `x`.
599+
600+-- - If the last rule used is `AppearsFreeIn.var`, then `t = x`, and from the
601+--   assumption that `t` is well typed under `Γ` we have immediately that `Γ`
602+--   assigns a type to `x`.
603+
604+-- - If the last rule used is `AppearsFreeIn.app1`, then `t = t₁ t₂` and `x`
605+--   appears free in `t₁`. Since `t` is well typed under `Γ`, we can see from
606+--   the typing rules that `t₁` must also be, and the IH then tells us that `Γ`
607+--   assigns `x` a type.
608+
609+-- - Almost all the other cases are similar: `x` appears free in a subterm of
610+--   `t`, and since `t` is well typed under `Γ`, we know the subterm of `t` in
611+--   which `x` appears is well typed under `Γ` as well, and the IH gives us
612+--   exactly the conclusion we want.
613+
614+-- - The only remaining case is `AppearsFreeIn.abs`. In this case
615+--   `t = λy:T₁. t₁` and `x` appears free in `t₁`, and we also know that `x` is
616+--   different from `y`. The difference from the previous cases is that, whereas
617+--   `t` is well typed under `Γ`, its body `t₁` is well typed under `y ↦ T₁; Γ`,
618+--   so the IH allows us to conclude that `x` is assigned some type by the
619+--   extended context `y ↦ T₁; Γ`. To conclude that `Γ` assigns a type to `x`,
620+--   we appeal to lemma `PartialMap.update_neq`, noting that `x` and `y` are
621+--   different variables.
622+
623+-- ### Exercise (2 stars): free_in_context ⭐⭐
624+
625+-- Complete the following proof.
626+
627+-- From the `free_in_context` lemma, it immediately follows that any term `t`
628+-- that is well typed in the empty context is closed (it has no free
629+-- variables).
630+
631+-- ### Exercise (2 stars): typable_empty__closed ⭐⭐
632+
633+theorem typable_empty_closed (t : Tm) (T : Ty) (hT : <{ ∅ ⊢ ~t ⦂ ~T }>) : t.Closed := by
634+  all_goals
635+    intro x ha
636+    obtain ⟨T', hc⟩ := free_in_context x t T ∅ ha hT
637+    rw [PartialMap.apply_empty] at hc
638+    cases hc
639+
640+-- Finally, we establish *context invariance*. It is useful in cases when we
641+-- have a proof of some typing relation `Γ ⊢ t ⦂ T`, and we need to replace
642+-- `Γ` by a different context `Γ'`. When is it safe to do this? Intuitively,
643+-- it must at least be the case that `Γ'` assigns the same types as `Γ` to all
644+-- the variables that appear free in `t`. In fact, this is the only condition
645+-- that is needed.
646+
647+theorem context_invariance (Γ Γ' : Context) (t : Tm) (T : Ty)
648+    (hT : <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~t ⦂ ~T }>) (hf : ∀ x, x ∈ᶠ t → Γ[x] = Γ'[x]) :
649+    <{ ~Γ' ⊢ ~t ⦂ ~T }> := by
650+  all_goals
651+    induction hT generalizing Γ' with
652+    | var _ x _ h => exact .var _ x _ ((hf x .var) ▸ h)
653+    | abs _ y _ _ _ _ ih =>
654+      refine .abs _ _ _ _ _ (ih _ ?_)
655+      intro z hz
656+      by_cases hyz : y = z
657+      · subst hyz; rw [PartialMap.update_eq, PartialMap.update_eq]
658+      -- The only tricky step.
659+      · rw [PartialMap.update_neq _ _ _ hyz, PartialMap.update_neq _ _ _ hyz]
660+        exact hf z (.abs y _ _ hyz hz)
661+    | app _ _ _ t₁ t₂ _ _ ih₁ ih₂ =>
662+      exact .app _ _ _ _ _ (ih₁ _ (fun z hz => hf z (.app1 t₁ t₂ hz)))
663+                           (ih₂ _ (fun z hz => hf z (.app2 t₁ t₂ hz)))
664+    | tru => exact .tru _
665+    | fls => exact .fls _
666+    | ite _ t₁ t₂ t₃ _ _ _ _ ih₁ ih₂ ih₃ =>
667+      exact .ite _ _ _ _ _ (ih₁ _ (fun z hz => hf z (.ite1 t₁ t₂ t₃ hz)))
668+                           (ih₂ _ (fun z hz => hf z (.ite2 t₁ t₂ t₃ hz)))
669+                           (ih₃ _ (fun z hz => hf z (.ite3 t₁ t₂ t₃ hz)))
670+
671+-- *Proof*: By induction on the derivation of `Γ ⊢ t ⦂ T`.
672+
673+-- - If the last rule in the derivation was `HasType.var`, then `t = x` and
674+--   `Γ x = T`. By assumption, `Γ' x = T` as well, and hence `Γ' ⊢ t ⦂ T` by
675+--   `HasType.var`.
676+
677+-- - If the last rule was `HasType.abs`, then `t = λy:T₂. t₁`, with
678+--   `T = T₂ → T₁` and `y ↦ T₂; Γ ⊢ t₁ ⦂ T₁`. The induction hypothesis states
679+--   that for any context `Γ''`, if `y ↦ T₂; Γ` and `Γ''` assign the same types
680+--   to all the free variables in `t₁`, then `t₁` has type `T₁` under `Γ''`. Let
681+--   `Γ'` be a context which agrees with `Γ` on the free variables in `t`; we
682+--   must show `Γ' ⊢ λy:T₂. t₁ ⦂ T₂ → T₁`.
683+
684+--   By `HasType.abs`, it suffices to show that `y ↦ T₂; Γ' ⊢ t₁ ⦂ T₁`. By the
685+--   IH (setting `Γ'' = y ↦ T₂;Γ'`), it suffices to show that `y ↦ T₂;Γ` and
686+--   `y ↦ T₂;Γ'` agree on all the variables that appear free in `t₁`.
687+
688+--   Any variable occurring free in `t₁` must be either `y` or some other
689+--   variable. `y ↦ T₂; Γ` and `y ↦ T₂; Γ'` clearly agree on `y`. Otherwise,
690+--   note that any variable other than `y` that occurs free in `t₁` also occurs
691+--   free in `t = λy:T₂. t₁`, and by assumption `Γ` and `Γ'` agree on all such
692+--   variables; hence so do `y ↦ T₂; Γ` and `y ↦ T₂; Γ'`.
693+
694+-- - If the last rule was `HasType.app`, then `t = t₁ t₂`, with
695+--   `Γ ⊢ t₁ ⦂ T₂ → T` and `Γ ⊢ t₂ ⦂ T₂`. One induction hypothesis states that
696+--   for all contexts `Γ'`, if `Γ'` agrees with `Γ` on the free variables in
697+--   `t₁`, then `t₁` has type `T₂ → T` under `Γ'`; there is a similar IH for
698+--   `t₂`. We must show that `t₁ t₂` also has type `T` under `Γ'`, given the
699+--   assumption that `Γ'` agrees with `Γ` on all the free variables in `t₁ t₂`.
700+--   By `HasType.app`, it suffices to show that `t₁` and `t₂` each have the same
701+--   type under `Γ'` as under `Γ`. But all free variables in `t₁` are also free
702+--   in `t₁ t₂`, and similarly for `t₂`; hence the desired result follows from
703+--   the induction hypotheses.
704+
705+-- ### Exercise (3 stars): context_invariance ⭐⭐⭐
706+

708+
709+-- The context invariance lemma can actually be used in place of the weakening
710+-- lemma to prove the crucial substitution lemma stated earlier.

733+-- ### Exercise (2 stars): stlc_variation1 (manually graded) ⭐⭐
734+
735+-- Suppose we add a new term `zap` with the following reduction rule
736+
737+--   ---------                  (ST_Zap)
738+--   t --> zap
739+
740+-- and the following typing rule:
741+
742+--   -------------------           (T_Zap)
743+--   Γ ⊢ zap ⦂ T
744+
745+-- Which of the following properties of the STLC remain true in the presence
746+-- of these rules? For each property, write either "remains true" or "becomes
747+-- false." If a property becomes false, give a counterexample.
748+
749+-- - Determinism of `step`
750+
751+-- - Becomes false. For instance `(if true then false else true) ⟶ false` and
752+--   `(if true then false else true) ⟶ zap`.
753+
754+-- - Progress
755+
756+-- - Remains true. Every term (including `zap`) can take a step to `zap`.
757+
758+-- - Preservation
759+
760+-- - Remains true. `zap` can have any type.
761+
762+-- ### Exercise (2 stars): stlc_variation2 (manually graded) ⭐⭐
763+
764+-- Suppose instead that we add a new term `foo` with the following reduction
765+-- rules:
766+
767+--   -----------------                (ST_Foo1)
768+--   (\x:A, x) --> foo
769+
770+--     ------------                   (ST_Foo2)
771+--     foo --> true
772+
773+-- Which of the following properties of the STLC remain true in the presence
774+-- of this rule? For each one, write either "remains true" or else "becomes
775+-- false." If a property becomes false, give a counterexample.
776+
777+-- - Determinism of `step`
778+
779+-- - Becomes false. The term [(\x:Bool, x) true] might step
780+-- to either [true] by the rule Step.appAbs or
781+-- to [foo true] by the rule Step.app1 and ST_Foo1.
782+
783+-- - Progress
784+
785+-- - Remains true. We are only adding to the step relation, and this can never
786+--   damage progress.
787+
788+-- - Preservation
789+
790+-- - Becomes false. For example,
791+-- [⊢ \x:Bool,x ⦂ Bool->Bool] and [(\x:Bool,x) --> foo] by (ST_Foo1),
792+-- but, since we have no typing rules for foo, we cannot prove that
793+-- [⊢ foo ⦂ Bool->Bool].
794+
795+-- ### Exercise (2 stars): stlc_variation3 (manually graded) ⭐⭐
796+
797+-- Suppose instead that we remove the rule `Step.app1` from the `step`
798+-- relation. Which of the following properties of the STLC remain true in the
799+-- presence of this rule? For each one, write either "remains true" or else
800+-- "becomes false." If a property becomes false, give a counterexample.
801+
802+-- - Determinism of `step`
803+
804+-- - Remains true. Removing reduction rules can only make `step` more
805+--   deterministic.
806+
807+-- - Progress
808+
809+-- - Becomes false. For example,
810+--   `((\x:Bool→Bool, \y:Bool→Bool, x) (λz:Bool. z)) (λz:Bool. z)` is well
811+--   typed, but stuck.
812+
813+-- - Preservation
814+
815+-- - Remains true. Removing reduction rules can't break preservation.
