875+-- ### Exercise (2 stars): stlc_variation6 ⭐⭐
876+
877+-- Suppose instead that we add the following new rule to the typing relation:
878+
879+--   Γ ⊢ t₁ ⦂ Bool
880+--   Γ ⊢ t₂ ⦂ Bool
881+--   ------------------------            (T_FunnyApp')
882+--   Γ ⊢ t₁ t₂ ⦂ Bool
883+
884+-- Which of the following properties of the STLC remain true in the presence
885+-- of this rule? For each one, write either "remains true" or else "becomes
886+-- false." If a property becomes false, give a counterexample.
887+
888+-- - Determinism of `step`
889+
890+-- - Remains true. We are not changing the `step` relation.
891+
892+-- - Progress
893+
894+-- - Becomes false. For instance, `true true` is a term that becomes typable (at
895+--   type `Bool`), but which is stuck.
896+
897+-- - Preservation
898+
899+-- - Remains true. There are 3 ways `t₁ t₂` can reduce. For `Step.app1` and
900+--   `Step.app2` we can still apply the induction hypothesis. To reduce `t₁ t₂`
901+--   using `Step.appAbs` `t₁` would need to be a function, but functions don't
902+--   have type `Bool`.
903+
904+-- ### Exercise (2 stars): stlc_variation7 ⭐⭐
905+
906+-- Suppose we add the following new rule to the typing relation of the STLC:
907+
908+--   ---------------------- (T_FunnyAbs)
909+--   ⊢ \x:Bool,t ⦂ Bool
910+
911+-- Which of the following properties of the STLC remain true in the presence
912+-- of this rule? For each one, write either "remains true" or else "becomes
913+-- false." If a property becomes false, give a counterexample.
914+
915+-- - Determinism of `step`
916+
917+-- - Remains true. We're not changing the `step` relation.
918+
919+-- - Progress
920+
921+-- - Becomes false. For instance [if (\x:Bool,false) then false
922+-- else false] is a term that would become typable, although it
923+-- is stuck.
924+
925+-- - Preservation
926+
927+-- - Remains true. `λx:Bool. t` doesn't step.
928+
929+end Stlc
930+
931+-- ### Exercise: STLC with Arithmetic
932+
933+-- To see how the STLC might function as the core of a real programming
934+-- language, let's extend it with a concrete base type of numbers and some
935+-- constants and primitive operators.
936+
937+-- The arithmetic we are adding is the arithmetic of the Slang chapter —
938+-- numeric constants and multiplication — together with the successor,
939+-- predecessor, and zero-test operations of the Types chapter. What is new is
940+-- the setting: those operations now live in a language that also has
941+-- variables, abstraction, and application, so an arithmetic computation can
942+-- be packaged up as a function and passed around as a value.
943+
944+namespace StlcArith
945+
946+-- To types, we add a base type of natural numbers (and remove booleans, for
947+-- brevity).
948+
949+inductive Ty where
950+  | arrow (T₁ T₂ : Ty)
951+  | nat
952+
953+-- To terms, we add natural number constants, along with successor,
954+-- predecessor, multiplication, and zero-testing.
955+
956+inductive Tm where
957+  | var (x : String)
958+  | app (t₁ t₂ : Tm)
959+  | abs (x : String) (T : Ty) (t : Tm)
960+  | const (n : Nat)
961+  | succ (t : Tm)
962+  | pred (t : Tm)
963+  | mult (t₁ t₂ : Tm)
964+  | ite0 (c t e : Tm)
965+
966+-- `StlcArith` is a **different** language from the STLC of this chapter, not
967+-- an extension of it, so it needs its own concrete syntax. Rather than invent
968+-- a new one, we reuse the grammars set up in the Stlc chapter — the syntax
969+-- categories `stlcTy`, `stlcTm`, and `stlcVar` — and give them a new meaning
970+-- here. Terms and types of this language are therefore written inside the
971+-- same `<{ … }>` brackets, with the same `~e` escape back to Lean.
972+
973+-- _Details:_ Notation encoding: types
974+
975+-- The type grammar needs no new productions: `Nat` is a bare identifier,
976+-- which the template already accepts, and arrows and parentheses are
977+-- unchanged. Only the `macro_rules` are new, and they differ from the STLC's
978+-- in just two places — the identifier `Nat` names this language's base type,
979+-- and the arrow builds this language's `StlcArith.Ty.arrow`.
980+
981+scoped macro_rules (kind := Stlc.tyBracket)
982+  | `(<{ ~$T:term }>)    => pure T
983+  | `(<{ ($T:stlcTy) }>) => `(<{ $T:stlcTy }>)
984+  | `(<{ $x:ident }>) =>
985+      match x.getId.toString with
986+      | "Nat" => `(Ty.nat)
987+      | _ => `(($x : Ty))
988+  | `(<{ $T₁:stlcTy → $T₂:stlcTy }>)  => `(Ty.arrow <{ $T₁:stlcTy }> <{ $T₂:stlcTy }>)
989+  | `(<{ $T₁:stlcTy -> $T₂:stlcTy }>) => `(Ty.arrow <{ $T₁:stlcTy }> <{ $T₂:stlcTy }>)
990+
991+-- _Details:_ Notation encoding: terms
992+
993+-- Terms do need new productions: a numeral, an infix `*`, and the zero test.
994+-- Multiplication binds looser than application and tighter than `λ`, so
995+-- `x * y z` multiplies `x` by the application `y z`; it associates to the
996+-- right, so `x * y * z` is `x * (y * z)`.
997+
998+-- `succ` and `pred` get no production of their own. Making them keywords
999+-- would reserve those words globally — and we would then be unable to write
1000+-- `succ` as a case name in a proof, including for Lean's own `Nat`. Instead
1001+-- they are written as though they were functions applied to an argument,
1002+-- `succ t`, and the application rule below recognizes them. `if0` **is** a
1003+-- keyword, since `then` and `else` leave no other option; that is why the
1004+-- constructor above is called `StlcArith.Tm.ite0` rather than `if0`, just as
1005+-- the STLC's conditional is `Stlc.Tm.ite`.
1006+
1007+scoped syntax:max num : stlcTm
1008+scoped syntax:60 stlcTm:61 " * " stlcTm:60 : stlcTm
1009+scoped syntax:50 "if0 " stlcTm:51 " then " stlcTm:50 " else " stlcTm:50 : stlcTm
1010+
1011+open Lean in
1012+scoped macro_rules (kind := Stlc.tmBracket)
1013+  | `(<{ ~$e:term }>)    => pure e
1014+  | `(<{ ($t:stlcTm) }>) => `(<{ $t:stlcTm }>)
1015+  | `(<{ $n:num }>)      => `(Tm.const $n)
1016+  | `(<{ $x:ident }>) =>
1017+      match x.getId.toString with
1018+      | "Nat"  => Macro.throwErrorAt x "`Nat` is a type, not a term"
1019+      | "succ" => Macro.throwErrorAt x "`succ` must be applied to an argument"
1020+      | "pred" => Macro.throwErrorAt x "`pred` must be applied to an argument"
1021+      | _      => `(Tm.var $(quote x.getId.toString))
1022+  | `(<{ $t₁:stlcTm $t₂:stlcTm }>) =>
1023+      match t₁ with
1024+      | `(stlcTm| $f:ident) =>
1025+          match f.getId.toString with
1026+          | "succ" => `(Tm.succ <{ $t₂:stlcTm }>)
1027+          | "pred" => `(Tm.pred <{ $t₂:stlcTm }>)
1028+          | _      => `(Tm.app <{ $t₁:stlcTm }> <{ $t₂:stlcTm }>)
1029+      | _ => `(Tm.app <{ $t₁:stlcTm }> <{ $t₂:stlcTm }>)
1030+  | `(<{ λ $x : $T . $t }>) => do
1031+      `(Tm.abs $(← Stlc.varStr x) <{ $T:stlcTy }> <{ $t:stlcTm }>)
1032+  | `(<{ $t₁:stlcTm * $t₂:stlcTm }>) => `(Tm.mult <{ $t₁:stlcTm }> <{ $t₂:stlcTm }>)
1033+  | `(<{ if0 $c then $t else $e }>) =>
1034+      `(Tm.ite0 <{ $c:stlcTm }> <{ $t:stlcTm }> <{ $e:stlcTm }>)
1035+
1036+-- _Details:_ Notation encoding: printing it back
1037+
1038+-- As in the Stlc chapter, a delaborator runs the grammar backwards, so that
1039+-- goals mentioning these terms and types read in the concrete syntax. The
1040+-- parenthesizers registered there are for the whole syntax category, so they
1041+-- serve this language too and are not repeated.
1042+
1043+open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
1044+/-- Rebuild `stlcTy` concrete syntax from a `Ty` value. -/
1045+partial def delabTyInner : DelabM (TSyntax `stlcTy) := do
1046+  let stx ←
1047+    match_expr ← getExpr with
1048+    | Ty.nat => `(stlcTy| $(mkIdent `Nat):ident)
1049+    | Ty.arrow _ _ => do
1050+        let a ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTyInner
1051+        let b ← withAppArg delabTyInner
1052+        `(stlcTy| $a → $b)
1053+    | _ => do
1054+        match ← delab with
1055+        | `($i:ident) => `(stlcTy| $i:ident)
1056+        | e => `(stlcTy| ~$e)
1057+  (⟨·⟩) <$> annotateTermInfo ⟨stx.raw⟩
1058+
1059+open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
1060+/-- Rebuild `stlcTm` concrete syntax from a `Tm` value. -/
1061+partial def delabTmInner : DelabM (TSyntax `stlcTm) := do
1062+  let stx ←
1063+    match_expr ← getExpr with
1064+    | Tm.var _ => do
1065+        match ← withAppArg delab with
1066+        | `($s:str) =>
1067+            if Stlc.isPlainName s.getString then
1068+              `(stlcTm| $(mkIdent (Name.mkSimple s.getString)):ident)
1069+            else `(stlcTm| ~($(⟨← delab⟩)))
1070+        | _ => `(stlcTm| ~($(⟨← delab⟩)))
1071+    | Tm.const _ => do
1072+        match ← withAppArg delab with
1073+        | `($n:num) => `(stlcTm| $n:num)
1074+        | _ => `(stlcTm| ~($(⟨← delab⟩)))
1075+    | Tm.app _ _ => do
1076+        let f ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTmInner
1077+        let a ← withAppArg delabTmInner
1078+        `(stlcTm| $f $a)
1079+    | Tm.abs _ _ _ => do
1080+        let x ← withAppFn <| withAppFn <| withAppArg Stlc.delabVarInner
1081+        let T ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTyInner
1082+        let t ← withAppArg delabTmInner
1083+        `(stlcTm| λ $x : $T . $t)
1084+    | Tm.succ _ => do
1085+        let t ← withAppArg delabTmInner
1086+        `(stlcTm| $(mkIdent `succ):ident $t)
1087+    | Tm.pred _ => do
1088+        let t ← withAppArg delabTmInner
1089+        `(stlcTm| $(mkIdent `pred):ident $t)
1090+    | Tm.mult _ _ => do
1091+        let a ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTmInner
1092+        let b ← withAppArg delabTmInner
1093+        `(stlcTm| $a * $b)
1094+    | Tm.ite0 _ _ _ => do
1095+        let c ← withAppFn <| withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTmInner
1096+        let t ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTmInner
1097+        let e ← withAppArg delabTmInner
1098+        `(stlcTm| if0 $c then $t else $e)
1099+    | _ => do
1100+        -- `subst` is defined below, so it is matched by name rather than with
1101+        -- `match_expr`; a substitution prints in its own bracket notation.
1102+        let e ← getExpr
1103+        if e.getAppFn.constName? == some `StlcArith.subst && e.getAppNumArgs == 3 then
1104+          let x ← withAppFn <| withAppFn <| withAppArg Stlc.delabVarInner
1105+          let s ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTmInner
1106+          let t ← withAppArg delabTmInner
1107+          `(stlcTm| [$x := $s] $t)
1108+        else
1109+          match ← delab with
1110+          | `($i:ident) => `(stlcTm| $i:ident)
1111+          | e => `(stlcTm| ~$e)
1112+  (⟨·⟩) <$> annotateTermInfo ⟨stx.raw⟩
1113+
1114+open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
1115+@[delab app.StlcArith.Ty.nat, delab app.StlcArith.Ty.arrow]
1116+def delabTy : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
1117+  guard <| match_expr ← getExpr with
1118+    | Ty.nat => true | Ty.arrow _ _ => true | _ => false
1119+  match ← delabTyInner with
1120+  | `(stlcTy| ~$e) => pure e
1121+  | e => `(<{ $e:stlcTy }>)
1122+
1123+open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
1124+@[delab app.StlcArith.Tm.var, delab app.StlcArith.Tm.app, delab app.StlcArith.Tm.abs,
1125+  delab app.StlcArith.Tm.const, delab app.StlcArith.Tm.succ, delab app.StlcArith.Tm.pred,
1126+  delab app.StlcArith.Tm.mult, delab app.StlcArith.Tm.ite0]
1127+def delabTm : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
1128+  guard <| match_expr ← getExpr with
1129+    | Tm.var _ => true | Tm.app _ _ => true | Tm.abs _ _ _ => true
1130+    | Tm.const _ => true | Tm.succ _ => true | Tm.pred _ => true
1131+    | Tm.mult _ _ => true | Tm.ite0 _ _ _ => true
1132+    | _ => false
1133+  match ← delabTmInner with
1134+  | `(stlcTm| ~$e) => pure e
1135+  | e => `(<{ $e:stlcTm }>)
1136+
1137+-- Note to developers (Claude):
1138+--     The Rocq source builds this grammar with custom entries, and a few
1139+--     pieces of that have no Lean counterpart: the `<{{ x }}>` quotation for
1140+--     shifting into type-parsing mode (Lean works out from context which of
1141+--     the two brackets is meant), the `$( t )` escape into arbitrary Rocq
1142+--     `constr` notation (our `~e` already does that, in both grammars), and
1143+--     the two coercions `tm_var : string >-> tm` and `tm_const : nat >-> tm`,
1144+--     which let a bare string or numeral stand for a term. Here a bare
1145+--     identifier and a bare numeral are productions of the term grammar
1146+--     itself, so no coercions are needed.
1147+
1148+-- In this extended exercise, your job is to finish formalizing the definition
1149+-- and properties of the STLC extended with arithmetic. Specifically:
1150+
1151+-- Fill in the core definitions for `StlcArith`, by starting with the rules
1152+-- and terms which are the same as the STLC. Then prove the key lemmas and
1153+-- theorems we provide. You will need to define and prove helper lemmas, as
1154+-- before.
1155+
1156+-- Make sure Lean accepts the whole file before submitting.
1157+
1158+-- ### Exercise (5 stars): StlcArith.subst ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐
1159+
1160+-- Substitution is defined exactly as it was for the STLC, with one clause per
1161+-- new constructor.
1162+
1163+-- _Details:_ Why the definition is wrapped in a section
1164+
1165+-- Substitution is written using its own `[x := s] t` notation, which is being
1166+-- defined at the same time, so — as in the Stlc chapter — the rule is first
1167+-- declared `local`, with hygiene off so that the `subst` in its expansion
1168+-- refers to the function being defined, and then declared again for real once
1169+-- the section closes.
1170+
1171+section
1172+set_option hygiene false in
1173+local macro_rules (kind := Stlc.tmBracket)
1174+  | `(<{ [$x := $s] $t }>) => do
1175+      `(subst $(← Stlc.varStr x) <{ $s:stlcTm }> <{ $t:stlcTm }>)
1176+
1177+def subst (x : String) (s : Tm) (t : Tm) : Tm := (
1178+  match t with
1179+  -- `.var y`, not `<{ ~y }>`: `y` is the variable's *name*, a `String`.
1180+  | .var y =>
1181+      if x = y then s else t
1182+  | <{ λ ~y : ~T . ~t₁ }> =>
1183+      if x = y then t else <{ λ ~y : ~T . [~x := ~s] ~t₁ }>
1184+  | <{ ~t₁ ~t₂ }> =>
1185+      <{ ([~x := ~s] ~t₁) ([~x := ~s] ~t₂) }>
1186+  | .const _ =>
1187+      t
1188+  | <{ succ ~t₁ }> =>
1189+      <{ succ ([~x := ~s] ~t₁) }>
1190+  | <{ pred ~t₁ }> =>
1191+      <{ pred ([~x := ~s] ~t₁) }>
1192+  | <{ ~t₁ * ~t₂ }> =>
1193+      <{ ([~x := ~s] ~t₁) * ([~x := ~s] ~t₂) }>
1194+  | <{ if0 ~t₁ then ~t₂ else ~t₃ }> =>
1195+      <{ if0 [~x := ~s] ~t₁ then [~x := ~s] ~t₂ else [~x := ~s] ~t₃ }>)
1196+end
1197+
1198+macro_rules (kind := Stlc.tmBracket)
1199+  | `(<{ [$x := $s] $t }>) => do
1200+      `(subst $(← Stlc.varStr x) <{ $s:stlcTm }> <{ $t:stlcTm }>)
1201+
1202+-- _Details:_ Notation encoding: substitution
1203+
1204+-- One more line registers substitutions with the printer, so that a goal
1205+-- mentioning one reads as `[x := s] t` rather than as a `subst` application.
1206+
1207+open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
1208+@[delab app.StlcArith.subst]
1209+def delabSubst : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
1210+  match ← delabTmInner with
1211+  | `(stlcTm| ~$e) => pure e
1212+  | e => `(<{ $e:stlcTm }>)
1213+
1214+-- You will also want one `@[simp]` simplification lemma per constructor,
1215+-- saying how your `subst` behaves on that constructor, in the style of the
1216+-- Stlc chapter — the substitution lemma below is proved by rewriting with
1217+-- them rather than by unfolding the definition. Two of the constructors need
1218+-- two lemmas apiece, since substitution treats a bound name differently
1219+-- depending on whether it is the name being substituted for.
1220+
1221+section
1222+variable (x y : String) (s t t₁ t₂ t₃ : Tm) (T : Ty) (n : Nat)
1223+@[simp] theorem subst_var_eq : <{ [~x := ~s] ~(Tm.var x) }> = s := by
1224+  simp [subst]
1225+
1226+@[simp] theorem subst_var_ne (h : x ≠ y) : <{ [~x := ~s] ~(Tm.var y) }> = .var y := by
1227+  simp [subst, h]
1228+
1229+@[simp] theorem subst_abs_eq : <{ [~x := ~s] (λ ~x : ~T . ~t) }> = <{ λ ~x : ~T . ~t }> := by
1230+  simp [subst]
1231+
1232+@[simp] theorem subst_abs_ne (h : x ≠ y) :
1233+    <{ [~x := ~s] (λ ~y : ~T . ~t) }> = <{ λ ~y : ~T . [~x := ~s] ~t }> := by
1234+  simp [subst, h]
1235+
1236+@[simp] theorem subst_app :
1237+    <{ [~x := ~s] (~t₁ ~t₂) }> = <{ ([~x := ~s] ~t₁) ([~x := ~s] ~t₂) }> := rfl
1238+
1239+@[simp] theorem subst_const : <{ [~x := ~s] ~(Tm.const n) }> = .const n := rfl
1240+
1241+@[simp] theorem subst_succ :
1242+    <{ [~x := ~s] (succ ~t₁) }> = <{ succ ([~x := ~s] ~t₁) }> := rfl
1243+
1244+@[simp] theorem subst_pred :
1245+    <{ [~x := ~s] (pred ~t₁) }> = <{ pred ([~x := ~s] ~t₁) }> := rfl
1246+
1247+@[simp] theorem subst_mult :
1248+    <{ [~x := ~s] (~t₁ * ~t₂) }> = <{ ([~x := ~s] ~t₁) * ([~x := ~s] ~t₂) }> := rfl
1249+
1250+@[simp] theorem subst_ite0 :
1251+    <{ [~x := ~s] (if0 ~t₁ then ~t₂ else ~t₃) }> =
1252+      <{ if0 [~x := ~s] ~t₁ then [~x := ~s] ~t₂ else [~x := ~s] ~t₃ }> := rfl
1253+end
1254+
1255+-- Next, the values. In the pure STLC, function abstractions were the only
1256+-- values; now the numbers are values too.
1257+
1258+inductive Tm.IsValue : Tm → Prop where
1259+  | abs (x : String) (T₂ : Ty) (t₁ : Tm) : Tm.IsValue <{ λ ~x : ~T₂ . ~t₁ }>
1260+  | const (n : Nat) : Tm.IsValue (.const n)
1261+
1262+-- Now the reduction relation. The three rules for application are the STLC's;
1263+-- the rest say how the arithmetic operators evaluate their arguments and what
1264+-- they compute once those arguments are numbers.
1265+
1266+section
1267+set_option hygiene false in
1268+local notation:40 t:41 " ⟶ " t':41 => Step t t'
1269+
1270+inductive Step : Tm → Tm → Prop where
1271+  | appAbs (x : String) (T : Ty) (t v : Tm) (hv : v.IsValue) :
1272+      <{ (λ ~x : ~T . ~t) ~v }> ⟶ <{ [~x := ~v] ~t }>
1273+  | app1 (t₁ t₁' t₂ : Tm) (h : t₁ ⟶ t₁') :
1274+      <{ ~t₁ ~t₂ }> ⟶ <{ ~t₁' ~t₂ }>
1275+  | app2 (v₁ t₂ t₂' : Tm) (hv : v₁.IsValue) (h : t₂ ⟶ t₂') :
1276+      <{ ~v₁ ~t₂ }> ⟶ <{ ~v₁ ~t₂' }>
1277+  | succ (t₁ t₁' : Tm) (h : t₁ ⟶ t₁') :
1278+      <{ succ ~t₁ }> ⟶ <{ succ ~t₁' }>
1279+  | succConst (n : Nat) :
1280+      <{ succ ~(Tm.const n) }> ⟶ Tm.const (1 + n)
1281+  | pred (t₁ t₁' : Tm) (h : t₁ ⟶ t₁') :
1282+      <{ pred ~t₁ }> ⟶ <{ pred ~t₁' }>
1283+  | predConst (n : Nat) :
1284+      <{ pred ~(Tm.const n) }> ⟶ Tm.const (n - 1)
1285+  | multConst (n₁ n₂ : Nat) :
1286+      <{ ~(Tm.const n₁) * ~(Tm.const n₂) }> ⟶ Tm.const (n₁ * n₂)
1287+  | mult1 (t₁ t₁' t₂ : Tm) (h : t₁ ⟶ t₁') :
1288+      <{ ~t₁ * ~t₂ }> ⟶ <{ ~t₁' * ~t₂ }>
1289+  | mult2 (v₁ t₂ t₂' : Tm) (hv : v₁.IsValue) (h : t₂ ⟶ t₂') :
1290+      <{ ~v₁ * ~t₂ }> ⟶ <{ ~v₁ * ~t₂' }>
1291+  | if0Step (t₁ t₁' t₂ t₃ : Tm) (h : t₁ ⟶ t₁') :
1292+      <{ if0 ~t₁ then ~t₂ else ~t₃ }> ⟶ <{ if0 ~t₁' then ~t₂ else ~t₃ }>
1293+  | if0Zero (t₂ t₃ : Tm) :
1294+      <{ if0 0 then ~t₂ else ~t₃ }> ⟶ t₂
1295+  | if0Nonzero (n : Nat) (t₂ t₃ : Tm) :
1296+      <{ if0 ~(Tm.const (n + 1)) then ~t₂ else ~t₃ }> ⟶ t₃
1297+end
1298+
1299+scoped notation:40 t:41 " ⟶ " t':41 => Step t t'
1300+scoped notation:40 t:41 " ⟶* " t':41 => Multi Step t t'
1301+
1302+-- An example:
1303+
1304+theorem Nat_step_example : ∃ t, <{ (λ x : Nat . λ y : Nat . x * y) 3 2 }> ⟶* t := by
1305+  all_goals
1306+    refine ⟨<{ 6 }>, ?_⟩
1307+    apply Multi.step (y := <{ (λ y : Nat . 3 * y) 2 }>)
1308+    · exact .app1 _ _ _ (.appAbs "x" _ _ _ (.const 3))
1309+    apply Multi.step (y := <{ 3 * 2 }>)
1310+    · exact .appAbs "y" _ _ _ (.const 2)
1311+    apply Multi.step (y := <{ 6 }>)
1312+    · exact .multConst 3 2
1313+    · rfl
1314+
1315+-- Note to developers (before next release):
1316+--     The reduction example above ought to be joined by a bigger one —
1317+--     something to replace the factorial example that used to live here.
1318+
1319+-- A typing context is a partial map from variables to types, exactly as
1320+-- before.
1321+
1322+abbrev Context := PartialMap String Ty
1323+
1324+-- _Details:_ Notation encoding: contexts and judgments
1325+
1326+-- The context grammar `stlcCtx` is reused as well; only the map it denotes is
1327+-- new, since the types it stores are this language's. As with `subst`, the
1328+-- judgment rule is introduced twice: `local` and hygiene-free while the
1329+-- relation is being declared, then again for real.
1330+
1331+open Lean in
1332+/-- The `Context` denoted by a context expression. -/
1333+partial def ctxTerm (G : TSyntax `stlcCtx) : MacroM Term :=
1334+  match G with
1335+  | `(stlcCtx| ∅)   => `((∅ : Context))
1336+  | `(stlcCtx| ~$e) => pure e
1337+  | `(stlcCtx| $x:stlcVar ↦ $T:stlcTy ; $G:stlcCtx) => do
1338+      `(PartialMap.update $(← ctxTerm G) $(← Stlc.varStr x) <{ $T:stlcTy }>)
1339+  | _ => Macro.throwUnsupported
1340+
1341+section
1342+set_option hygiene false in
1343+local macro_rules (kind := Stlc.judgeBracket)
1344+  | `(<{ $G:stlcCtx ⊢ $t:stlcTm ⦂ $T:stlcTy }>) => do
1345+      `(HasType $(← ctxTerm G) <{ $t:stlcTm }> <{ $T:stlcTy }>)
1346+
1347+-- The typing rules for variables, abstraction, and application are the
1348+-- STLC's. The remaining four are the typing rules for arithmetic expressions.
1349+
1350+inductive HasType : Context → Tm → Ty → Prop where
1351+  | var (Γ : Context) (x : String) (T₁ : Ty) (h : Γ[x] = some T₁) :
1352+      <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~(Tm.var x) ⦂ ~T₁ }>
1353+  | abs (Γ : Context) (x : String) (T₁ T₂ : Ty) (t₁ : Tm)
1354+      (h : <{ ~x ↦ ~T₂ ; ~Γ ⊢ ~t₁ ⦂ ~T₁ }>) :
1355+      <{ ~Γ ⊢ λ ~x : ~T₂ . ~t₁ ⦂ ~T₂ → ~T₁ }>
1356+  | app (Γ : Context) (T₁ T₂ : Ty) (t₁ t₂ : Tm)
1357+      (h₁ : <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~t₁ ⦂ ~T₂ → ~T₁ }>) (h₂ : <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~t₂ ⦂ ~T₂ }>) :
1358+      <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~t₁ ~t₂ ⦂ ~T₁ }>
1359+  | const (Γ : Context) (n : Nat) :
1360+      <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~(Tm.const n) ⦂ Nat }>
1361+  | succ (Γ : Context) (t₁ : Tm) (h : <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~t₁ ⦂ Nat }>) :
1362+      <{ ~Γ ⊢ succ ~t₁ ⦂ Nat }>
1363+  | pred (Γ : Context) (t₁ : Tm) (h : <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~t₁ ⦂ Nat }>) :
1364+      <{ ~Γ ⊢ pred ~t₁ ⦂ Nat }>
1365+  | mult (Γ : Context) (t₁ t₂ : Tm)
1366+      (h₁ : <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~t₁ ⦂ Nat }>) (h₂ : <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~t₂ ⦂ Nat }>) :
1367+      <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~t₁ * ~t₂ ⦂ Nat }>
1368+  | ite0 (Γ : Context) (t₁ t₂ t₃ : Tm) (T₀ : Ty)
1369+      (h₁ : <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~t₁ ⦂ Nat }>) (h₂ : <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~t₂ ⦂ ~T₀ }>)
1370+      (h₃ : <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~t₃ ⦂ ~T₀ }>) :
1371+      <{ ~Γ ⊢ if0 ~t₁ then ~t₂ else ~t₃ ⦂ ~T₀ }>
1372+
1373+-- _Details:_ Notation encoding: the judgment, for real
1374+
1375+-- Closing the section retires the hygiene-free rule; the same rule is then
1376+-- declared again, hygienically, for every later use, and a pair of
1377+-- unexpanders prints judgments back in their own notation.
1378+
1379+end
1380+
1381+scoped macro_rules (kind := Stlc.judgeBracket)
1382+  | `(<{ $G:stlcCtx ⊢ $t:stlcTm ⦂ $T:stlcTy }>) => do
1383+      `(HasType $(← ctxTerm G) <{ $t:stlcTm }> <{ $T:stlcTy }>)
1384+
1385+open Lean PrettyPrinter in
1386+/-- Rebuild `stlcCtx` syntax from the term syntax of a `Context`, so that a
1387+context prints as `x ↦ Nat ; Γ` rather than as a chain of map updates. -/
1388+partial def unexpandCtx : Term → UnexpandM (TSyntax `stlcCtx)
1389+  | `(∅) => `(stlcCtx| ∅)
1390+  | `($x:str →ₚ $T ; $G) => do
1391+      let G' ← unexpandCtx G
1392+      let x' : TSyntax `stlcVar ←
1393+        if Stlc.isPlainName x.getString then
1394+          `(stlcVar| $(mkIdent (Name.mkSimple x.getString)):ident)
1395+        else `(stlcVar| ~$x)
1396+      match T with
1397+      | `(<{ $T':stlcTy }>) => `(stlcCtx| $x':stlcVar ↦ $T' ; $G')
1398+      | _                   => `(stlcCtx| $x':stlcVar ↦ ~($T) ; $G')
1399+  | G => `(stlcCtx| ~($G))
1400+
1401+open Lean PrettyPrinter in
1402+@[app_unexpander StlcArith.HasType]
1403+def HasType.unexpand : Unexpander
1404+  | `($_ $G <{ $t:stlcTm }> <{ $T:stlcTy }>) =>
1405+      do `(<{ $(← unexpandCtx G) ⊢ $t ⦂ $T }>)
1406+  | `($_ $G <{ $t:stlcTm }> $T) =>
1407+      do `(<{ $(← unexpandCtx G) ⊢ $t ⦂ ~($T) }>)
1408+  | `($_ $G $t <{ $T:stlcTy }>) =>
1409+      do `(<{ $(← unexpandCtx G) ⊢ ~($t) ⦂ $T }>)
1410+  | `($_ $G $t $T) =>
1411+      do `(<{ $(← unexpandCtx G) ⊢ ~($t) ⦂ ~($T) }>)
1412+  | _ => throw ()
1413+
1414+-- An example:
1415+
1416+theorem Nat_typing_example : <{ ∅ ⊢ (λ x : Nat . λ y : Nat . x * y) 3 2 ⦂ Nat }> :=
1417+  (
1418+    .app _ _ Ty.nat _ _
1419+      (.app _ _ Ty.nat _ _
1420+        (.abs _ _ _ _ _ (.abs _ _ _ _ _ (.mult _ _ _ (.var _ "x" _ rfl) (.var _ "y" _ rfl))))
1421+        (.const _ 3))
1422+      (.const _ 2))
1423+
1424+-- #### The Technical Theorems
1425+
1426+-- The next lemmas are proved *exactly* as before.
1427+
1428+-- ### Exercise (4 stars): StlcArith.weakening ⭐⭐⭐⭐
1429+
1430+theorem weakening (Γ Γ' : Context) (t : Tm) (T : Ty)
1431+    (hi : Γ ⊆ Γ') (hT : <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~t ⦂ ~T }>) : <{ ~Γ' ⊢ ~t ⦂ ~T }> := by
1432+  all_goals
1433+    induction hT generalizing Γ' with
1434+    | var _ x _ h => exact .var _ x _ (hi x _ h)
1435+    | abs _ x _ _ _ _ ih => exact .abs _ x _ _ _ (ih _ (PartialMap.update_subset _ _ _ _ hi))
1436+    | app _ _ _ _ _ _ _ ih₁ ih₂ => exact .app _ _ _ _ _ (ih₁ _ hi) (ih₂ _ hi)
1437+    | const _ n => exact .const _ n
1438+    | succ _ _ _ ih => exact .succ _ _ (ih _ hi)
1439+    | pred _ _ _ ih => exact .pred _ _ (ih _ hi)
1440+    | mult _ _ _ _ _ ih₁ ih₂ => exact .mult _ _ _ (ih₁ _ hi) (ih₂ _ hi)
1441+    | ite0 _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ ih₁ ih₂ ih₃ =>
1442+      exact .ite0 _ _ _ _ _ (ih₁ _ hi) (ih₂ _ hi) (ih₃ _ hi)
1443+
1444+-- The two helper lemmas that weakening is for are also proved just as they
1445+-- were for the STLC.
1446+
1447+theorem weakening_empty (Γ : Context) (t : Tm) (T : Ty) (hT : <{ ∅ ⊢ ~t ⦂ ~T }>) :
1448+    <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~t ⦂ ~T }> :=
1449+  (
1450+    weakening _ _ _ _
1451+      (fun x T h => by rw [PartialMap.apply_empty] at h; cases h) hT)
1452+
1453+theorem substitution_preserves_typing (Γ : Context) (x : String) (U : Ty)
1454+    (t v : Tm) (T : Ty)
1455+    (hT : <{ ~x ↦ ~U ; ~Γ ⊢ ~t ⦂ ~T }>) (hv : <{ ∅ ⊢ ~v ⦂ ~U }>) :
1456+    <{ ~Γ ⊢ [~x := ~v] ~t ⦂ ~T }> := by
1457+  all_goals
1458+    induction t generalizing Γ T with
1459+    | var y =>
1460+      cases hT with
1461+      | var _ _ _ h =>
1462+        by_cases hxy : x = y
1463+        · subst hxy
1464+          rw [PartialMap.update_eq] at h
1465+          rw [subst_var_eq]
1466+          have hUT : U = T := Option.some.inj h
1467+          subst hUT
1468+          exact weakening_empty _ _ _ hv
1469+        · rw [PartialMap.update_neq _ _ _ hxy] at h
1470+          rw [subst_var_ne _ _ _ hxy]
1471+          exact .var _ y _ h
1472+    | app t₁ t₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
1473+      cases hT with
1474+      | app _ _ _ _ _ h₁ h₂ =>
1475+        rw [subst_app]; exact .app _ _ _ _ _ (ih₁ _ _ h₁) (ih₂ _ _ h₂)
1476+    | abs y S t₁ ih =>
1477+      cases hT with
1478+      | abs _ _ _ _ _ h =>
1479+        by_cases hxy : x = y
1480+        · subst hxy
1481+          rw [subst_abs_eq]
1482+          rw [PartialMap.update_shadow] at h
1483+          exact .abs _ _ _ _ _ h
1484+        · rw [subst_abs_ne _ _ _ _ _ hxy]
1485+          rw [PartialMap.update_permute _ _ _ _ _ (Ne.symm hxy)] at h
1486+          exact .abs _ _ _ _ _ (ih _ _ h)
1487+    | const n => cases hT with | const => rw [subst_const]; exact .const _ n
1488+    | succ t₁ ih => cases hT with | succ _ _ h => rw [subst_succ]; exact .succ _ _ (ih _ _ h)
1489+    | pred t₁ ih => cases hT with | pred _ _ h => rw [subst_pred]; exact .pred _ _ (ih _ _ h)
1490+    | mult t₁ t₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
1491+      cases hT with
1492+      | mult _ _ _ h₁ h₂ => rw [subst_mult]; exact .mult _ _ _ (ih₁ _ _ h₁) (ih₂ _ _ h₂)
1493+    | ite0 t₁ t₂ t₃ ih₁ ih₂ ih₃ =>
1494+      cases hT with
1495+      | ite0 _ _ _ _ _ h₁ h₂ h₃ =>
1496+        rw [subst_ite0]
1497+        exact .ite0 _ _ _ _ _ (ih₁ _ _ h₁) (ih₂ _ _ h₂) (ih₃ _ _ h₃)
1498+
1499+-- #### Preservation
1500+
1501+-- ### Exercise (4 stars): StlcArith.preservation ⭐⭐⭐⭐
1502+
1503+-- *Hint*: you will need to define and prove the same helper lemmas we used
1504+-- before.
1505+
1506+theorem preservation (t t' : Tm) (T : Ty)
1507+    (hT : <{ ∅ ⊢ ~t ⦂ ~T }>) (hs : t ⟶ t') : <{ ∅ ⊢ ~t' ⦂ ~T }> := by
1508+  all_goals
1509+    generalize hΓ : (∅ : Context) = Γ at hT
1510+    induction hT generalizing t' with
1511+    | var => cases hs
1512+    | abs => cases hs
1513+    | const => cases hs
1514+    | app Γ T₁ T₂ t₁ t₂ h₁ h₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
1515+      subst hΓ
1516+      cases hs with
1517+      | appAbs _ _ _ _ _ =>
1518+        -- The one interesting case: the desired result is the substitution lemma.
1519+        cases h₁ with
1520+        | abs _ _ _ _ _ hb => exact substitution_preserves_typing _ _ _ _ _ _ hb h₂
1521+      | app1 _ t₁' _ h => exact .app _ _ _ _ _ (ih₁ t₁' h rfl) h₂
1522+      | app2 _ _ t₂' _ h => exact .app _ _ _ _ _ h₁ (ih₂ t₂' h rfl)
1523+    | succ Γ t₁ h ih =>
1524+      subst hΓ
1525+      cases hs with
1526+      | succ _ t₁' hst => exact .succ _ _ (ih t₁' hst rfl)
1527+      | succConst n => exact .const _ _
1528+    | pred Γ t₁ h ih =>
1529+      subst hΓ
1530+      cases hs with
1531+      | pred _ t₁' hst => exact .pred _ _ (ih t₁' hst rfl)
1532+      | predConst n => exact .const _ _
1533+    | mult Γ t₁ t₂ h₁ h₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
1534+      subst hΓ
1535+      cases hs with
1536+      | multConst _ _ => exact .const _ _
1537+      | mult1 _ t₁' _ hst => exact .mult _ _ _ (ih₁ t₁' hst rfl) h₂
1538+      | mult2 _ _ t₂' _ hst => exact .mult _ _ _ h₁ (ih₂ t₂' hst rfl)
1539+    | ite0 Γ t₁ t₂ t₃ T₀ h₁ h₂ h₃ ih₁ ih₂ ih₃ =>
1540+      subst hΓ
1541+      cases hs with
1542+      | if0Step _ t₁' _ _ hst => exact .ite0 _ _ _ _ _ (ih₁ t₁' hst rfl) h₂ h₃
1543+      | if0Zero => exact h₂
1544+      | if0Nonzero => exact h₃
1545+
1546+-- #### Progress
1547+
1548+-- ### Exercise (4 stars): StlcArith.progress ⭐⭐⭐⭐
1549+
1550+theorem progress (t : Tm) (T : Ty) (hT : <{ ∅ ⊢ ~t ⦂ ~T }>) :
1551+    t.IsValue ∨ ∃ t', t ⟶ t' := by
1552+  all_goals
1553+    generalize hΓ : (∅ : Context) = Γ at hT
1554+    induction hT with
1555+    | var Γ x T₁ h =>
1556+      subst hΓ
1557+      -- Contradictory: variables cannot be typed in an empty context.
1558+      rw [PartialMap.apply_empty] at h
1559+      cases h
1560+    | abs => exact .inl (.abs ..)
1561+    | const _ n => exact .inl (.const n)
1562+    | app Γ T₁ T₂ t₁ t₂ h₁ h₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
1563+      right
1564+      subst hΓ
1565+      cases ih₁ rfl with
1566+      | inl hv₁ =>
1567+        cases ih₂ rfl with
1568+        | inl hv₂ =>
1569+          -- `t₁` is a value of arrow type, so it is an abstraction, not a number.
1570+          cases hv₁ with
1571+          | abs x T u => exact ⟨<{ [~x := ~t₂] ~u }>, .appAbs x T u t₂ hv₂⟩
1572+          | const n => cases h₁
1573+        | inr hs₂ =>
1574+          obtain ⟨t₂', h⟩ := hs₂; exact ⟨<{ ~t₁ ~t₂' }>, .app2 t₁ t₂ t₂' hv₁ h⟩
1575+      | inr hs₁ =>
1576+        obtain ⟨t₁', h⟩ := hs₁; exact ⟨<{ ~t₁' ~t₂ }>, .app1 t₁ t₁' t₂ h⟩
1577+    | succ Γ t₁ h ih =>
1578+      right
1579+      subst hΓ
1580+      cases ih rfl with
1581+      | inl hv =>
1582+        cases hv with
1583+        | abs => cases h
1584+        | const n => exact ⟨.const (1 + n), .succConst n⟩
1585+      | inr hs => obtain ⟨t₁', hst⟩ := hs; exact ⟨<{ succ ~t₁' }>, .succ t₁ t₁' hst⟩
1586+    | pred Γ t₁ h ih =>
1587+      right
1588+      subst hΓ
1589+      cases ih rfl with
1590+      | inl hv =>
1591+        cases hv with
1592+        | abs => cases h
1593+        | const n => exact ⟨.const (n - 1), .predConst n⟩
1594+      | inr hs => obtain ⟨t₁', hst⟩ := hs; exact ⟨<{ pred ~t₁' }>, .pred t₁ t₁' hst⟩
1595+    | mult Γ t₁ t₂ h₁ h₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
1596+      right
1597+      subst hΓ
1598+      cases ih₁ rfl with
1599+      | inl hv₁ =>
1600+        cases ih₂ rfl with
1601+        | inl hv₂ =>
1602+          cases hv₁ with
1603+          | abs => cases h₁
1604+          | const n₁ =>
1605+            cases hv₂ with
1606+            | abs => cases h₂
1607+            | const n₂ => exact ⟨.const (n₁ * n₂), .multConst n₁ n₂⟩
1608+        | inr hs₂ =>
1609+          obtain ⟨t₂', hst⟩ := hs₂
1610+          exact ⟨<{ ~t₁ * ~t₂' }>, .mult2 t₁ t₂ t₂' hv₁ hst⟩
1611+      | inr hs₁ =>
1612+        obtain ⟨t₁', hst⟩ := hs₁; exact ⟨<{ ~t₁' * ~t₂ }>, .mult1 t₁ t₁' t₂ hst⟩
1613+    | ite0 Γ t₁ t₂ t₃ T₀ h₁ h₂ h₃ ih₁ ih₂ ih₃ =>
1614+      right
1615+      subst hΓ
1616+      cases ih₁ rfl with
1617+      | inl hv₁ =>
1618+        cases hv₁ with
1619+        | abs => cases h₁
1620+        | const n =>
1621+          cases n with
1622+          | zero => exact ⟨t₂, .if0Zero t₂ t₃⟩
1623+          | succ n' => exact ⟨t₃, .if0Nonzero n' t₂ t₃⟩
1624+      | inr hs₁ =>
1625+        obtain ⟨t₁', hst⟩ := hs₁
1626+        exact ⟨<{ if0 ~t₁' then ~t₂ else ~t₃ }>, .if0Step t₁ t₁' t₂ t₃ hst⟩
1627+
1628+end StlcArith
1629+

24---  Our next major topic is *type systems* — static program analyses that
25---  classify expressions according to the "shapes" of their results. We'll
26---  begin with a typed version of the simplest imaginable language, to
27---  introduce the basic ideas of types and typing rules and the fundamental
28---  theorems about type systems: *type preservation* and *progress*. In the
29---  next chapter we'll move on to the *simply typed lambda-calculus*, which
30---  lives at the core of every modern functional programming language
31---  (including Lean!).
32-
33---  ## Typed Arithmetic Expressions
34-
35---  To motivate the discussion of type systems, let's begin as usual with a
36---  tiny toy language. We want it to have the potential for programs to go
37---  wrong because of runtime type errors, so we endow it with two kinds of
38---  data — numbers and booleans — where not every operation is defined on
39---  both types of data. For example, program terms like `5 + true` and
40---  `if 42 then 0 else 1` use undefined operator/data-type combinations.
41-
42---  The language definition is completely routine.

45-
46---  Here is the syntax of program terms, informally:
47-
48---  t ::= true
49---      | false
50---      | if t then t else t
51---      | 0
52---      | succ t
53---      | pred t
54---      | iszero t

56---  And here it is formally:
19+--     LATER: There are a bunch of slides from earlier offerings of CIS500
20+--     that might be wonderful additions to the TERSE notes.
21+--     https://www.seas.upenn.edu/~cis500/cis500-f06/lectures/1002.pdf

23+
24+-- Our next major topic is *type systems* — static program analyses that
25+-- classify expressions according to the "shapes" of their results. We'll
26+-- begin with a typed version of the simplest imaginable language, to
27+-- introduce the basic ideas of types and typing rules and the fundamental
28+-- theorems about type systems: *type preservation* and *progress*. In the
29+-- next chapter we'll move on to the *simply typed lambda-calculus*, which
30+-- lives at the core of every modern functional programming language
31+-- (including Lean!).
32+
33+-- ## Typed Arithmetic Expressions
34+
35+-- To motivate the discussion of type systems, let's begin as usual with a
36+-- tiny toy language. We want it to have the potential for programs to go
37+-- wrong because of runtime type errors, so we endow it with two kinds of data
38+-- — numbers and booleans — where not every operation is defined on both types
39+-- of data. For example, program terms like `5 + true` and
40+-- `if 42 then 0 else 1` use undefined operator/data-type combinations.
41+

69---  #### Notation
70-
71---  Writing terms as raw constructors (`.ite .fls .zero (.succ .zero)`)
72---  gets unreadable quickly. We introduce a *concrete syntax* so that a
73---  term can be written inside `<{ … }>` — for example
74---  `<{ if false then 0 else succ 0 }>` — mirroring the informal grammar
75---  above. A bare identifier is spliced as a Lean term (so a variable `t`
76---  is written just `t`); `~e` escapes an arbitrary Lean expression, and
77---  `( … )` groups.
78-

81---  it is worth seeing the pattern once:

84---    `tm`, the terms of this chapter's language.
85-
86---  - Each `syntax` directive declares one production of that non-terminal,
87---    with annotations fixing precedence, and the last one declares the
88---    `<{ … }>` brackets that let a `tm` appear where Lean expects a term.
89-
90---  - `macro_rules` then translates the resulting syntax forms into the
91---    corresponding constructors of `Tm`.

70+
71+-- Writing terms as raw constructors (`.ite .fls .zero (.succ .zero)`) gets
72+-- unreadable quickly. We introduce a *concrete syntax* so that a term can be
73+-- written inside `<{ … }>` — for example `<{ if false then 0 else succ 0 }>`
74+-- — mirroring the informal grammar above. A bare identifier is spliced as a
75+-- Lean term (so a variable `t` is written just `t`); `~e` escapes an
76+-- arbitrary Lean expression, and `( … )` groups.
77+
78+-- You do not need to understand exactly how the declarations below work;
79+-- every object language in this book is given its syntax the same way, so it
80+-- is worth seeing the pattern once:
81+
82+-- - `declare_syntax_cat` adds a new non-terminal to Lean's grammar — here `tm`,
83+--   the terms of this chapter's language.
84+
85+-- - Each `syntax` directive declares one production of that non-terminal, with
86+--   annotations fixing precedence, and the last one declares the `<{ … }>`
87+--   brackets that let a `tm` appear where Lean expects a term.
88+
89+-- - `macro_rules` then translates the resulting syntax forms into the
90+--   corresponding constructors of `Tm`.

275+-- ### Normal Forms and Values
276+
277+-- The first interesting thing to notice about this `Tm.Step` relation is that
278+-- the strong progress theorem from the Smallstep chapter fails here. That is,
279+-- there are terms that are normal forms (they can't take a step) but not
280+-- values (they are not included in our definition of possible "results of
281+-- reduction").
282+
283+-- Such terms are *stuck*.

493---  Some questions about this relation (answers inline):
494-
495---  - Is `⇢` deterministic (`∀ t t' t'', t ⇢ t' → t ⇢ t'' → t' = t''`)? No:
496---    `pred (succ (pred 0))` steps to both `pred 0` (by `predSucc`) and
497---    `pred (succ 0)` (by `predStep`, since `pred 0 ⇢ 0`).
498-
499---  - Is every `Tm.Step` normal form also a `⇢` normal form? No:
500---    `pred (succ true)` is stuck for `Tm.Step` but steps under `⇢` (to
501---    `true`, by `predSucc`, now that the `Tm.IsNValue` premise is gone).
502-
503---  - Is every `⇢` normal form also a `Tm.Step` normal form? Yes —
504---    `Tm.Step` is a subrelation of `⇢`, so anything stuck for `⇢` is stuck
505---    for `Tm.Step`.
506-
507---  - Is every value reachable by `Tm.Step` (in many steps) also reachable
508---    by `⇢` (in many steps)? Yes, for the same subrelation reason.
509-
510---  - Conversely? No: `iszero (succ true)` reaches the value `false` under
511---    `⇢` but is stuck under `Tm.Step`.
512-

557-
558---  The next critical observation is that, although this language has stuck
559---  terms, they are always nonsensical, mixing booleans and numbers in a
560---  way that we don't even *want* to have a meaning. We can easily exclude
561---  such ill-typed terms by defining a *typing relation* that relates terms
562---  to the types (either numeric or boolean) of their final results.
563-
564---  The *typing relation* `⊢ t ⦂ T` relates terms to the types of their
565---  results. In informal notation it is often written `⊢ t ⦂ T` and
566---  pronounced "`t` has type `T`." The `⊢` symbol is called a "turnstile."
567---  The `⦂` between the term and its type is a dedicated type-colon glyph
568---  (distinct from an ordinary `:`); in the editor you enter it with the
569---  Lean input abbreviation `\tc` followed by a space. Below, we're going
570---  to see richer typing relations where one or more additional "context"
571---  arguments are written to the left of the turnstile. For the moment, the
572---  context is always empty.

552+-- ### Typing
553+
554+-- The next critical observation is that, although this language has stuck
555+-- terms, they are always nonsensical, mixing booleans and numbers in a way
556+-- that we don't even *want* to have a meaning. We can easily exclude such
557+-- ill-typed terms by defining a *typing relation* that relates terms to the
558+-- types (either numeric or boolean) of their final results.
559+
560+-- The *typing relation* `⊢ t ⦂ T` relates terms to the types of their
561+-- results. In informal notation it is often written `⊢ t ⦂ T` and pronounced
562+-- "`t` has type `T`." The `⊢` symbol is called a "turnstile." The `⦂` between
563+-- the term and its type is a dedicated type-colon glyph (distinct from an
564+-- ordinary `:`); in the editor you enter it with the Lean input abbreviation
565+-- `\tc` followed by a space. Below, we're going to see richer typing
566+-- relations where one or more additional "context" arguments are written to
567+-- the left of the turnstile. For the moment, the context is always empty.
568+
569+-- -------------                (tru)
570+--                      ⊢ true ⦂ Bool
571+
572+--                      --------------               (fls)
573+--                      ⊢ false ⦂ Bool
574+
575+--           ⊢ t1 ⦂ Bool    ⊢ t2 ⦂ T    ⊢ t3 ⦂ T
576+--           -----------------------------------     (ite)
577+--               ⊢ if t1 then t2 else t3 ⦂ T
578+
579+--                        ---------                  (zero)
580+--                        ⊢ 0 ⦂ Nat
581+
582+--                       ⊢ t1 ⦂ Nat
583+--                     ---------------               (succ)
584+--                     ⊢ succ t1 ⦂ Nat
585+
586+--                       ⊢ t1 ⦂ Nat
587+--                     ---------------               (pred)
588+--                     ⊢ pred t1 ⦂ Nat
589+
590+--                       ⊢ t1 ⦂ Nat
591+--                    ------------------             (isZero)
592+--                    ⊢ iszero t1 ⦂ Bool
593+
594+-- Here are the formal rules.
595+
596+-- The typing judgment is written `<{ ⊢ t ⦂ T }>`: the whole judgment is
597+-- wrapped in `<{ … }>`, the term is in the object grammar (bare variables, no
598+-- inner `<{ }>`) and the type as `Bool`/`Nat` (a type variable is spliced,
599+-- `~T` escapes to a Lean `Ty`). As with `Tm.Step`, we define the relation
600+-- using its own notation, inside a `section` with `set_option hygiene false`
601+-- so the bare name `Tm.HasType` in the expansion resolves to the relation
602+-- being defined; after the `section` we re-declare the same rules
603+-- hygienically for real use. Unlike `⟶`, the judgment builds on the custom
604+-- `tm` syntactic category, so it must use `syntax`/`macro_rules` rather than
605+-- `notation` — which is why it still needs the `app_unexpander` to print the
606+-- judgment back.
612607

614609   | bool
668663 example : <{ ⊢ if false then 0 else succ 0 ⦂ Nat }> :=
669664   .ite _ _ _ _ .fls .zero (.succ _ .zero)

683+-- ### Canonical forms
684+
685+-- The following two lemmas capture the fundamental fact that the definitions
686+-- of boolean and numeric values agree with the typing relation: a well-typed
687+-- value of type `Bool` is a boolean value, and of type `Nat` a numeric value.
694688 
695689 theorem bool_canonical (t : Tm) (hT : <{ ⊢ t ⦂ Bool }>) (hv : Tm.IsValue t) : Tm.IsBValue t := by
696690   cases hv with
704698   | inl hb => cases hb <;> cases hT
705699   | inr hn => exact hn
706700 
707---  ### Progress
708-
709---  The typing relation enjoys two critical properties.
710-
711---  The first is that well-typed normal forms are not stuck — or
712---  conversely, if a term is well typed, then either it is a value or it
713---  can take at least one step. We call this *progress*.

703+-- The typing relation enjoys two critical properties.
704+
705+-- The first is that well-typed normal forms are not stuck — or conversely, if
706+-- a term is well typed, then either it is a value or it can take at least one
707+-- step. We call this *progress*.

778---  *Theorem*: If `⊢ t ⦂ T`, then either `t` is a value or else `t ⟶ t'`
779---  for some `t'`.
780-
781---  *Proof*: By induction on a derivation of `⊢ t ⦂ T`.
782-
783---  - If the last rule in the derivation is `ite`, then
784---    `t = if t1 then t2
785---        else t3`, with `⊢ t1 ⦂ Bool`, `⊢ t2 ⦂ T` and
786---    `⊢ t3 ⦂ T`. By the IH, either `t1` is a value or else `t1` can step
787---    to some `t1'`.
788-
789---    - If `t1` is a value, then by the canonical forms lemmas and the fact
790---      that `⊢ t1 ⦂ Bool` we have that `t1` is a boolean value
791---      (`Tm.IsBValue`) — i.e., it is either `true` or `false`. If
792---      `t1 = true`, then `t` steps to `t2` by `ifTrue`, while if
793---      `t1 = false`, then `t` steps to `t3` by `ifFalse`. Either way, `t`
794---      can step, which is what we wanted to show.
795-
796---    - If `t1` itself can take a step, then, by `ifStep`, so can `t`.
797-
798---  - If the last rule in the derivation is `tru`, then `t = true`, which
799---    is a boolean value and hence a value.  The cases for `fls` and `zero`
800---    are similar.
801-
802---  - If the last rule in the derivation is `succ`, then `t = succ t1`, with
803---    `⊢ t1 ⦂ Nat`.  By the IH, either `t1` is a value or else `t1` can step
804---    to some `t1'`.
805-
806---    - If `t1` is a value, then by the canonical forms lemma `t1` is an
807---      `nvalue`, and hence `t` is also an `nvalue` (and hence a value) by
808---      `succ`.
809-
810---    - If `t1` can take a step, then by `succStep`, so can `t`.
811-
812---  - If the last rule in the derivation is `pred`, then `t = pred t1`, with
813---    `⊢ t1 ⦂ Nat`.  By the IH, either `t1` is a value or else `t1` can step
814---    to some `t1'`.
815-
816---    - If `t1` is a value, then (by the same argument as in the previous
817---      case) it must be an `nvalue`.  By case analysis on the `nvalue`
818---      judgement, there are two cases:
819-
820---      - If `t1 = 0`, then `t` can take a step by `predZero`.
821-
822---      - Otherwise, `t1 = succ t1'`, with `t1'` an `nvalue`.  Hence `t` can
823---        again take a step, this time by `predSucc`.
824-
825---    - Finally, if `t1` can take a step, then by `predStep`, so can `t`.
826-
827---  - If the last rule in the derivation is `isZero`, then `t = iszero t1`,
828---    with `⊢ t1 ⦂ Nat`.  By the IH, either `t1` is a value or else `t1` steps
829---    to some `t1'`.
830-
831---    - If `t1` is a value, it must be an `nvalue`, and there are two cases to
832---      consider:
833-
834---      - If `t1 = 0`, then `t` can take a step by `isZeroZero`.
835-
836---      - Otherwise, `t1 = succ t1'` where `t1'` is an `nvalue`.  Hence `t` can
837---        take a step by `isZeroSucc`.
838-
839---    - If `t1` can take a step, then so can `t`, by `isZeroStep`.
840-
841---  This theorem is more interesting than the strong progress theorem that
842---  we saw in the Smallstep chapter, where *all* normal forms were values.
843---  Here a term can be stuck, but only if it is ill typed.

778+-- - If the last rule in the derivation is `ite`, then
779+--   `t = if t1 then t2
780+--       else t3`, with `⊢ t1 ⦂ Bool`, `⊢ t2 ⦂ T` and
781+--   `⊢ t3 ⦂ T`. By the IH, either `t1` is a value or else `t1` can step to some
782+--   `t1'`.
783+
784+--   - If `t1` is a value, then by the canonical forms lemmas and the fact that
785+--     `⊢ t1 ⦂ Bool` we have that `t1` is a boolean value (`Tm.IsBValue`) — i.e.,
786+--     it is either `true` or `false`. If `t1 = true`, then `t` steps to `t2` by
787+--     `ifTrue`, while if `t1 = false`, then `t` steps to `t3` by `ifFalse`.
788+--     Either way, `t` can step, which is what we wanted to show.
789+
790+--   - If `t1` itself can take a step, then, by `ifStep`, so can `t`.
791+
792+-- - If the last rule in the derivation is `tru`, then `t = true`, which
793+--   is a boolean value and hence a value.  The cases for `fls` and `zero`
794+--   are similar.
795+
796+-- - If the last rule in the derivation is `succ`, then `t = succ t1`, with
797+--   `⊢ t1 ⦂ Nat`.  By the IH, either `t1` is a value or else `t1` can step
798+--   to some `t1'`.
799+
800+--   - If `t1` is a value, then by the canonical forms lemma `t1` is an
801+--     `nvalue`, and hence `t` is also an `nvalue` (and hence a value) by
802+--     `succ`.
803+
804+--   - If `t1` can take a step, then by `succStep`, so can `t`.
805+
806+-- - If the last rule in the derivation is `pred`, then `t = pred t1`, with
807+--   `⊢ t1 ⦂ Nat`.  By the IH, either `t1` is a value or else `t1` can step
808+--   to some `t1'`.
809+
810+--   - If `t1` is a value, then (by the same argument as in the previous
811+--     case) it must be an `nvalue`.  By case analysis on the `nvalue`
812+--     judgement, there are two cases:
813+
814+--     - If `t1 = 0`, then `t` can take a step by `predZero`.
815+
816+--     - Otherwise, `t1 = succ t1'`, with `t1'` an `nvalue`.  Hence `t` can
817+--       again take a step, this time by `predSucc`.
818+
819+--   - Finally, if `t1` can take a step, then by `predStep`, so can `t`.
820+
821+-- - If the last rule in the derivation is `isZero`, then `t = iszero t1`,
822+--   with `⊢ t1 ⦂ Nat`.  By the IH, either `t1` is a value or else `t1` steps
823+--   to some `t1'`.
824+
825+--   - If `t1` is a value, it must be an `nvalue`, and there are two cases to
826+--     consider:
827+
828+--     - If `t1 = 0`, then `t` can take a step by `isZeroZero`.
829+
830+--     - Otherwise, `t1 = succ t1'` where `t1'` is an `nvalue`.  Hence `t` can
831+--       take a step by `isZeroSucc`.
832+
833+--   - If `t1` can take a step, then so can `t`, by `isZeroStep`.
834+
835+-- This theorem is more interesting than the strong progress theorem that we
836+-- saw in the Smallstep chapter, where *all* normal forms were values. Here a
837+-- term can be stuck, but only if it is ill typed.
838+

872+-- ### Type Preservation
873+
874+-- The second critical property of typing is that, when a well-typed term
875+-- takes a step, the result is a well-typed term (of the same type).
876+

933+--           Bool`. The

945+--   show that `t` steps is `succStep`, in which case `t1` steps to some
946+--   `t1'`.  So, by the IH, `⊢ t1' ⦂ Nat`, and hence `t' = succ t1'` also has

1050+-- ### Exercise (3 stars): subject_expansion ⭐⭐⭐
1051+
1052+-- Having seen the subject reduction property, one might wonder whether the
1053+-- opposite property — subject *expansion* — also holds. That is, is it always
1054+-- the case that, if `t ⟶ t'` and `⊢ t' ⦂ T`, then `⊢ t ⦂ T`? If so, prove it.
1055+-- If not, give a counter-example.
1056+
1057+-- Subject expansion does not hold in this language (or most interesting
1058+-- languages).  For example, `if false then true else 0` is ill typed, but
1059+-- it reduces to the well-typed term `0`.

1196---  ### Exercise (4 stars): prog_pres_bigstep (Advanced, manually graded) ⭐⭐⭐⭐
1197-
1198---  Suppose our evaluation relation is defined in the big-step style. State
1199---  appropriate analogs of the progress and preservation properties. (You
1200---  do not need to prove them.)
1201-
1202---  Can you see any limitations of either of your properties? Do they allow
1203---  for nonterminating programs? Why might we prefer the small-step
1204---  semantics for stating preservation and progress?
1205-
1206---  The type preservation property for the big-step semantics is similar to
1207---  the one we gave for the small-step semantics: if a well-typed term
1208---  evaluates to some final value, then this value has the same type as the
1209---  original term.  The proof is similar to the one we gave.  However,
1210---  preservation for small-step semantics implies that all intermediate states
1211---  (i.e., all states reachable in multi-step) are well-typed, whereas big-step
1212---  semantics only relates a term to its final evaluation result, with no
1213---  notion of "intermediate state" about which preservation can make
1214---  guarantees.
1215-
1216---  The situation with the progress property is more interesting.  A direct
1217---  analog (if a term is well typed then it evaluates to some other term)
1218---  makes a much stronger claim than the progress theorem we have given: it
1219---  says that every well-typed term can be evaluated to some final value---that
1220---  is, that evaluation always terminates on well-typed terms.  For arithmetic
1221---  expressions, this happens to be the case, but for more interesting
1222---  languages (languages involving general recursion, for example) it will
1223---  often not be true.  For such languages, we simply have no progress property
1224---  in the big-step style: in effect, there is no way to tell the difference
1225---  between reaching an error state and failing to terminate.  This is one
1226---  reason that language theorists generally prefer the small-step style.

1177+-- ### Exercise (1 star): remove_pred0 (manually graded) ⭐
1178+
1179+-- The reduction rule `predZero` is a bit counter-intuitive: we might feel
1180+-- that it makes more sense for the predecessor of `0` to be undefined, rather
1181+-- than being defined to be `0`. Can we achieve this simply by removing the
1182+-- rule from the definition of `Tm.Step`? Would doing so create any problems
1183+-- elsewhere?

1186+-- be to raise an exception in this case, but this requires that we add
1187+-- exceptions to the language we're formalizing!

1189+-- ### Exercise (4 stars): prog_pres_bigstep (Advanced, manually graded) ⭐⭐⭐⭐
1190+
1191+-- Suppose our evaluation relation is defined in the big-step style. State
1192+-- appropriate analogs of the progress and preservation properties. (You do
1193+-- not need to prove them.)
1194+
1195+-- Can you see any limitations of either of your properties? Do they allow for
1196+-- nonterminating programs? Why might we prefer the small-step semantics for
1197+-- stating preservation and progress?
1198+
1199+-- The type preservation property for the big-step semantics is similar to
1200+-- the one we gave for the small-step semantics: if a well-typed term
1201+-- evaluates to some final value, then this value has the same type as the
1202+-- original term.  The proof is similar to the one we gave.  However,
1203+-- preservation for small-step semantics implies that all intermediate states
1204+-- (i.e., all states reachable in multi-step) are well-typed, whereas big-step
1205+-- semantics only relates a term to its final evaluation result, with no
1206+-- notion of "intermediate state" about which preservation can make
1207+-- guarantees.
1208+
1209+-- The situation with the progress property is more interesting.  A direct
1210+-- analog (if a term is well typed then it evaluates to some other term)
1211+-- makes a much stronger claim than the progress theorem we have given: it
1212+-- says that every well-typed term can be evaluated to some final value---that
1213+-- is, that evaluation always terminates on well-typed terms.  For arithmetic
1214+-- expressions, this happens to be the case, but for more interesting
1215+-- languages (languages involving general recursion, for example) it will
1216+-- often not be true.  For such languages, we simply have no progress property
1217+-- in the big-step style: in effect, there is no way to tell the difference
1218+-- between reaching an error state and failing to terminate.  This is one
1219+-- reason that language theorists generally prefer the small-step style.
